title: CPAT-AI Model
text:
CPAT-AI Model

The CPAT-AI model is one model in two forms. Excel-AI computes it in the rows of a workbook; CPAT Python computes it in small functions, one per equation. Both use the same equations, the same variable codes and the same order of calculation, and they agree number for number. This book explains that shared model, block by block, as the Methodology explains legacy CPAT, and links to the methodology wherever the model follows it, simplifies it or departs from it.

title: 1  Overview, notation and policies
text:
1.1 What the model is
This chapter opens the book. It says what the shared model is, how a run is organised, and in which order the model computes. It fixes the notation, the units and the conventions that every later chapter uses. It then explains the first two blocks of the model: the header of macro series (block M0) and the policies (block M1 and its adjustments A1), which turn the scenario inputs into a price signal for every year, fuel and sector.
The model is shared by two implementations. Excel-AI (the Excel prototype, tab CPAT Excel-AI) computes each equation in workbook rows. CPAT Python (Coded CPAT, tab CPAT Python) computes the same equation in one function. Both use the same variable codes and the same order of calculation, and CPAT Python is checked against Excel-AI code by code and year by year.
The model is the mitigation module of the IMF and World Bank Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), together with its distribution module. It answers one question: what do carbon pricing and related policies do to energy prices, energy use, emissions, government revenue, GDP and households, year by year to 2041?
It follows the method of legacy CPAT, described in the methodology (methodology, section 3.1.2): a reduced-form model in which fuel use responds to income, prices and efficiency, with a techno-economic model of the power sector. It departs from legacy CPAT only where legacy has a bug (always fixed) or where a decision was taken and recorded (the boxes “Differences from legacy CPAT” list them).
The methodology’s own summary of the policies CPAT can assess is in its user guide (methodology, section 1.1).

title: 1  Overview, notation and policies
text:
Policies in
Carbon tax; new emissions trading system (ETS) with a cap; feebates; energy efficiency regulations (as shadow prices); fuel excises (fuel price reform); consumer subsidy, price-control and producer subsidy phase-outs; methane fee; existing carbon taxes and ETS; power-sector policies; road vehicle policies


Results out
Retail energy prices; fuel use in 16 subsectors and 9 fuels; electricity generation, capacity and prices; revenue; CO2, other greenhouse gases and local air pollutants; GDP effects; the gap to the country’s NDC; household effects by decile


Country
One country at a time in Excel-AI, any number of countries at once in CPAT Python. Equations contain no country numbers: every country value comes from the data, looked up by the country code










NoteIn Excel-AI and CPAT Python






Excel-AI: workbook CPAT-AI-Mitigation-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm. The model is sheet Mitigation, run top to bottom, one section per step with the section numbers of legacy CPAT (0 header, 1 policies, 2 prices, 3 power, 5-8 sectors, 11 totals, 12 revenues, 13-15 emissions, 16-18 GDP, indicators, welfare), and sheet Distribution. The inputs are on ScenarioDefinition (the rows of legacy MTInputs), Settings, Constants and Manual inputs; the country data on the data tabs. The formula of every row is listed in excel_ai/mitigation/docs/Formulas.md.
CPAT Python: package coded/cpat_model/. The run is cpat_model.run() (core/loop.py); the order of the blocks is written once, in mitigation/chain.py; the blocks are in mitigation/ and distribution/.

title: 1  Overview, notation and policies
text:
1.2 How a run is organised
A run takes one scenario set and a choice of countries, and returns every result by output code, country, scenario and year.

1.2.1 Countries, scenarios and scenario sets
A scenario is one full column of inputs: one value for each policy input (the rows of legacy MTInputs and Excel-AI’s additions). A scenario set is a table of such columns, numbered from 1.

Scenario 1 is the baseline (\(o = B\)): no new policy, only what the price data already contain (existing taxes, subsidies and carbon pricing).
Scenarios 2 to \(n\) are policy scenarios (\(o = P\)). Each runs with the same equations and its own inputs.

In Excel-AI each scenario is a group of year columns on the Mitigation sheet: group 1 is the baseline and group 2 the live policy scenario. In CPAT Python a scenario set is a CSV file (data/inputs/scenarios_<name>.csv, one column per scenario), and any number of scenarios run one after another.
A few inputs are read from the baseline column for every scenario: they are run settings, not policies. They include the results year, the last historical price year, the social cost of carbon settings, the effectiveness of output-based allocation, the price-control (pass-through) choice and the price floor.


1.2.2 Baseline and comparisons
Most results are reported against the baseline. Write \(X^{B}\) for the value of \(X\) in the baseline (scenario 1) in the same year and country. The change against the baseline is
\[
\Delta X_t = X_t - X^{B}_t
\tag{1.1}\]
where \(X\) is any result (fuel use, CO2, revenue, GDP) and \(t\) the year. Percent changes are \(\Delta X_t / X^{B}_t\).
Policy scenarios also read some baseline values as inputs: the baseline CO2 by ETS sector (for the ETS cap), the calibration values of the GHG inventory year, and the same-year baseline revenue (for the fiscal space and so for GDP in the next year). This is why the baseline always runs first.


1.2.3 Years
The model runs year by year from the base year \(t_0\) to 2041.

The macro series of the header (block M0) run over a longer range, the macro years 2018 to 2045, so that growth rates and averages of earlier years exist.


1.2.4 Money: the results year and real USD
Every money value is in real US dollars of the results year \(R\) (input ResultsYear, read from the baseline column; 2026 by default), per unit of the quantity (USD/GJ, USD/tCO2, USD million). A constant real price is a constant number: there is no inflation in the projection, and fuel use responds only to real price changes.
Two indices, both equal to 1 in \(R\), convert nominal values to real ones (block M0, Equation 1.5):

the CPI index \(\nu_t\) (US consumer prices) converts nominal domestic values: the price data, existing taxes, the nominal option of the carbon price, producer subsidies;
the deflator index \(\delta_t\) (US GDP deflator) converts nominal international prices and GDP.

Policy inputs are real (results-year USD) unless an input says otherwise: only the carbon price has a nominal option. The methodology describes the currency rules in its user guide (methodology, section 1.2.11).






WarningDifferences from legacy CPAT






Two indices, as legacy. Legacy uses the CPI for domestic values and the deflator for international prices; the model keeps that split. Up to 2030 the two differ by up to 1.2% (2022: 1.137 against 1.124; 2030: 0.918 against 0.929), so a single index would not reproduce legacy.
Horizon. Legacy holds the US CPI flat after the WEO horizon (2031) but not the deflator; so does the model. The model computes to 2041, the horizon of the legacy power block; values after 2030 were not a target of the comparisons with legacy.

title: 1  Overview, notation and policies
text:
1.3 The calculation chain
The model never solves a system of equations. Each year reads only that year and earlier years, so the whole run is one pass in a fixed order. This section gives that order; each later chapter explains one link of it.

1.3.1 Three stages, baseline first
Each scenario runs in three stages.

Prepare (all years at once). Everything that depends on no model quantity: the macro header, the policy paths, the international and retail prices before and after policies, the power cost paths (including the forward-looking levelised costs). Because prices and policies are known for all years before any quantity is computed, a later year’s price can be used in an earlier year’s decision without a circular reference.
Year loop (\(t = t_0, \dots, 2041\)). Every block of the year, in a fixed order. The base year sets the starting values.
Finish (all years). Rows that need the whole path: the NDC targets and the gap.

The baseline runs first, then each policy scenario in turn, because policy scenarios read baseline values. After all scenarios, the distribution module computes household effects in its analysis year, every scenario against the baseline.

Two links run across years. The GDP effect of year \(t\) moves the GDP level of year \(t+1\) (the only feedback from policy to activity). Power reads last year’s electricity price for demand, and its capacities and vintages are recursions on \(t-1\). The only look-aheads read exogenous paths built in the prepare stage, such as the levelised variable cost of power over \([t, 2041]\).






TipPseudocode: a run



settings = run_settings(scenario_set.column(1))       # results year, last price year, ... from the baseline
for o in [1, 2, ..., n]:                              # baseline first
    state = {}
    for block in PREPARE:                             # header, policies, prices, power costs, fuel prices, ...
        block(state, inputs[o], baseline)             # all years at once
    for t in range(base_year, 2041 + 1):
        for block in YEAR:                            # gdp.start, power.step, fuel_use.step, totals, emissions,
            block(state, inputs[o], baseline, t)      # revenues, indicators, gdp.effects, road, welfare, ...
    for block in FINISH:                              # NDC gap
        block(state, inputs[o], baseline)
    if o == 1:
        baseline = state                              # read by every policy scenario
    results[o] = state
if 'YearDistn' in inputs[1]:
    results.distribution = distribution(results, year=YearDistn)   # every scenario against the baseline








NoteIn Excel-AI and CPAT Python






Excel-AI: sheet Mitigation computes every row for every year in its scenario groups: group 1 is the baseline, group 2 the live scenario (each group is 22 columns wide: the code column, the years 2022-2041 and a spacer; constant MitGW). Each year reads only that year and earlier years. Baseline values that policy scenarios read are stored on sheet BaselineCO2 (CO2 by ETS sector, methane activity). Sheet Distribution reads both groups.
CPAT Python: core/loop.py (run_scenarios, run_one); the stages are the lists PREPARE, YEAR and FINISH of mitigation/chain.py. Every function works on all countries at once (an array dimension). Each block and its tests are listed in the blocks.
Outside the passes, in both: the ETS goal seek, which repeats whole runs until emissions meet the cap (only on request; Chapter 6).

title: 1  Overview, notation and policies
text:
1.6 Conventions
A few conventions hold in every chapter.

Indicator. \(\mathbb{1}[\cdot]\) is 1 if the condition holds and 0 otherwise. For example \(\mathbb{1}[o \ne B]\) is 1 in a policy scenario.
Switches. Yes/No inputs are switches of the scenario. A text switch counts as Yes when it starts with “Yes” (so “Yes” and “Yes*” both count; the test is on the first three letters, ignoring case). A tick box is TRUE or FALSE; in arithmetic TRUE is 1 and FALSE or a blank cell is 0.
Defaults. An asterisk marks the default option of a dropdown input (“Medium”, ”Real”, “Linear*“). Numbers in parentheses in the parameter tables of this book are defaults of sheet Constants or Settings, not country data.
Blank inputs read as 0, as an Excel lookup of an empty cell does.
Baseline and previous year. \(X^{B}_t\) is the baseline value in the same year; \(X_{t-1}\) the value of the previous year in the same scenario.
Codes. Every variable has a short code (ener, atp, cptraj, …), the same in Excel-AI (row codes) and CPAT Python (variable names). A full output code adds the country, module, sector, fuel and scenario, for example egy.mit.co2.tot.tot.2.
Equation ids. Each equation of the model has an id (M1.2, A2.5, …) in the equation lists of the appendices; CPAT Python cites it in the code (EQ-M1.2). This book links them, for example (M1.1).

title: 1  Overview, notation and policies
text:
1.7 Header: the macro series (M0)
The header turns the IMF World Economic Outlook (WEO) data of the country into the series every later block reads: the price indices that make money values real, real GDP in US dollars and local currency, the exchange rate and the baseline growth of GDP. It depends on no model quantity, so it is computed for all years in the prepare stage. The methodology lists the macro data and their sources in methodology, section 3.9.1.

1.7.1 Macro series past the last data year
Each WEO series is data up to its own last data year \(T^{WEO}_x\) and is then extended by a rule of its own (M0.1):
\[
x_t = \begin{cases} x^{WEO}_t & t \le T^{WEO}_x \\ \text{extension rule of } x & t > T^{WEO}_x \end{cases}
\tag{1.3}\]
over the macro years 2018 to 2045. The rules are:








Series
WEO code
Extension past the last data year




US GDP deflator
USA.NGDP_D
Linear trend: \(x_t = 2x_{t-1} - x_{t-2}\)


US CPI
USA.PCPI
Held flat: \(x_t = x_{t-1}\)


Real GDP growth
NGDP_RPCH
Held, or eased off when falling (Equation 1.4)


Real GDP, local currency
NGDP_R
Grown with real growth: \(x_t = x_{t-1}(1 + g_t)\)


Nominal GDP, local currency
NGDP
Grown with its last growth rate, held from the last data year


Nominal GDP, USD
NGDPD
Grown with the nominal growth rate of local-currency GDP


Exchange rate
XDC_USD.PA_RT
Held flat; a euro country takes the euro area’s rate (WEO G163)


Population
LP
Grown with its last growth factor: \(x_t = x_{t-1}\,x_{t-1}/x_{t-2}\)



Real GDP growth is held at its last value, unless it was falling. Then it eases off: it keeps at least half of the average of the last three years, and otherwise follows the linear trend of the last two:
\[
g_t = \begin{cases} g_{t-1} & g_{t-1} \ge g_{t-2} \\[4pt] \max\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\bar{g}_{t-3..t-1},\; 2g_{t-1} - g_{t-2}\right) & g_{t-1} < g_{t-2} \end{cases}
\tag{1.4}\]
where

\(g_t\) is real GDP growth in year \(t\) (share per year);
\(\bar{g}_{t-3..t-1}\) is the average of the growth rates of the three previous years;
\(\tfrac{1}{2}\) is the constant GdpExtHalf (0.5).

Nominal GDP in local currency grows with the growth rate of its last data year; in Excel-AI that rate is the one of the year before the last data year, and CPAT Python does the same.


1.7.2 Price indices, real GDP and the exchange rate
The header rows of the model read these series (M0.2):
\[
\nu_t = \frac{CPI^{US}_{R}}{CPI^{US}_t}, \qquad \delta_t = \frac{D^{US}_{R}}{D^{US}_t}
\tag{1.5}\]
where

\(\nu_t\) (infl) is the CPI index: it converts nominal domestic prices and nominal policy inputs of year \(t\) to real USD of \(R\);
\(\delta_t\) (defl) is the deflator index: it converts nominal international prices;
\(CPI^{US}_t\), \(D^{US}_t\) are the US CPI and GDP deflator (WEO, extended as above);
\(R\) is the results year.

Both indices equal 1 in \(R\), are above 1 before it and below 1 after it.
Real GDP in US dollars (gdp.usd, USD billion of \(R\)) is converted from nominal GDP in the historical years and grown with real growth from the base year on:
\[
Y^{USD}_t = \begin{cases} \dfrac{Y^{n}_t}{e^{n}_t}\,\delta_t & t < t_0 \\[8pt] Y^{USD}_{t-1}\,(1 + g_t) & t \ge t_0 \end{cases}
\tag{1.6}\]
where \(Y^{n}_t\) is nominal GDP in local currency, \(e^{n}_t\) the market exchange rate (local currency per USD) and \(g_t\) real GDP growth (gdp.base, the baseline growth that the GDP block starts from; Chapter 7).
Real GDP in local currency (gdp.lcu) is the WEO real GDP series, \(Y^{LCU}_t = Y^{R}_t\). The exchange rate the model uses is the ratio of the two real GDP series:
\[
e_t = \frac{Y^{LCU}_t}{Y^{USD}_t}
\tag{1.7}\]
in local currency per real US dollar (xr). From the base year on both series grow at the same rate, so \(e_t\) is constant in real terms. GDP per capita is \(Y^{USD}_t\) divided by population (times 1000, population being in thousands).

title: 1  Overview, notation and policies
text:
1.8 Policies (M1 and A1)
The policies block turns the inputs of a scenario into price signals: a rate per tonne of CO2 or per unit of fuel, for each year, sector and fuel. Every later block reads these signals. Prices add them to the retail price (Chapter 2); fuel use and power respond to the price and to the shadow price (Chapter 3, Chapter 4); revenues collect them (Chapter 7). The block depends on no model quantity, so it is computed for all years in the prepare stage.
The methodology describes the policy options in its user guide (methodology, section 1.3.2.3) and the price notation in methodology, section 3.2.2.

Power-sector policies (renewable subsidies, PPAs, rebates, new investment bans, the electricity excise) are set in the same scenario column and explained in Chapter 4; road vehicle policies (vehicle feebates, EV subsidies, purchase taxes, distance taxes) in Chapter 5; revenue recycling in Chapter 7 and Chapter 8.


1.8.2 The policy path
Every policy is a path from a start year to a target year, set per scenario: zero before the start year, linear from a start level to a target level, and then either held or continued (M1.1).
\[
\Lambda(t;\, T_0, T_1, x_0, x_1) = \begin{cases} 0 & t < T_0 \\[4pt] x_0 + (x_1 - x_0)\,\dfrac{t - T_0}{\max(T_1 - T_0,\,1)} & t \ge T_0 \end{cases}
\tag{1.8}\]
where

\(T_0\) is the start year and \(T_1\) the target year of the policy (inputs);
\(x_0\) is the level in the start year and \(x_1\) the level in the target year (inputs);
\(\max(T_1 - T_0, 1)\) guards against a target year equal to the start year.

\(\Lambda\) continues the line after \(T_1\). The path held flat after the target year reads the line at \(\min(t, T_1)\):
\[
\bar{\Lambda}(t;\, T_0, T_1, x_0, x_1) = \Lambda\big(\min(t, T_1);\, T_0, T_1, x_0, x_1\big) \quad \text{for } t \ge T_0
\tag{1.9}\]
and 0 before \(T_0\). Which form a policy takes after its target year:

TipPseudocode: the policy path



def path(t, t0, t1, x0, x1, hold=True):
    if t < t0:
        return 0
    tt = min(t, t1) if hold else t          # hold: flat after the target year
    return x0 + (x1 - x0) / max(t1 - t0, 1) * (tt - t0)




1.8.3 Carbon tax
The carbon tax is a charge per tonne of CO2 on the fuels and sectors it covers. It is added to the fuel price as the rate times the fuel’s emission factor (Chapter 2). The methodology’s notation is \(NCT\) for the new carbon tax and \(\varphi_{NCT}\) for its coverage (methodology, section 3.9.3.1.1).
The carbon price path. The national carbon price follows the policy path, made real if the inputs are nominal (M1.2):
\[
\tau_t = \Lambda^{*}(t;\, T^{cp}_0, T^{cp}_1, x^{cp}_0, x^{cp}_1)\; n_t, \qquad n_t = \begin{cases} \nu_t & \text{inputs nominal} \\ 1 & \text{inputs real} \end{cases}
\tag{1.10}\]
where

\(\tau_t\) (cptraj, methodology \(NCT_t\)) is the carbon price in real USD/tCO2;
\(\Lambda^{*}\) is \(\Lambda\) if ExtendCarbonPriceBeyondOutro = Linear*, else \(\bar{\Lambda}\);
\(T^{cp}_0\), \(T^{cp}_1\) are CPIntro, CPOutro; \(x^{cp}_0\), \(x^{cp}_1\) are CPLevelStart, CPLevelTarget;
\(n_t\) (cp.nom) is the CPI index \(\nu_t\) if NomorReal starts with “Nominal”, else 1 (default Real*).

Explicit or shadow pricing. The input ScenarioSelected picks a main scenario from the legacy table of main scenarios. It says whether the carbon price path is an explicit tax or a shadow price (Section 1.8.5). The explicit carbon price is
\[
\tau^{x}_t = \tau_t\; \mathbb{1}[\text{main scenario prices explicitly}]
\tag{1.11}\]
(cpx, cp.exp). A text that is not in the table counts as explicit pricing, as the shipped ” - Carbon tax”.
Coverage by fuel and by sector. The tax covers a fuel and a sector through two sets of switches, one per fuel (MCovCoa, …, MCovOop; biomass CTaxCoversBiomass; jet fuel reads the kerosene switch) and one per coverage sector (MCovPow, MCovRod, …, MCovOen). Unticked fuels and sectors are exempt. An exemption can be phased out: in a policy scenario with ExemptPhaseout = TRUE, an uncovered fuel or sector becomes taxed linearly over ExemptPhaseoutPeriod years from YearPha:
\[
\varphi_{t} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{switch ticked} \\[4pt] \mathbb{1}[o \ne B]\;\mathbb{1}[\text{ExemptPhaseout}]\;\mathbb{1}[t \ge T^{cp}_0]\;\min\!\left(\max\!\left(\dfrac{t + 1 - T^{pha}}{N^{pha}},\, 0\right),\, 1\right) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{1.12}\]
where

\(\varphi_t\) (ctcov) is the coverage of one fuel (\(\varphi_{NCT,f}\)) or one sector (\(\varphi_{NCT,s}\)), a share;
\(T^{pha}\) is YearPha, \(N^{pha}\) is ExemptPhaseoutPeriod;
the phase-out share itself is exph.

A fuel used in a sector is taxed by the product of the two coverages: the sector coverage enters the rate by sector below, the fuel coverage the rate per GJ (M2.4, Chapter 2).
The rate by sector. Where the new ETS covers a sector, the ETS replaces the carbon tax. The carbon tax rate of coverage sector \(s\) is (M1.3):
\[
T_{s,t} = \tau^{x}_t\; c_{s,t}\; (1 - \kappa_{s,t}), \qquad c_{s,t} = \begin{cases} 1 - \text{xcov}_{j(s),\min(t, T_x)} & \text{tax complementary to an existing ETS} \\ \varphi_{NCT,s,t} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{1.13}\]
where

\(T_{s,t}\) (ctr, methodology \(NCT_{s,t}\)) is the carbon tax rate of sector \(s\) in USD/tCO2;
\(\kappa_{s,t}\) is the new ETS coverage of the sector (Equation 1.15);
\(c_{s,t}\) is the sector coverage of the tax. If CTaxComplimentaryToETS = Yes, the new tax covers what the country’s existing national ETS does not: one minus the existing ETS coverage \(\text{xcov}\) of the sector’s ECP sector \(j(s)\) in the data year of \(t\). Otherwise new instruments add to existing ones.

Residential LPG and kerosene. With AlwaysExemptResLPGKer = Yes (default No*), the new carbon tax, the new ETS cost and the new excise of residential LPG and kerosene are zero. The model applies this through an exemption factor \(x_{s,f}\) (exf) that multiplies each new policy per unit of fuel:
\[
x_{s,f} = \begin{cases} 0 & f \in \{\text{LPG, kerosene}\},\ s = \text{residential},\ \text{switch Yes} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{1.14}\]
Existing taxes, existing carbon pricing and subsidy phase-outs still apply to these fuels, and the shadow price is not exempted (Chapter 2).

for t in years:
    tt = t if ExtendCarbonPriceBeyondOutro == 'Linear*' else min(t, CPOutro)
    cp_nom[t] = infl[t] if NomorReal.startswith('Nominal') else 1
    cptraj[t] = 0 if t < CPIntro else (CPLevelStart + (CPLevelTarget - CPLevelStart)
                                       / max(CPOutro - CPIntro, 1) * (tt - CPIntro)) * cp_nom[t]
    cpx[t] = cptraj[t] * explicit(ScenarioSelected)          # 1 unless a shadow-pricing scenario
    exph[t] = 0
    if scenario > 1 and ExemptPhaseout and t >= CPIntro:
        exph[t] = clip((t + 1 - YearPha) / ExemptPhaseoutPeriod, 0, 1)
    for x in fuels + coverage_sectors:                        # MCov* switches
        ctcov[x][t] = 1 if switch[x] else exph[t]
    for s in coverage_sectors:
        if CTaxComplimentaryToETS starts with 'Yes':
            cover = 1 - existing_ets_coverage[ecp_sector(s)][min(t, last_ecp_year)]
        else:
            cover = ctcov[s][t]
        ctr[s][t] = cpx[t] * cover * (1 - etsc[s][t])
exf['all'] = 1
exf['res'] = 0 if AlwaysExemptResLPGKer starts with 'Yes' else 1   # read by residential LPG and kerosene




1.8.4 New emissions trading system
A new ETS sets a cap on the emissions of the sectors it covers. The model does not clear the permit market inside a run: it estimates the permit price that would meet the cap, applies it like a carbon tax, and reports how far emissions end up from the cap. A goal seek outside the run then refines the price (Chapter 6). The methodology’s user guide describes the option in methodology, section 1.3.2.4.2.
On and coverage. The ETS applies from its start year if NewETS = Yes; it covers the sectors whose switch (ETSCovPow, …, ETSCovOen) is ticked:
\[
\text{on}_t = \mathbb{1}[\text{NewETS}]\;\mathbb{1}[t \ge T^{E}_0], \qquad \kappa_{s,t} = \text{on}_t\;\mathbb{1}[\text{ETS covers } s]
\tag{1.15}\]
where \(T^{E}_0\) is ETSIntro and \(\kappa_{s,t}\) (etsc) the effective coverage of sector \(s\).
Free allocation. Part of the permits can be allocated free, in proportion to output (output-based allocation, OBR). The benchmark of a group is the share of its emission intensity allocated free; it runs from one minus the auctioned share at the start year to one minus the auctioned share at the target year, and is held after:
\[
B_{G,t} = \bar{\Lambda}\big(t;\, T^{E}_0, T^{E}_1,\, 1 - a_0,\, 1 - a_1\big), \qquad \omega_{s,t} = \min\big(1, \max(0, B_{G(s),t})\big)
\tag{1.16}\]
where

\(B_{G,t}\) (etsb) is the benchmark of ETS group \(G\) (power, transport, residential, industry);
\(a_0\), \(a_1\) are ETSAuctStart, ETSAuctTarget, the same for every group (default: nothing auctioned, so \(B = 1\));
\(T^{E}_1\) is ETSOutro;
\(\omega_{s,t}\) (obr) is the OBR share of sector \(s\), the benchmark of its group \(G(s)\) bounded to \([0, 1]\).

The cap. The cap is a change against the baseline emissions of the covered sectors:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathit{bce}_t &= \sum_s \mathit{CO2}^{B}_{s,t}\;\kappa_{s,t} \\
\mathit{chg}_t &= \bar{\Lambda}\big(t;\, T^{E}_0, T^{E}_1,\, \mathit{chg}_0,\, \mathit{chg}_1\big) \\
\mathit{cap}_t &= \begin{cases} \mathit{cap}_{t-1} & t > T^{E}_1 \text{ and the cap is held Constant} \\ \text{on}_t\; \mathit{bce}_t\,(1 + \mathit{chg}_t) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.17}\]
where

\(\mathit{bce}_t\) (ets.bce, MtCO2) is the baseline covered emissions;
\(\mathit{CO2}^{B}_{s,t}\) (bco2) is the baseline CO2 of ETS sector \(s\), stored from scenario 1 as data;
\(\mathit{chg}_0\), \(\mathit{chg}_1\) are ETSChangeRelStart, ETSChangeRelTarget (for example \(-0.05\) and \(-0.20\));
ETSCapCont = Constant holds the cap at its last level after the target year (and only while the ETS is on); otherwise the relative change is held.

Volatility. A volatile permit price raises the cost of abatement: firms act as if the price were lower. The volatility adjustment converts the permit price into a tax-equivalent price:
\[
V = \frac{1 + r\, i}{1 + v\, i}
\tag{1.18}\]
where

\(V\) (ets.vadj) is the tax-equivalent price per USD of permit price;
\(v\) (ets.vol) is the assumed annual price volatility of the ETS, and \(i\) (ets.imp) the abatement-cost increase per unit of volatility, both read by label from the table below;
\(r\) is the carbon tax policy risk (ETSCTRisk, 0.2).











Label (ETSVolatility, ETSVolImpact)
Medium*
High
Low
Zero

0.42

0.5

At Medium, \(V = (1 + 0.2 \times 0.5)/(1 + 0.42 \times 0.5) = 1/1.1\).
The fast price estimate. With one semi-elasticity of covered emissions to the price, the price that brings covered emissions from \(bce\) to the cap solves \(cap = bce\; e^{\bar{\sigma} V p}\) (A1.1):
\[
\bar{\sigma}_t = \frac{\sum_s \mathit{CO2}^{B}_{s,t}\,\kappa_{s,t}\,\sigma_s\,\big(1 - (1 - \vartheta)\,\omega_{s,t}\big)}{\mathit{bce}_t}
\tag{1.19}\]
\[
\hat{p}_t = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\ln(\mathit{cap}_t / \mathit{bce}_t)}{\bar{\sigma}_t\, V} & \text{on}_t = 1,\ 0 < \mathit{cap}_t < \mathit{bce}_t,\ \bar{\sigma}_t < 0 \\[8pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{1.20}\]
where

\(\bar{\sigma}_t\) (ets.se, per USD/tCO2) is the effective semi-elasticity of covered emissions, 0 when nothing is covered;
\(\sigma_s\) is the semi-elasticity of the sector’s semi-elasticity group (power, transport, residential, industry; legacy table ETS+LTS, by country);
\(\vartheta\) is the effectiveness of output-based allocation (setting ETSOBREffectiveness, 0.5): a permit allocated free has half the effect of an auctioned one;
\(\hat{p}_t\) (ets.est) is the fast estimate of the permit price in USD/tCO2.

Permit price, tax-equivalent price, revenue factor.
\[
p^{E}_t = \text{on}_t \begin{cases} \text{override}_t \ (\text{blank: } \tau_t) & \text{ETSPriceOverride = Yes} \\ \hat{p}_t & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \qquad \tilde{p}^{E}_t = p^{E}_t\, V, \qquad \rho = \frac{1}{V}
\tag{1.21}\]
where \(p^{E}_t\) (ets.p, methodology \(NETSP\)) is the permit price, \(\tilde{p}^{E}_t\) (ets.pe) the tax-equivalent price that enters behaviour, and \(\rho\) (ets.rf) the revenue factor: permit revenue per USD of tax-equivalent cost. The override row holds prices pasted from the goal seek (Chapter 6).
The ETS cost by sector. The tax-equivalent price splits by the OBR share. The auctioned part enters the fuel price like a tax; the free part acts only on efficiency, through the shadow price (Equation 1.25):
\[
A_{s,t} = \tilde{p}^{E}_t\;\kappa_{s,t}\;(1 - \omega_{s,t})
\tag{1.22}\]
where \(A_{s,t}\) (etr) is the ETS cost in the fuel price of sector \(s\), USD/tCO2 (M1.3). Revenue counts the auctioned part times \(\rho\), the permit price; the free part raises none (Chapter 7).






TipPseudocode: new ETS



for t in years:
    on[t] = NewETS starts with 'Yes' and t >= ETSIntro
    for s in coverage_sectors:                                   # power + 16 subsectors
        etsc[s][t] = on[t] * ETSCov[s]
    for G in ['pow', 'tra', 'res', 'ind']:
        etsb[G][t] = path(t, ETSIntro, ETSOutro, 1 - ETSAuctStart, 1 - ETSAuctTarget, hold=True)
    for s in coverage_sectors:
        obr[s][t] = clip(etsb[ets_group(s)][t], 0, 1)
    vadj = (1 + ETSCTRisk * imp[ETSVolImpact]) / (1 + vol[ETSVolatility] * imp[ETSVolImpact])
    bce[t] = sum(bco2[s][t] * etsc[s][t] for s in coverage_sectors)     # stored baseline CO2
    chg[t] = path(t, ETSIntro, ETSOutro, ETSChangeRelStart, ETSChangeRelTarget, hold=True)
    cap[t] = on[t] * bce[t] * (1 + chg[t])
    if ETSCapCont starts with 'Constant' and t > ETSOutro:
        cap[t] = cap[t-1] if on[t] else 0
    se[t] = sum(bco2[s][t] * etsc[s][t] * semi[semi_group(s)] * (1 - (1 - obr_eff) * obr[s][t])
                for s in coverage_sectors) / bce[t]   if bce[t] > 0 else 0
    est[t] = log(cap[t] / bce[t]) / (se[t] * vadj)   if on[t] and 0 < cap[t] < bce[t] and se[t] < 0 else 0
    p[t] = (override[t] or cptraj[t]) if ETSPriceOverride starts with 'Yes' else est[t]
    p[t] = p[t] if on[t] else 0
    pe[t] = p[t] * vadj                                         # tax-equivalent price
    rf = 1 / vadj                                               # revenue factor
    for s in coverage_sectors:
        etr[s][t] = pe[t] * etsc[s][t] * (1 - obr[s][t])        # auctioned part, in the fuel price




1.8.5 Feebates and regulations: the shadow price
Feebates and regulations make energy use more efficient without raising the price of energy. A feebate charges above-average emitters and rebates below-average ones, so it is revenue neutral; a regulation sets a standard. The model represents both as a shadow price per tonne of CO2 that acts only on the efficiency margin of fuel use (Chapter 3) and on power (Chapter 4), and raises no revenue. The user guide describes feebates in methodology, section 1.3.2.4.3 and regulations in section 1.3.2.6.
Feebate rates. One rate per feebate group \(G\) (power, transport, residential, industry), linear from FeebateIntro to FeebateOutro and held after:
\[
b_{G,t} = \bar{\Lambda}\big(t;\, T^{b}_0, T^{b}_1,\, b_{G,0},\, b_{G,1}\big)
\tag{1.23}\]
where \(b_{G,t}\) (fb) is in USD/tCO2 and \(b_{G,0}\), \(b_{G,1}\) are Feb_Level_Start_<group>, Feb_Level_Target_<group>. Food and forestry and services take the residential rate; other energy use the industry rate.
Regulations. The main scenario (ScenarioSelected) decides whether the carbon price path is an explicit tax or a shadow price, which efficiency adjustment applies and which sectors the shadow price covers:

The adjustments are the inputs SPPEffAdjEnergyEfficiencyRegulations (1), SPPEffAdjVehicleFuelEconomy (2), SPPEffAdjRes (3), SPPEffAdjInd (4) and SPPEffAdjFeebates (5): the share of the shadow price that reaches the efficiency margin (Egypt: 0.7 for the regulations, 1 for feebates). Under shadow pricing there is no explicit carbon tax (\(\tau^x = 0\)), and the carbon price path becomes the shadow carbon price:
\[
\mathit{reg}_{s,t} = (\tau_t - \tau^{x}_t)\; a^{reg}\; \mathbb{1}[\text{main scenario covers } s]
\tag{1.24}\]
where \(\mathit{reg}_{s,t}\) (reg) is the regulation shadow price of sector \(s\), \(\tau_t - \tau^x_t\) the shadow carbon price (cp.shd) and \(a^{reg}\) (regadj) the efficiency adjustment of the main scenario.
The shadow price by sector. Feebates, regulations and the free part of the ETS add up (M1.4):
\[
\Sigma_{s,t} = b_{G(s),t}\; a^{fb}\; \mathbb{1}[\text{feebate covers } s] \;+\; \mathit{reg}_{s,t} \;+\; \tilde{p}^{E}_t\;\kappa_{s,t}\;\omega_{s,t}
\tag{1.25}\]
where

\(\Sigma_{s,t}\) (shpx) is the shadow price of sector \(s\) in USD/tCO2;
\(a^{fb}\) is SPPEffAdjFeebates, the share of the feebate on the efficiency margin; the product \(a^{fb}\,\mathbb{1}[\cdot]\) is ssc;
the feebate coverage switches are FbCovPow, …, FbCovOen.

Other regulation inputs act directly on efficiency rather than through a price: the additional policy-induced efficiency gains AdditionalEfficiencyRoadVehicle, AdditionalEfficiencyResidential, AdditionalEfficiencyIndustrial (Chapter 3) and AdditionalEfficiencyPower (Chapter 4). The road engineer model’s vehicle feebate uses the road regulation shadow price (Chapter 5).






TipPseudocode: shadow prices



scn = position of ScenarioSelected in main_scenarios (0 if not found)
explicit = 1 if scn == 0 else main_scenarios[scn].explicit
regadj   = 0 if scn == 0 or main_scenarios[scn].adjustment == 0 \
           else [SPPEffAdjEnergyEfficiencyRegulations, SPPEffAdjVehicleFuelEconomy,
                 SPPEffAdjRes, SPPEffAdjInd, SPPEffAdjFeebates][main_scenarios[scn].adjustment - 1]
for t in years:
    for G in ['pow', 'tra', 'res', 'ind']:
        fb[G][t] = path(t, FeebateIntro, FeebateOutro, fb_start[G], fb_target[G], hold=True)
    cpx[t] = cptraj[t] * explicit
    shadow[t] = cptraj[t] - cpx[t]
    for s in coverage_sectors:
        regc = scn > 0 and main_scenarios[scn].covers[s]
        reg[s][t] = shadow[t] * regadj * regc
        ssc[s] = FbCov[s] * SPPEffAdjFeebates
        shpx[s][t] = fb[feebate_group(s)][t] * ssc[s] + reg[s][t] + ets_pe[t] * etsc[s][t] * obr[s][t]




1.8.6 Fuel excises: the fuel price reform
A new excise is a tax per unit of fuel, set in the fuel’s own price unit (USD/liter for gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene, USD/bbl for other oil products, USD/GJ for coal, gas and biomass, USD/kWh for electricity). The model calls it the fuel price reform: one increase path per price block, all with the same start and target year (FprIntro, FprOutro). The methodology describes new excises in methodology, section 3.9.3.1.4.
Up to the target year the path is linear; after it, the input ExtendCarbonPriceBeyondOutro (the same as for the carbon price) chooses how it continues (M1.5):
\[
F_{g,f,t} = \begin{cases} 0 & t < T^{F}_0 \\[2pt] x_0 + j\,(t - T^{F}_0) & t < T^{F}_1 \text{ or Linear*} \\[2pt] \hat{x}\,(1 + k)^{\,t - T^{F}_1 + 1} & \text{Percentage} \\[2pt] x_1 & \text{otherwise (held)} \end{cases}
\tag{1.26}\]
with
\[
j = \frac{x_1 - x_0}{T^{F}_1 - T^{F}_0}, \qquad k = \left(\frac{x_1}{x_0}\right)^{1/(T^{F}_1 - T^{F}_0)} - 1, \qquad \hat{x} = x_0 + j\,\max(T^{F}_1 - T^{F}_0 - 1,\, 0)
\tag{1.27}\]
where

\(F_{g,f,t}\) (fpr) is the excise increase of price block \((g,f)\) in its price unit;
\(x_0\), \(x_1\) are the start and final increases (FprStart<Fuel><Sector>, FprFinal<Fuel><Sector>);
\(j\) (fprj) is the annual step, 0 if the target year is not after the start year;
\(k\) (fprk) is the average annual growth rate of the path; where the start is zero it divides by \(x_0 + j\) instead of \(x_0\); it is 0 if both levels are zero or the years do not increase;
\(\hat{x}\) (fprp) is the value of the year before the target year; the value after the target year is fpra;
if the target year is not after the start year, the held value is \(x_0\).

The new excise of a price block. The gross new excise (ntxg) is the reform path, plus the Pigouvian tax when AddEfficientTaxes = Yes (Section 1.8.12). It applies in policy scenarios only:
\[
N^{x}_{g,f,t} = \mathbb{1}[o \ne B]\; F_{g,f,t}
\tag{1.28}\]
(ntxb). Prices divide it by the GJ per price unit and multiply it by the exemption factor \(x_{s,f}\) to get the new excise per GJ of each subsector (Chapter 2). The electricity blocks reach the electricity price through the power block, together with the manual electricity excise of AdditionalExcise (A4.7, Chapter 4).






TipPseudocode: fuel price reform



for (g, f) in price_blocks + [('res', 'ecy'), ('ind', 'ecy')]:      # 14 blocks
    s0, s1 = FprStart[g, f], FprFinal[g, f]
    j = (s1 - s0) / (FprOutro - FprIntro) if FprOutro > FprIntro else 0
    k = 0
    if FprOutro > FprIntro and max(s0, s1) > 0:
        k = (s1 / (s0 if s0 > 0 else s0 + j)) ** (1 / (FprOutro - FprIntro)) - 1
    before_target = s0 + j * max(FprOutro - FprIntro - 1, 0)
    for t in years:
        if ExtendCarbonPriceBeyondOutro == 'Percentage':
            after = before_target * (1 + k) ** (t - FprOutro + 1)
        else:
            after = s1 if FprOutro > FprIntro else s0
        if t < FprIntro:
            fpr[g, f][t] = 0
        elif t < FprOutro or ExtendCarbonPriceBeyondOutro == 'Linear*':
            fpr[g, f][t] = s0 + j * (t - FprIntro)
        else:
            fpr[g, f][t] = after
        ntxg[g, f][t] = fpr[g, f][t]                    # + Pigouvian tax if AddEfficientTaxes (Excel-AI only)
        ntxb[g, f][t] = ntxg[g, f][t] * (scenario > 1)




1.8.7 Subsidy and price-control phase-outs
Many countries subsidise fuels, either explicitly (a consumer or producer subsidy) or by controlling the retail price so that it does not follow the supply cost. The model can phase out three kinds of support, each with its own switch, start year, period and share: producer subsidies, consumer subsidies and price controls. The methodology describes these reforms in methodology, section 3.9.3.1.6 and section 3.9.3.1.7.
The phase-out factor. For each phase-out \(k\), the share of the original support still in place (M1.7):
\[
\phi_{k,t} = \max\!\left(1 - \bar{s}_k,\;\; \begin{cases} 1 - \bar{s}_k\,\dfrac{t - T_k}{\max(N_k, 1)} & \text{on}_k \text{ and } t > T_k \\[6pt] 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\right)
\tag{1.29}\]
where

\(\phi_{k,t}\) (pof) is the share of the original subsidy (or floating tax) kept, from 1 down to \(1 - \bar{s}_k\);
\(T_k\) is the start year (YearProdSubPha, YearConsSubPha, YearPrcContPha);
\(N_k\) (po.n) is the phase-out period in years, \(\bar{s}_k\) (po.sh) the share phased out, and \(\text{on}_k\) (po.on) whether the phase-out applies.

The baseline can phase out subsidies too (a reform already decided). The baseline and policy scenarios read different inputs:

A switch counts as on when it is TRUE or starts with “Yes”. Price controls are phased out only where the policy switch is on (and, in the baseline, the baseline switch too), and they use the consumer-subsidy shares (issue I48).
Scope by fuel and sector. Scope switches let a reform cover some price blocks or fuels only:
\[
\psi^{cs}_{g,f,t} = 1 - i^{cs}_{g,f}\,(1 - \phi_{cs,t}), \qquad \psi^{pc}_{g,f,t} = 1 - i^{pc}_{g,f}\,(1 - \phi_{pc,t}), \qquad \psi^{ps}_{f,t} = 1 - i^{ps}_{f}\,(1 - \phi_{ps,t})
\tag{1.30}\]
where

\(\psi^{cs}\) (csf), \(\psi^{pc}\) (pcf) are the consumer-subsidy and price-control factors of each of the 12 fuel price blocks, and \(\psi^{ps}\) (psf) the producer-subsidy factor of each producer fuel (coal, gas, oil, biomass, electricity);
\(i^{cs}\), \(i^{pc}\), \(i^{ps}\) (csi, pci, psi) are the scope switches (ConsSubPhaseScope_<fuel>_<sector>, PriceCtrlPhaseScope_<fuel>_<sector>, ProdSubPhaseScope_<fuel>), 1 where the reform applies.

The factors become wedges in the after-tax price: the consumer-subsidy reform removes part of the fixed subsidy, the price-control phase-out part of the floating tax or subsidy that absorbs supply-cost changes (Chapter 2). The saved subsidy is revenue (Chapter 7). Subsidy reforms of electricity prices are part of the power block (Chapter 4).






TipPseudocode: phase-out factors



for k in ['ps', 'cs', 'pc']:
    if k == 'pc':
        on = PrcContPha and (scenario > 1 or PrcContPhaBaseline)
        share = ShareofConsSubPhaBA if scenario == 1 else max(ShareofConsSubPhaBA, ShareOfConsSubPha)
    else:
        on = baseline_switch[k] if scenario == 1 else policy_switch[k]
        share = share_BA[k] if scenario == 1 else max(share_BA[k], share_policy[k])
    period = period_BA[k] if scenario == 1 else period_policy[k]
    for t in years:
        pof[k][t] = max(1 - share,
                        1 - share * (t - start_year[k]) / max(period, 1) if on and t > start_year[k] else 1)
for (g, f) in price_blocks:                                  # 12 blocks
    csf[g, f] = 1 - csi[g, f] * (1 - pof['cs'])
    pcf[g, f] = 1 - pci[g, f] * (1 - pof['pc'])
for f in ['coa', 'nga', 'oil', 'bio', 'ecy']:
    psf[f] = 1 - psi[f] * (1 - pof['ps'])




1.8.8 Producer subsidy reform
A producer subsidy lowers the cost of supplying a fuel. The model reads the subsidy of each fuel from the price data, spreads it over the demand it supports to get a subsidy per unit, and lowers it with the producer phase-out factor after the last historical price year (A2.5):
\[
\mathit{ps}_{f,t} = \begin{cases} -\dfrac{\mathit{PROS}_{f,t}}{D_{f,t}} & t \le L \\[8pt] \mathit{ps}_{f,L}\;\psi^{ps}_{f,t} & t > L \end{cases}
\tag{1.31}\]
where

\(\mathit{ps}_{f,t}\) (psu) is the producer subsidy per unit of fuel \(f\) (negative: USD/liter for oil, USD/GJ for coal, gas and biomass);
\(\mathit{PROS}_{f,t}\) (pros) is the producer subsidy (price data, USD billion nominal, times the CPI index and 1000: USD million real; held after \(L\)), times \(10^6\) to get USD;
\(D_{f,t}\) (psd) is the demand that carries the subsidy: world demand times liters per ktoe for oil; the average of world demand and domestic consumption (excluding electricity and heat) times GJ per ktoe for coal and gas; domestic consumption times GJ per ktoe for biomass;
\(\psi^{ps}_{f,t}\) is the producer-subsidy factor psf of Equation 1.30.

The per-unit subsidy enters the supply cost of each price block of the fuel, so the floating taxes and price controls absorb part of a phase-out, as in legacy (Chapter 2). The subsidy itself is a fiscal line (rpsu, Chapter 7). The electricity producer subsidy is allocated between user groups in the power block (Chapter 4).


1.8.9 Methane fee
The methane fee is a charge per tonne of CO2-equivalent of methane from the sources it covers (fuel supply, gas distribution, agriculture, waste). It drives methane abatement and raises revenue (Chapter 6, Chapter 7). The methodology describes methane in methodology, section 3.5.4.2.
\[
m_t = \Lambda\big(t;\, T^{m}_0, T^{m}_1, m_0, m_1\big)\;\mathbb{1}[o \ne B] \;+\; \tau_t\;\mathbb{1}[\text{carbon tax applies to methane}]
\tag{1.32}\]
where

\(m_t\) (mfee) is the methane fee in USD/tCO2e; the path alone is mfee.p;
\(T^{m}_0\), \(T^{m}_1\), \(m_0\), \(m_1\) are MPIntro, MPOutro, MPLevelStart, MPLevelTarget; the path continues linearly after the target year;
the fee path applies only in policy scenarios; the carbon price \(\tau_t\) is added in any scenario where CTforMethane = Yes (M1.8).

Which methane sources the fee covers is set by switches per source (Excel-AI sheet Manual inputs; Chapter 6).


1.8.10 Existing carbon pricing
Some countries already price carbon. The IMF retail prices contain whatever existing carbon pricing the country had in the price data, so the model adds only the change against that level: a scheme switched off lowers the price by its embedded level, growth or new data raise it. The data are the World Bank Carbon Pricing Dashboard and ICAP (legacy sheet ECP, as of 1 April 2025; 52 countries). The methodology describes the options in methodology, section 3.9.3.1.3.
Data by ECP sector and fuel. For each ECP sector \(j\) (power, transport, residential, industry), fuel \(f\) and data year \(y\) (2021 to \(T_x = 2025\)), in real USD/tCO2:
\[
\mathit{XT}_{j,f,y} = r_{f,y}\; k^{T}_{j,y}\; l^{T}_{f,y}, \qquad \mathit{XE}_{j,f,y} = p^{nat}_y\; k^{N}_{j,y}\; l^{N}_{f,y} \;+\; p^{EU}_y\; k^{EU}_{j,y}\; l^{EU}_{f,y}
\tag{1.33}\]
where

\(\mathit{XT}\) is the existing carbon tax and \(\mathit{XE}\) the existing ETS price of the sector and fuel;
\(r_{f,y}\) is the carbon tax rate of the fuel where the country has fuel rates and no “single price” flag, otherwise the single rate; \(k^{T}\), \(l^{T}\) its sector and fuel coverage;
\(p^{nat}\) is the national ETS price with sector and fuel coverage \(k^{N}\), \(l^{N}\); \(p^{EU}\) the EU ETS price with the country’s regional coverage \(k^{EU}\), \(l^{EU}\), counted only if the country is in the EU ETS (flag Yes or Both);
prices are made real with the CPI index of the data year; blank coverage is 0.

Scenario factors. Each scheme can be switched off or grown after the last data year:
\[
\phi^{ct}_t = \mathbb{1}[\text{ExistingCTApply}]\,(1 + \gamma^{ct})^{\max(0,\, t - T_x)}, \qquad \phi^{ets}_t = \mathbb{1}[\text{ExistingETSApply}]\,(1 + \gamma^{ets})^{\max(0,\, t - T_x)}
\tag{1.34}\]
where \(\phi^{ct}\) (xct.p), \(\phi^{ets}\) (xets.p) multiply the data of year \(t^* = \min(t, T_x)\) (xct.c), and \(\gamma^{ct}\), \(\gamma^{ets}\) are ExistingCTGrowth, ExistingETSGrowth. The level per GJ is then the emission factor times \(\mathit{XT}\,\phi^{ct} + \mathit{XE}\,\phi^{ets}\); the price block takes the change against the level embedded in the price data, of year \(\min(L, T_x)\) (A2.2, Chapter 2). The change also enters the variable cost of power plants (Chapter 4).






TipPseudocode: existing carbon pricing



eu = country in EU ETS ('Yes' or 'Both')
for y in [2021, ..., 2025]:
    for f in fuels:
        rate[f][y] = single_rate[y] if single_price or no fuel rate else fuel_rate[f][y]
        rate[f][y] *= infl[y]                                         # real USD of the results year
    for j in ['pow', 'trs', 'res', 'ind']:
        for f in fuels:
            xct[j, f][y] = rate[f][y] * tax_sector_cov[j][y] * tax_fuel_cov[f][y]
            xets[j, f][y] = (nat_price[y] * infl[y] * nat_sector_cov[j][y] * nat_fuel_cov[f][y]
                             + eu * eu_price[y] * infl[y] * eu_sector_cov[j][y] * eu_fuel_cov[f][y])
for t in years:
    xct_c[t] = column of min(t, 2025)
    xct_p[t] = (1 + ExistingCTGrowth) ** max(0, t - 2025) if ExistingCTApply starts with 'Yes' else 0
    xets_p[t] = (1 + ExistingETSGrowth) ** max(0, t - 2025) if ExistingETSApply starts with 'Yes' else 0




1.8.11 Social cost of carbon
The social cost of carbon values a tonne of CO2. It does not change behaviour by itself: it is used by the climate part of the Pigouvian tax (Section 1.8.12) and by the welfare results (Chapter 7). The methodology discusses it in methodology, section 3.7. Five paths are computed, each growing at the rate \(g^{scc}\) (M1.6):
\[
\mathit{SCC}^{tgt}_t = \mathit{SCC}^{*}\,(1 + g^{scc})^{t - T^{*}}, \qquad \mathit{SCC}^{x}_t = \mathit{SCC}^{x}\,(1 + g^{scc})^{t - t_0} \quad (x = \text{Ricke national, Ricke global, EPA})
\tag{1.35}\]

The national and the global SCC are each chosen by NSCCSource and GSCCSource (by first letter: Target, Ricke, Manual, US EPA; default Target*). These settings are read from the baseline column.


1.8.12 Pigouvian (efficient) taxes
With AddEfficientTaxes = Yes, the new excise of each price block adds a Pigouvian tax: the external cost of a unit of fuel that its price does not already cover (A1.2). It has three parts:

air pollution: the value of averted PM2.5 (from the air pollution module) times the module’s concentration coefficients of the source times the combustion factors of the fuel, per GJ, weighted by base-year fuel use (residential coal only where coal is above ApCoalResMin, 0.1% of buildings fuel use);
climate (if ClimateEffTax): the national SCC times the generic CO2 factor of the fuel;
road transport: accident, congestion and road-damage costs per km (from the transport co-benefits module), converted per unit of fuel with base-year fuel economy, the elasticity share of usage and the road share of the fuel.

The sum is phased in over AddEfficientTaxesPhaseInYears from CPIntro. Where an existing pre-tax wedge already covers part of it, the new excise is \(\min\big(n,\ \max(0,\ n - w\,\gamma)\big)\), with \(n\) the gross excise, \(w\) the existing wedge per GJ and \(\gamma\) the GJ per price unit (issue I113). The module values enter in the prepare stage, so the Pigouvian tax is exogenous to the year loop (issue I151).






NoteIn Excel-AI and CPAT Python






Excel-AI: sheet Mitigation, section 1 (rows of Formulas.md E7-E235): the input rows read from ScenarioDefinition, then the carbon price (cp.t, cp.nom, exph, ctcov, cptraj), fuel price reform (fprj … fpr), SCC (scc), Pigouvian taxes (rows 185-418: pig.*, airpol.mc, cc.code, pigx, ntxg, xcpb, xpre, ntxb), new ETS (ets.on … ets.rf), feebates (fb, fbcov), main scenario (scn, cp.exp, cpx, cp.shd, regadj, regc, reg, ssc), sector rates (ctr, etr, shpx), existing carbon pricing (xct.c, xct.p, xets.p), phase-outs (po.on … psu), exf, methane fee (mfee.p, mfee). title: 2  Energy prices
text:
2.1 The price chain at a glance
This chapter explains how the model builds the price of every fuel in every sector, year by year. Prices are the first link of the model’s chain: a carbon tax, an ETS, an excise reform or a subsidy reform changes fuel use, power dispatch, emissions and revenue only through the prices computed here.
The chapter follows the order of the calculation. It starts with international prices, builds the domestic price before new policies (supply cost, excise and other taxes, VAT), adds the existing carbon pricing, the subsidy and price-control reforms and the new policies, and ends with the average prices and price indices that the model reports. The welfare use of the Pigouvian prices and the revenue raised at these prices belong to Chapter 7; electricity prices belong to Chapter 4.
The methodology describes prices in methodology, section 3.2 and, in more detail, in Appendix C. This chapter says where the model follows, simplifies or departs from it.
Assumptions you need here. The notation, dimensions and policy paths are set out in Chapter 1. Four of them matter for every equation of this chapter:
A fuel price is built in layers. The first layers are prices before new policies: what the country pays today, projected forward with the international price. The last layers are wedges that policies add, each passed through to the consumer with VAT.
flowchart TD
    GP["International price gp"] --> SP["Supply cost sp"]
    PS["Producer subsidy ps"] --> SP
    SP --> TXO["Excise and other taxes txo<br/>(pass-through pcc)"]
    TXO --> PBC["Price before new policies pbc<br/>(sp + txo) x (1 + VAT)"]
    PBC --> ATP["After-tax price atp"]
    NCE["New policies nce<br/>carbon tax, ETS cost, excise"] --> ATP
    XCP["Change in existing<br/>carbon pricing xcpd"] --> ATP
    W["Subsidy and price-control<br/>wedges csw, pcw"] --> ATP
    ATP --> D["Fuel use (sec-demand)"]
    SHP["Shadow price shp"] --> D
The methodology writes the same identity in its own terms: retail price = supply price + VAT + excise and other taxes, with the excise term holding every carbon price and subsidy (methodology, section 3.2.1). The model keeps the same identity but stores the pieces separately: txo holds only the existing taxes and subsidies, and the carbon prices and reforms are wedges on top (Section 2.13).

section: 2.2 Price blocks: fuels and price sectors

2.2 Price blocks: fuels and price sectors
Prices are kept by price block: a fuel and a price sector, as in the IMF price dataset. There are 12 blocks. Coal and natural gas have one block each for power, residential and industry; the oil products and biomass have a single block for all sectors. Electricity prices are left to the power module (Chapter 4), but the electricity rows ecy.res and ecy.ind appear where a policy path is set per price fuel (fuel price reform, Pigouvian taxes), which makes 14 policy rows.

The road and residential sectors therefore pay the residential coal and gas prices; food, services and the transport modes other than road pay the industry prices.
Layout of a block, as a model concept. Each block is a small stack of rows that reads from top to bottom:

its settings: the pass-through, the VAT rate, GJ per price unit and the position of its international price;
the international reference price gpi, the fixed supply cost spf, the producer subsidy ps;
the build-up before new policies: sp, txf, txo, fadtx, cs, etx, esub, esubpu, vat, ending with pbc, the retail price before new policies;
the subsidy-reform wedges pcsw and ppcw;
the new policies averaged over the subsectors priced by the block (pnq, pctx, etsnew, pntx, pxcd, pvatn, pnce) and the retail price including new policies rpn (Section 2.16).

New policies themselves act by subsector and fuel (rows 9 of the chain), because coverage, exemptions and emission factors differ by subsector. The block shows their fuel-use weighted averages.

title: 2  Energy prices
section: 2.3 Units, real values and the two indices
text:
2.3 Units, real values and the two indices
All money values are converted to real USD of the results year as soon as they are read. Two different indices do the conversion, both equal to 1 in the results year:
\[
\iota_t = \frac{\text{CPI}^{US}_R}{\text{CPI}^{US}_t}, \qquad \delta_t = \frac{\text{Defl}^{US}_R}{\text{Defl}^{US}_t}
\tag{2.1}\]
where

\(\iota_t\) is the CPI index (code infl; US CPI from the IMF WEO), used for nominal domestic values: the IMF price dataset, margins and production costs, producer subsidies, existing carbon tax rates and permit prices, and a nominal carbon price;
\(\delta_t\) is the deflator index (code defl; US GDP deflator, WEO), used for nominal international prices;
\(R\) is the results year (2026).

This is the legacy split (legacy rows 456/725 for the CPI index, 467 for the deflator). The two differ by up to 1.2% before 2030 (2022: 1.137 against 1.124; 2030: 0.918 against 0.929), so one index alone would not reproduce legacy. The CPI index is held flat after 2031 (the WEO horizon); the deflator is not.

title: 2  Energy prices
text:
2.4 International prices
International prices drive the projection of every supply cost. The model reads a forecast of each commodity from the source chosen for the scenario, converts it to real terms and applies the High or Low adjustment. The methodology describes the sources in Appendix C, choices of the sources.
\[
gp_{m,t} = gpn_{m,t}\;\delta_t\;h_{m,t}, \qquad
h_{m,t} = \begin{cases} 1 & t \le L \text{ or Base} \\ h^{High}_m \text{ or } h^{Low}_m & t > L \end{cases}
\tag{2.2}\]
where

\(gp_{m,t}\) is the real international price of commodity \(m\) (code gp, source units);
\(gpn_{m,t}\) is the nominal price of \(m\) from the chosen source (code gpn; equation list A2.3); it is 1 for biomass, whose “commodity” is a flat line;
\(\delta_t\) is the deflator index (Equation 2.1);
\(h_{m,t}\) is the adjustment factor (code gp.adj holds the choice: 1 none, 2 High, 3 Low).

The commodity \(m\) of a block is crude oil for the five oil products, coal for coal, the gas of the country’s gas market for natural gas, and the flat line for biomass. The block reads its commodity’s price as its reference price gpi.

section: 2.5 Europe gas market: shift to LNG
text:
2.5 Europe gas market: shift to LNG
For countries in the European gas market the model follows Europe’s move away from Russian pipeline gas. The gas price these countries face moves from the European hub price towards the LNG price as the share of gas from outside Russia grows.
\[
gpn^{eus}_t = gpn^{eur}_t\,(1 - s_t) + gpn^{lng}_t\,s_t
\tag{2.3}\]
where

\(gpn^{eus}_t\) is the gas price of the European market (series nga.eus, by source);
\(gpn^{eur}_t\), \(gpn^{lng}_t\) are the Europe and LNG series of the same source;
\(s_t\) is the share of gas from outside Russia (Inputs_pint row 3; legacy rows 699, 706).

title: 2  Energy prices
section: 2.6 Historical domestic prices and forecasting coefficients
text:
2.6 Historical domestic prices and forecasting coefficients
Up to the last historical year the domestic price of each block is data: the IMF price dataset gives the supply cost, the excise and other taxes, the VAT rate and the retail price. The same data step also sets the coefficients the projection uses: the pass-through, the fixed part of the supply cost and the VAT rate. The methodology describes the data in section 3.2.3 and Appendix C, price reconstruction.

2.6.1 Supply cost and taxes in the historical years
For each historical year \(y\) (data 2021 to \(L\)):
\[
sp_y = \frac{sp^{n}_y\,\iota_y}{u}, \qquad
txo_y = \frac{\iota_y}{u}\begin{cases} \dfrac{rp^{n}_y}{1 + vatrate_y} - sp^{n}_y & \text{coal, gas, biomass} \\[2mm] txo^{n}_y & \text{oil products} \end{cases}
\tag{2.4}\]
where

\(sp^n_y\), \(rp^n_y\), \(txo^n_y\) are the dataset’s supply cost, retail price and excise and other taxes, nominal USD per price unit (mit.sp.<block>, mit.rp.<block>, mit.txo.<block>);
\(vatrate_y\) is the VAT rate of the year (below);
\(\iota_y\) is the CPI index of the year and \(u\) GJ per price unit (A2.4).

So for coal, gas and biomass the taxes are the residual of the dataset’s retail price after VAT and supply cost; for the oil products they are the dataset’s own tax column, and the retail price is rebuilt as \((sp + txo)(1 + vatrate)\), as legacy does.
Manual values. Where Settings DomPrTax is on, a value typed in the manual price tables replaces the dataset value for the codes sp, vatrate, txo, rp and pros. A blank dataset cell reads as 0.


2.6.2 Pass-through (price controls)
The pass-through \(pcc\) says how much of a change in the supply cost reaches the consumer: 1 in a liberalised market, 0 where the government fixes the retail price. It is set once per block. Settings GovPriceControls chooses how:







Option
Pass-through




Bucketed (default)
the dataset’s base-year value (mit.ps.<block>; blank = 0; biomass 1), bucketed: up to PassLo (0.25) → 0; up to PassHi (0.5) → PassMid (0.5); above → 1


Manual
the retail price control of the block from sheet Manual inputs J167:J180 (legacy addresses), by the code in column G (mit.rp.<fuel>.<sector>.ctrl; legacy default 0.8 for every block); a blank cell gives 1, as legacy rows 747-760. The electricity rows J178:J179 are not read: electricity prices come from Chapter 4


None
1 for every block



Egypt, bucketed: coal 1; gas 0; gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene and other oil products 0; biomass 1.


2.6.3 Fixed part of the supply cost
The supply cost has a fixed part (margins over the international price and, for coal and gas, the cost of domestic production) and a part that floats with the international price. The fixed part is set once:
\[
fixsp = \frac{mar\;\iota_{y^m} + dsh\;pcost\;\iota_{t_0}}{u}
\tag{2.5}\]
where

\(fixsp\) is the fixed part of the supply cost (code spf, USD/GJ real, constant over the years);
\(mar\) is the margin over international prices (mit.mar.<block>, nominal USD per price unit) read in year \(y^m\): 2024 for coal and gas (a typed year, as legacy: issue I101), the base year for the oil products; 0 for biomass;
\(dsh\) is the share of the fuel produced domestically (mit.coa.prod, mit.nga.prod in the base year, clipped to \([0, 1]\); 0 for the other fuels);
\(pcost\) is the domestic production cost (mit.coa.prod.cost, mit.nga.prod.cost, base year; 0 for the other fuels);
\(\iota_{y^m}\), \(\iota_{t_0}\) are the CPI indices of the margin year and of the base year.

Other oil products take their pass-through and margin from the dataset like the other oil products (Egypt: 0 and 7.95 USD/bbl).


2.6.4 VAT rate
The VAT rate of a block is the dataset’s rate where it is filled. Where the cell is blank, consumers pay the general VAT rate of the country (VAT_WEO of the year; Egypt 14%) and firms pay none:







Block
VAT rate where the data are blank




coa.res, nga.res; gso.all, die.all, lpg.all, ker.all, oop.all
general rate


coa.pow, coa.ind, nga.pow, nga.ind
0 (VAT is credited to firms)


bio.all
0 (largely informal)



The rate used in the projection is the rate of year \(L\). For gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene it is then multiplied by the household share of the product (sheet OilProductShares; a blank share counts as 1), because only households pay VAT on the product; firms reclaim it:
\[
vatrate = vatrate_L \times hsh
\tag{2.6}\]
where \(hsh\) is the household share of the oil product (Egypt: gasoline 1, diesel 0.03, LPG 0.99, kerosene 0.39). Other oil products and the other fuels take the full rate.






TipPseudocode: historical prices and coefficients of a block



for block in PRICES:                              # 12 blocks
    u = gj_per_unit[fuel]
    pcc_raw = 1.0 if fuel == 'bio' else data(t0, 'mit.ps.' + block)
    pcc_bucket = 0 if pcc_raw <= PassLo else (PassMid if pcc_raw <= PassHi else 1)
    pcc = {'Bucketed': pcc_bucket, 'Manual': manual_ctrl[block] or 1, 'None': 1}[GovPriceControls]
    mar_year = 2024 if fuel in ('coa', 'nga') else t0
    mar = 0 if fuel == 'bio' else data(mar_year, 'mit.mar.' + block)
    dsh = clip(data(t0, 'mit.' + fuel + '.prod'), 0, 1) if fuel in ('coa', 'nga') else 0
    pcost = data(t0, 'mit.' + fuel + '.prod.cost') if fuel in ('coa', 'nga') else 0
    spf = (mar * infl[mar_year] + dsh * pcost * infl[t0]) / u
    for y in hist_years:                          # 2021 .. L
        vr_y = data(y, 'mit.vatrate.' + block)
        if blank(vr_y):
            vr_y = VAT_WEO[y] if block in VAT_CONSUMER else 0
        sp[y] = data(y, 'mit.sp.' + block) * infl[y] / u
        if fuel in ('coa', 'nga', 'bio'):
            txo[y] = (data(y, 'mit.rp.' + block) / (1 + vr_y) - data(y, 'mit.sp.' + block)) * infl[y] / u
        else:
            txo[y] = data(y, 'mit.txo.' + block) * infl[y] / u
    vr = vr_L * (household_share[fuel] if block in OIL_SHARE else 1)








NoteIn Excel-AI and CPAT Python






Excel-AI: sheet Inputs_prices (build_inputs_prices; Inputs rows 158-169) from sheet Prices_dom (or the manual tables where DomPrTax is on); Settings GovPriceControls, PassLo, PassMid, PassHi; sheet Manual inputs J167:J180; sheet OilProductShares.
CPAT Python: cpat_model/mitigation/prices_data.py, domestic_prices() and DomesticData; equation A2.4.










WarningDifferences from legacy CPAT






LD2 (decision), L13. Legacy hardcodes the pass-through of other oil products to 1 and their margin to 0. The model takes both from the dataset. Under the legacy rule their retail price fell with the oil price to the 0.01 floor (3.79 USD/GJ in 2024, 0.23 in 2030) and their fuel use rose tenfold by 2030.
LD3 (VAT where the data are blank). The general VAT rate for residential coal and gas and the all-sector oil products; 0 for power, industry and biomass. Only blank cells are filled (user decision).
LD5, issue I39 (household share). VAT on gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene is charged on the household share only, as legacy rows 797-816.
LD16, L172 (margins and production cost in real terms). Legacy adds the margin and the production cost in nominal USD to real prices. The model converts each with the CPI index of the year it is read.
LD80 (production-cost weight, as legacy). The production cost is weighted by the share produced domestically (legacy P747:P752), not by the bucketed pass-through (an earlier prototype rule).
I101. Coal and gas margins are read at the typed year 2024, as legacy.
LD4, I150 (Egypt data). The Egypt price data equal legacy’s cell by cell, except the spot coal and gas cells, which legacy 465 fills with a year and 0; the model keeps the module values (no effect unless the spot option is chosen).
I89 (price vintage). The last historical price year is 2024, as legacy 456/465 (price data through 2024, projection from 2025).

title: 2  Energy prices
text:
2.7 Producer subsidies
A producer subsidy lowers the cost at which a fuel is supplied, so it sits inside the supply cost, before any tax. The dataset gives each producer subsidy as a total amount; the model spreads it over the demand that carries it, to get a subsidy per unit. The methodology treats producer subsidies as part of the supply price (section 3.2.4).
Amount. For each producer fuel (coal, gas, oil, biomass, electricity):
\[
pros_{f,t} = \begin{cases} PROS^{n}_{f,t}\;\iota_t \times 1000 & t \le L \\ pros_{f,t-1} & t > L \end{cases}
\tag{2.7}\]
where \(pros_{f,t}\) is the producer subsidy before the phase-out (USD million real) and \(PROS^n_{f,t}\) the dataset value (mit.pros.<fuel>.all, USD billion nominal, or a manual value).
Demand that carries it. The subsidy is spread over:








Fuel
Demand \(D_f\) (code psd)
Unit




Oil
world demand × liters per ktoe (1,108,792)
liters


Coal
average of world demand and domestic consumption × GJ per ktoe (41,868)
GJ


Gas
average of world demand and domestic consumption × GJ per ktoe
GJ


Biomass
domestic consumption × GJ per ktoe
GJ



World demand is the global production of the fuel in the IEA scenario chosen by GlobalEnergyDemand (stated policies, announced pledges or sustainable development; Mtoe × 1000). Domestic consumption is the energy use of the fuel in sheet EnergyCons, excluding electricity output and international bunkers.
Per unit, after the phase-out.
\[
psu_{f,t} = \begin{cases} -\dfrac{pros_{f,t} \times 10^6}{D_{f,t}} & t \le L \\[2mm] psu_{f,L}\;psf_{f,t} & t > L \end{cases}
\tag{2.8}\]
where

\(psu_{f,t}\) is the producer subsidy per unit after the phase-out (negative; USD per liter for oil, USD/GJ for coal, gas and biomass);
\(psf_{f,t}\) is the producer subsidy factor of the fuel: the share of the subsidy kept (Equation 2.15; 1 without a reform).

Per block. Each block reads the subsidy of its international-price commodity and converts it to USD/GJ:
\[
ps_{g,f,t} = \frac{psu_{m(f),t} \times (\text{liters per barrel if } f = \text{oop})}{u}
\tag{2.9}\]
where \(m(f)\) is oil for the five oil products, coal, gas, or biomass, and liters per barrel = 158.987. The producer subsidy enters the supply cost (Equation 2.10), so its phase-out raises the supply cost; the floating taxes then absorb \((1 - pcc)\) of the rise, as for any other change in the supply cost (A2.5).
The fiscal cost of producer subsidies after the phase-out, \(-\sum_f pros_f\,psf_f\) (code rpsu), is in the revenue totals (Chapter 7). The electricity producer subsidy is allocated in the power module (Chapter 4). Egypt has no producer subsidy data, so \(ps = 0\).

for f in ['oil', 'coa', 'nga', 'bio']:

        psd[f][t] = {'oil': world[f][t] * 1000 * LitersPerKtoeOil,

                     'nga': (world[f][t] * 1000 + cons[f]) / 2 * GJperKtoe,
                     'bio': cons[f] * GJperKtoe}[f]
        psu[f][t] = -pros[f][t] * 1e6 / psd[f][t] if t <= L else psu[f][L] * psf[f][t]
for block in PRICES:
    for t in years:
        ps[block][t] = psu[commodity[block]][t] * (LitersPerBbl if fuel == 'oop' else 1) / u[block]

title: 2  Energy prices
text:
2.8 Supply cost
After the last historical year the supply cost moves with the international price. Only its floating part moves: the fixed part (margins, production cost) stays, and the producer subsidy is added back at its current level.
\[
sp_{t} = fixsp + \left(sp_{t-1} - fixsp - ps_{t-1}\right)\frac{gp_t}{gp_{t-1}} + ps_t, \qquad t > L
\tag{2.10}\]
where

\(sp_t\) is the supply cost of the block (code sp, USD/GJ real; data up to \(L\), Equation 2.4);
\(fixsp\) is its fixed part (Equation 2.5);
\(gp_t\) is the block’s international reference price (gpi, Equation 2.2);
\(ps_t\) is the producer subsidy of the block (Equation 2.9).

This is the equation list’s M2.1. The methodology writes it as three parts, \(sp = fixsp + fltsp + ps\) with \(fltsp_t = fltsp_{t-1}\,gp_t / gp_{t-1}\) (Appendix C, calculations); the model’s equation is the same with \(fltsp_{t-1} = sp_{t-1} - fixsp - ps_{t-1}\).
Biomass has a flat international price, so its supply cost stays at its value of year \(L\).

title: 2  Energy prices
text:
2.9 Excise and other taxes: pass-through
The excise and other taxes txo are the net of every existing tax and consumer subsidy other than VAT. Their projection carries the price control: the share of a supply-cost change that is not passed through is absorbed by the taxes (or by the subsidy, which then floats). The methodology calls this the floating portion of taxes and subsidies (Appendix C, price liberalization).
Floating taxes. Each year the taxes absorb \((1 - pcc)\) of the change in the supply cost:
\[
\widetilde{txo}_t = \widetilde{txo}_{t-1} - \left(sp_t - sp_{t-1}\right)\left(1 - pcc\right), \qquad \widetilde{txo}_t = txo_t \text{ for } t \le L
\tag{2.11}\]
which adds up to \(\widetilde{txo}_t = txo_L + (sp_L - sp_t)(1 - pcc)\) (M2.2).
Floor on a positive tax. A tax that was positive in year \(L\) does not fall below that level; a subsidy floats freely:
\[
txo_t = \begin{cases} \max\left(txo_L,\ \widetilde{txo}_t\right) & txo_L \ge 0 \\ \widetilde{txo}_t & txo_L < 0 \end{cases}
\tag{2.12}\]
where \(\widetilde{txo}_t\) is the floating value (code txf) and \(txo_t\) the excise and other taxes before new policies (code txo, USD/GJ real; A2.1).
The two extreme cases make the rule clear:

\(pcc = 1\) (liberalised). Supply-cost changes are passed on in full; the taxes stay at \(txo_L\).
\(pcc = 0\) (fixed price). The price before new policies stays at its value of year \(L\); the subsidy (or the tax) absorbs every change in the supply cost. For Egypt’s gas and oil products, a fall in the oil price shrinks the subsidy and a rise widens it.

Here txo holds existing taxes and subsidies only. The methodology’s \(txo\) also holds the existing and new carbon prices and the new excise; the model keeps those apart as wedges (Section 2.12, Section 2.13).






WarningDifferences from legacy CPAT






L14 (fixed). With a pass-through of 0.5 or 0.8, legacy applies \((1 - pcc)\) twice in the first projected year (the floating subsidy is multiplied by \((1 - pcc)\) a second time), so other taxes jump. The model applies it once. No effect for Egypt (pass-through 0 or 1).
Methodology. The methodology averages the fixed and floating portions over five historical years (2018-2022) and multiplies the floating part by the price-control phase-out factor. The model, as legacy, projects from the single year \(L\) and keeps the phase-out as a separate wedge (Section 2.11).

title: 2  Energy prices
section: 2.10 VAT, the price before new policies and existing taxes
text:
2.10 VAT, the price before new policies and existing taxes
VAT is charged on the supply cost plus the other taxes. With it the block reaches its retail price before new policies, the price a consumer would pay if no new policy were introduced.
\[
vat_t = \left(sp_t + txo_t\right) vatrate, \qquad p^{0}_t = \left(sp_t + txo_t\right)\left(1 + vatrate\right)
\tag{2.13}\]
where

\(vat_t\) is the VAT payment before new policies (code vat, USD/GJ real);
\(vatrate\) is the block’s VAT rate (Equation 2.6; code vr in CPAT Python);
\(p^0_t\) is the retail price before new policies (code pbc; M2.3).

Existing taxes and subsidies. The net txo is split by sign, so that taxes and subsidies can be reported and reformed separately. Subsidies are negative throughout the model.

Revenue at these rates (fuel use in PJ × the rate) is in Chapter 7: existing taxes = excise + VAT + the change in existing carbon pricing with its VAT; existing subsidies = the subsidy (negative); net existing = taxes + subsidies.






TipPseudocode: the build-up of a block before new policies



for block in PRICES:
    txf[:L], txo[:L] = txo_hist, txo_hist        # data years
    for t in years after L:
        sp[t] = spf + (sp[t-1] - spf - ps[t-1]) * gpi[t] / gpi[t-1] + ps[t]
        txf[t] = txf[t-1] - (sp[t] - sp[t-1]) * (1 - pcc)
        txo[t] = max(txo[L], txf[t]) if txo[L] >= 0 else txf[t]
    for t in years:
        fadtx[t] = pcc * (txo[t] if t <= L else txo[L])
        cs[t] = txo[t] - fadtx[t]
        etx[t], esub[t] = max(txo[t], 0), min(txo[t], 0)
        esubpu[t] = esub[t] * u
        vat[t] = (sp[t] + txo[t]) * vr
        pbc[t] = (sp[t] + txo[t]) * (1 + vr)

title: 2  Energy prices
text:
2.11 Subsidy and price-control phase-outs
Two reforms remove the existing consumer support. The consumer subsidy reform removes the fixed subsidy; the price-control phase-out (price liberalisation) removes the floating part, so the consumer comes to pay the supply-cost changes. Both are separate policy lines, by price block: the price before new policies pbc is not changed, and the reforms are wedges added to the after-tax price like the new policies. The methodology describes them in Appendix C, fossil fuel subsidies reform and price liberalization.

2.11.1 Phase-out factors
There is one factor per reform \(k\): producer subsidies (ps), consumer subsidies (cs) and price controls (pc). Each is the share of the original support still kept, the same in every year for every line:
\[
pof_{k,t} = \begin{cases} \max\!\left(1 - \bar{s}_k,\ 1 - \bar{s}_k\,\dfrac{t - T_k}{\max(N_k, 1)}\right) & \text{the reform is on and } t > T_k \\[2mm] 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{2.14}\]
where

\(pof_{k,t}\) is the phase-out factor (code pof; M1.7);
\(\bar{s}_k\) is the share to phase out (po.sh), \(T_k\) the start year and \(N_k\) the period in years (po.n).

The inputs come from ScenarioDefinition. Scenario 1 reads the baseline switch, period and share; the other scenarios read the policy switch and period, with the share the larger of the baseline and the policy share (legacy rows 264-274). The price-control phase-out applies only if its policy switch is on and either the scenario is a policy scenario or its baseline switch is on. It uses the consumer-subsidy shares (issue I48) and the same period in every scenario. A switch counts as on if it is TRUE or starts with “Yes”.



Table 2.5: Phase-out inputs (ScenarioDefinition rows 123-137 and 191-195)

Which blocks and fuels a reform covers. Inclusion switches on ScenarioDefinition, per scenario, let a reform cover some fuels and sectors only: ConsSubPhaseScope_<block> (\(csi\)) and PriceCtrlPhaseScope_<block> (\(pci\)) for the 12 price blocks, and ProdSubPhaseScope_<fuel> (\(psi\)) for coal, gas, oil, biomass and electricity. Each turns the reform factor into the factor of its line:
\[
csf = 1 - csi\,(1 - pof_{cs}), \qquad pcf = 1 - pci\,(1 - pof_{pc}), \qquad psf_f = 1 - psi_f\,(1 - pof_{ps})
\tag{2.15}\]


2.11.2 The wedges
Each block splits its taxes into the fixed part fadtx and the floating part cs (Section 2.10). The consumer subsidy reform removes the share \((1 - csf)\) of a fixed subsidy; the price-control phase-out removes the share \((1 - pcf)\) of the floating part, whether that is a subsidy or a tax:
\[
pcsw_t = -\left(1 - csf_t\right)\min\left(fadtx_t,\ 0\right), \qquad
ppcw_t = -\left(1 - pcf_t\right) cs_t
\tag{2.16}\]
where

\(pcsw_t\) is the consumer subsidy reform wedge of the block (USD/GJ, before VAT);
\(ppcw_t\) is the price-control phase-out wedge of the block (USD/GJ, before VAT).

Because the two wedges act on different parts of txo, using both reforms does not count a subsidy twice. For Egypt every subsidised fuel has pass-through 0, so its whole subsidy floats: only the price-control phase-out removes it, as in legacy.
Every subsector reads the wedges of its block as csw and pcw and adds them, with VAT, to its after-tax price (Equation 2.24). The revenue of the reforms, \(F\,\theta\,(csw + pcw)(1 + vatrate)\) (code rsr: the subsidy saved plus the VAT on it), and the producer-subsidy line rpsu are in Chapter 7; the net existing revenue rnet stays the pre-reform one.






TipPseudocode: phase-outs and wedges



for k in ['ps', 'cs', 'pc']:
    on, start, period, share = phaseout_inputs(k, scenario)    # baseline or policy columns
    for t in years:
        pof[k][t] = max(1 - share, 1 - share * (t - start) / max(period, 1)) if on and t > start else 1
for block in PRICES:
    for t in years:
        csf[block][t] = 1 - csi[block] * (1 - pof['cs'][t])
        pcf[block][t] = 1 - pci[block] * (1 - pof['pc'][t])
        pcsw[block][t] = -(1 - csf[block][t]) * min(fadtx[block][t], 0)
        ppcw[block][t] = -(1 - pcf[block][t]) * cs[block][t]
for f in ['coa', 'nga', 'oil', 'bio', 'ecy']:
    for t in years:
        psf[f][t] = 1 - psi[f] * (1 - pof['ps'][t])
