title: 2  Energy prices
text:
2.12 Existing carbon pricing
Some countries already price carbon, with a carbon tax, a national ETS or the EU ETS. The IMF retail prices already contain whatever existing carbon pricing a country had, so the model adds only the change against that level: growth after the last data year, new data, or a scheme switched off. A country’s history is never counted twice. The methodology describes existing carbon pricing in section 3.2.4 and Appendix C, policy options.

2.12.1 Data and tables
The data are the World Bank Carbon Pricing Dashboard and ICAP data of sheet ECP (as of 1 April 2025; 52 countries; Egypt has none), read at their legacy addresses. Each code is looked up in its own legacy block (sheet Inputs_ecp, columns K:L give each block’s first and last row):








Scheme
Codes
Legacy rows of sheet ECP




Carbon tax
single rate ecr.all, fuel rates ecr.<fuel>, sector coverage ecs.<sector>, fuel coverage ecf.<fuel>
69-559


National ETS
price eer.all, coverage ees.<sector>, eef.<fuel>
600-615, 619-737, 1040-1093


EU ETS (regional)
the EU price (row 616), the country’s regional coverage
738-1036, 1094-1223




Prices are made real with the CPI index of the data year.
Coverage is that of each data year (2021-2025; blank = 0, as legacy); the last data year holds after it.
The carbon tax rate of a fuel is the fuel rate where the country has one and no “single price” flag (general information, column E); otherwise the single rate (legacy rows 1752-1764).
The EU ETS counts where the country’s “EU ETS?” flag (general information, column K) is Yes or Both (legacy row 1695).

From these the model builds two tables by ECP sector \(j\) (power, transport, buildings, industry), fuel \(f\) and data year \(y\), in USD/tCO2:
\[
XT_{j,f,y} = rate_{f,y}\;scov_{j,y}\;fcov_{f,y}, \qquad
XE_{j,f,y} = p^{nat}_y\;ncov_{j,y}\;nfcov_{f,y} + p^{EU}_y\;rcov_{j,y}\;rfcov_{f,y}
\tag{2.17}\]
where \(XT\) is the existing carbon tax and \(XE\) the existing ETS price of the sector and fuel. The national and the EU schemes add up, as legacy. Existing coverage is fractional; coverage of the new policies is a yes/no switch.
ECP sector of a price. Coal and gas take their price sector (power, residential, industry); the oil products, biomass and jet fuel take transport; other oil products take industry; power takes power.


2.12.2 Factors, level and change
ScenarioDefinition decides, per scenario, whether each scheme applies and how its real price grows after the last data year \(T_x\) (2025):
\[
\varphi^{ct}_t = \mathbb{1}[\texttt{ExistingCTApply}]\,(1 + \gamma^{ct})^{\max(0,\,t - T_x)}, \qquad
\varphi^{ets}_t = \mathbb{1}[\texttt{ExistingETSApply}]\,(1 + \gamma^{ets})^{\max(0,\,t - T_x)}
\tag{2.18}\]
where \(\gamma^{ct}\) is ExistingCTGrowth and \(\gamma^{ets}\) is ExistingETSGrowth (real growth per year; codes xct.p, xets.p).
Then, per subsector and fuel:
\[
xcp_{s,f,t} = ef_{s,f}\left(XT_{j,f,t^*}\,\varphi^{ct}_t + XE_{j,f,t^*}\,\varphi^{ets}_t\right), \qquad
\Delta xcp_{s,f,t} = xcp_{s,f,t} - ef_{s,f}\,XCP^{0}_{j,f}
\tag{2.19}\]
where

\(xcp_{s,f,t}\) is the level of existing carbon pricing (code xcp, USD/GJ);
\(\Delta xcp_{s,f,t}\) is its change against the price data (code xcpd, USD/GJ; A2.2);
\(ef_{s,f}\) is the calibrated CO2 emission factor (tCO2/GJ; Chapter 6);
\(t^* = \min(t, T_x)\) is the data column of the year (code xct.c), \(j = j(s,f)\) the ECP sector;
\(XCP^0_{j,f} = XT_{j,f,y_e} + XE_{j,f,y_e}\) is the existing carbon pricing embedded in the price data, the tables in the year \(y_e = \min(L, T_x)\) (2024).

Only \(\Delta xcp\) enters the after-tax price (Equation 2.24). Switching a scheme off therefore lowers the price by its embedded level; growth or new data raise it.
Power. The same change per kWh (the power row of the tables) is part of the variable cost before new policies, so dispatch, investment and electricity prices respond (Chapter 4).
New carbon tax beside an existing ETS. If CTaxComplimentaryToETS = Yes (legacy rows 2270-2288), the new carbon tax of a sector covers 1 − the national ETS sector coverage of the year (Chapter 1). Otherwise new instruments add to existing ones.
Revenue. The existing-tax revenue includes \(\Delta xcp\,(1 + vatrate)\); a memo shows the level, fuel use × \(xcp\). Existing ETS revenue is valued at the full permit price, as legacy; legacy’s free-allocation and revenue data (ECP rows 560-597, 1225-1322) are not used, in legacy’s model either (Chapter 7).

    xets_p[t] = (1 + ExistingETSGrowth) ** max(0, t - Tx) if ExistingETSApply == 'Yes' else 0

            xcpd[s, f, t] = ef[s, f] * (level - xcp0)

title: 2  Energy prices
section: 2.13 New policies and the after-tax price
text:
2.13 New policies and the after-tax price
The new policies of a scenario act per subsector and fuel, because coverage, exemptions and emission factors differ by subsector. Each policy is turned into a cost per GJ and added, with VAT, to the price before new policies of the subsector’s block. The result is the after-tax price, the price that drives fuel use. The methodology describes the new carbon price and the new excise in section 3.2.4 and in Appendix C, policy coverage and exemptions.

2.13.1 New carbon tax, ETS cost and excise per GJ
\[
nct_{s,f} = NCT_s\;ef_{s,f}\;\varphi_{NCT,f}\;x_{s,f}, \qquad
netsp_{s,f} = NETSP_s\;ef_{s,f}\;x_{s,f}, \qquad
nexc_{s,f} = \frac{F^{x}_{c(s,f)}}{u_f}\;x_{s,f}
\tag{2.20}\]
where

\(nct_{s,f}\), \(netsp_{s,f}\), \(nexc_{s,f}\) are the new carbon tax, the new ETS cost and the new excise (codes ctxnew, ets, ntx; USD/GJ; M2.4);
\(NCT_s\) is the new carbon tax rate of the sector (USD/tCO2; code ctr): the explicit carbon price where the sector is covered and not in a new ETS (Chapter 1);
\(NETSP_s\) is the ETS cost in the price of the sector (code etr): the tax-equivalent permit price × ETS coverage × the auctioned share (Chapter 6);
\(ef_{s,f}\) is the calibrated CO2 emission factor (tCO2/GJ);
\(\varphi_{NCT,f}\) is the carbon-tax coverage of the fuel (code ctcov: 1 if covered, else the exemption phase-out path; biomass is covered with emission factor 0);
\(F^x_c\) is the new excise of the price fuel \(c(s,f)\) in price units (code ntxb; Equation 2.21), and \(u_f\) GJ per price unit of the fuel row;
\(x_{s,f}\) is the exemption factor (code exf, below).

The new excise. The fuel price reform path fpr (Chapter 1, M1.5) is set per price fuel in price units (USD/liter, USD/bbl, USD/GJ). It acts only in the policy scenarios:
\[
F^x_{c,t} = \mathbb{1}[o \ne B]\;ntxg_{c,t}, \qquad ntxg_{c,t} = fpr_{c,t} + \mathbb{1}[\texttt{AddEfficientTaxes}]\;pigx_{c,t}
\tag{2.21}\]
where \(ntxg\) is the gross new excise (code ntxg) and \(pigx\) the Pigouvian tax (Section 2.15; with AddEfficientTaxes = Yes the formula of \(F^x\) changes, Equation 2.31). Jet fuel reads the kerosene reform per liter and divides it by its own GJ per liter.
Total new policy:
\[
nce_{s,f} = nct_{s,f} + netsp_{s,f} + nexc_{s,f}
\tag{2.22}\]
Residential LPG and kerosene always exempted. ScenarioDefinition AlwaysExemptResLPGKer (row 268, by scenario; default No) exempts these two rows from every new policy. If the switch starts with “Yes” (Yes or Yes), the exemption factor of the residential LPG and kerosene rows is 0; every other row has factor 1:
\[
x_{s,f} = \begin{cases} 0 & f \in \{\text{LPG, kerosene}\},\ s = \text{residential},\ \texttt{AlwaysExemptResLPGKer} \text{ starts with "Yes"} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{2.23}\]
Their new carbon tax, ETS cost and new excise are then 0, so neither is the VAT on them, nor their new-policy revenue (rnew, the excise revenue rex and the VAT on new policies in rvt). Existing taxes, the change in existing carbon pricing and the subsidy phase-outs stay, as legacy (row 2651, the price before new policies). The shadow price is not exempted, as legacy. ETS-covered emissions still count them where the residential sector is in an ETS (Chapter 6), and the residential leakage to biomass reads the row’s own nce, so an exempt fuel does not leak (Chapter 3).


2.13.2 The after-tax price
\[
p_{s,f} = \max\!\Big(p^{0}_{g,f} + \big(nce_{s,f} + \Delta xcp_{s,f} + csw_{s,f} + pcw_{s,f}\big)\left(1 + vatrate_{g,f}\right),\ \underline{p}\Big)
\tag{2.24}\]
where

\(p_{s,f}\) is the after-tax price of fuel \(f\) in subsector \(s\) (code atp, USD/GJ real; M2.5);
\(g\) is the price sector of \((s,f)\), so \(p^0_{g,f}\) is the price before new policies of the block (Equation 2.13) and \(vatrate_{g,f}\) its VAT rate;
\(\Delta xcp_{s,f}\) is the change in existing carbon pricing (Equation 2.19);
\(csw_{s,f}\), \(pcw_{s,f}\) are the subsidy and price-control wedges of the block (Equation 2.16);
\(\underline{p}\) is the price floor (PriceFloor, 0.01 USD/GJ, legacy’s).

New policies are passed through in full and pay VAT, as legacy’s VAT on txo with nce inside it. With the exemption, the residential LPG and kerosene price is \(\max(p^0 + (\Delta xcp + csw + pcw)(1 + vatrate), \underline{p})\).






TipPseudocode: new policies and the after-tax price



for c in price_fuels_14:                         # 12 blocks + ecy.res, ecy.ind
    for t in years:
        ntxg[c][t] = fpr[c][t] + (pigx[c][t] if AddEfficientTaxes == 'Yes' else 0)
        ntxb[c][t] = ntxg[c][t] if scenario > 1 else 0          # (Pigouvian netting: see below)
for s in subsectors:
    for f in fuels:
        block = price_block(s, f)                # e.g. ('nga', 'res') for road gas
        x = exf['res'] if (s, f) in [('res', 'lpg'), ('res', 'ker')] else exf['all']
        for t in years:
            ctxnew[s, f, t] = ctr[s][t] * ef[s, f] * ctcov[f][t] * x
            ets[s, f, t] = etr[s][t] * ef[s, f] * x
            ntx[s, f, t] = ntxb[price_fuel(s, f)][t] / u[f] * x
            nce[s, f, t] = ctxnew[s, f, t] + ets[s, f, t] + ntx[s, f, t]
            csw[s, f, t], pcw[s, f, t] = pcsw[block][t], ppcw[block][t]
            atp[s, f, t] = max(pbc[block][t]
                               + (nce[s, f, t] + xcpd[s, f, t] + csw[s, f, t] + pcw[s, f, t]) * (1 + vr[block]),
                               PriceFloor)
            shp[s, f, t] = shpx[s][t] * ef[s, f]

WarningDifferences from legacy CPAT

title: 2  Energy prices
text:
2.14 The shadow price
Some policies change behaviour without changing what consumers pay: feebates, efficiency regulations and the part of a new ETS that is allocated free. The model represents them as a shadow price per GJ. Demand responds to it on the efficiency margin only, and it raises no revenue.
\[
sh_{s,f} = \Sigma_s\;ef_{s,f}
\tag{2.25}\]
where

\(sh_{s,f}\) is the shadow price per GJ (code shp; M2.6);
\(\Sigma_s\) is the shadow price of sector \(s\) per tonne (code shpx; M1.4): the feebate rate × the share of the feebate on the efficiency margin, plus the shadow price of regulations, plus the tax-equivalent ETS price × ETS coverage × the share allocated free (Chapter 1).

The demand equation uses the after-tax price twice: alone in the usage term, and with the shadow price in the efficiency term, \(\big((p + sh)_t / (p + sh)_{t-1}\big)^{\varepsilon_F (1 + \varepsilon_U)}\) (Chapter 3). The shadow price is not exempted by AlwaysExemptResLPGKer, as legacy.






NoteIn Excel-AI and CPAT Python

CPAT Python: policies.py (shpx), fuel_use.py, prepare() (shp).

title: 2  Energy prices
text:
2.15 Pigouvian components
The model can compute an efficient (Pigouvian) tax per price unit: the cost of the local air pollution, the climate damage and the road-transport externalities of one more unit of the fuel. Here they are prices; their welfare use and the efficient prices of the subsidy estimates are in Chapter 7. The methodology describes the external costs in section 3.7.2.
The components are computed in every run; they enter prices only if ScenarioDefinition AddEfficientTaxes = Yes, which CPAT Python does not support yet (Section 2.17). All are by price code \(c\) (the 12 blocks and the two electricity rows) in USD per price unit (A1.2).

2.15.1 Phase-in
\[
\phi_t = \min\!\left(\frac{\max(t - T_0 + 1,\ 0)}{\max(n,\ 1)},\ 1\right)
\tag{2.26}\]
where \(\phi_t\) is the phase-in share (code pig.phi), \(T_0\) the carbon-pricing start year (CPIntro) and \(n\) AddEfficientTaxesPhaseInYears.


2.15.2 Air pollution
The marginal damage of air pollution per GJ of fuel \(f\) in subsector \(s\) is the value of averted PM2.5 times the PM2.5 concentration one GJ adds:
\[
mc^{ap}_{s,f,t} = v_t\;\Big[(1 - w_t)\,d^{(0)}_{s,f} + w_t\,d^{(1)}_{s,f}\Big]\;\frac{10^9}{\theta \cdot 10^6}
\tag{2.27}\]
where

\(mc^{ap}_{s,f,t}\) is the marginal air-pollution damage (code airpol.mc, USD/GJ; power: by plant type);
\(v_t\) is the value of averted modelled ambient PM2.5 (code pig.vpm, USD billion per µg/m³, from the air pollution module, typed FromAirPollution; the base year reads the next year, because legacy has no change in PM2.5 in 2022);
\(d^{(0)}\), \(d^{(1)}\) are the µg/m³ per ktoe of the fuel: the module’s concentration coefficients \(\kappa\) of the source (road, ground level for residential, services and construction, food, other; coal, gas and other power plants) times the combustion emission factors of each pollutant, with base-year and final (EFEndYear, 2039) factors;
\(w_t\) is the weight of the final factors (code pig.efw): EFFinShare × \((t - t_0)/(\text{EFEndYear} - t_0)\), with EFFinShare 0 for constant factors, 1 for variable and 0.5 otherwise;
\(\theta\) is PJ per ktoe.

By price code (code pig.ap), the subsector damages are averaged with base-year fuel use as weights (the plain average where all weights are 0) and converted to price units:








Price code
Average over
Notes




coa.pow, nga.pow

coa.res

nga.res

gso.all, die.all, lpg.all, ker.all

× GJ per liter

× GJ per barrel (L194 fixed)

2.15.3 Climate
\[
cc_{c,t} = SCC^{nat}_t\;\overline{ef}_{f(c)}\;u_c
\tag{2.28}\]
where \(cc_{c,t}\) is the climate damage per price unit (code cc.code), \(SCC^{nat}_t\) the national social cost of carbon (M1.6) and \(\overline{ef}_f\) the generic, uncalibrated CO2 factor of the fuel (averaged over its emission-factor sectors; IEA for other oil products; issue I116).


2.15.4 Road transport
Accidents, congestion and road damage are costs per vehicle-km. The model turns them into costs per liter with the base-year kilometres driven per liter of the fuel’s total use, then lets them grow with the cost per km:
\[
tr_{c,t} = \sum_{k} cost^{km}_{k,t_0}\;kpl_f\;\big(1 - \omega_f\big)^{[k = rdm]}\;\frac{cost^{km}_{k,t}}{cost^{km}_{k,t_0}}, \qquad kpl_f = \overline{fe}_f\;\mu_f\;\rho_f
\tag{2.29}\]
where

\(tr_{c,t}\) is the road-transport cost per liter (code pig.tr; gasoline: accidents and congestion; diesel: also road damage, for the freight share only, issue I118; 0 for the other price codes);
\(cost^{km}_{k,t}\) is the cost per vehicle-km of kind \(k\) (accidents, congestion, road damage) from the transport co-benefits module (typed FromTransportCB); the ratio is the growth against the base year (codes pig.trg.*); the products \(cost^{km}_{k,t_0}\,kpl_f\) are the base-year costs per liter (codes pig.trb.*);
\(\overline{fe}_f\) is the base-year fuel economy (code pig.fe0, km/liter): passenger and light vehicles weighted by ownership, then mixed with 2-3 wheelers (gasoline) or freight (diesel) by the share \(\omega_f\);
\(\omega_f\) is the passenger and light share of the road use of the fuel (code pig.wsh): gasoline 1 − the cycle share; diesel 1 − freight / (1 − bus);
\(\mu_f\) is the driving share of the fuel’s response (code pig.mu0): gasoline \(\varepsilon_U / (\varepsilon_U + \varepsilon_F)\); diesel \((\varepsilon^{die}_U + \omega(\varepsilon^{gso}_U - \varepsilon^{die}_U)) / (\varepsilon^{die}_U + \varepsilon^{die}_F + \omega(\varepsilon^{gso}_U + \varepsilon^{gso}_F - \varepsilon^{die}_U - \varepsilon^{die}_F))\);
\(\rho_f\) is the base-year road share of the fuel’s use over all subsectors (code pig.rsh0).



2.15.5 The Pigouvian tax and its netting
\[
pigx_{c,t} = \phi_t\left(ap_{c,t} + \mathbb{1}[\texttt{ClimateEffTax}]\;cc_{c,t} + tr_{c,t}\right)
\tag{2.30}\]
where \(ap_{c,t}\) is the air-pollution cost per price unit (pig.ap). With AddEfficientTaxes = Yes the gross new excise \(ntxg = fpr + pigx\) (Equation 2.21) is netted against the existing taxes, so the Pigouvian tax tops up what is already there:
\[
F^x_{c,t} = \mathbb{1}[o \ne B]\;\min\!\Big(ntxg_{c,t},\ \max\big(0,\ ntxg_{c,t} - xpre_{c,t}\,u_c\big)\Big), \qquad
xpre_{c,t} = txo_{c,t} + pcsw_{c,t} + ppcw_{c,t} + xcpb_{c,t}
\tag{2.31}\]
where

\(xpre_{c,t}\) is the existing taxes before new policy of the block (code xpre, USD/GJ; 0 for electricity);
\(xcpb_{c,t} = \overline{ef}_f\,(XT\,\varphi^{ct}_t + XE\,\varphi^{ets}_t - XCP^0)\) is the change in existing carbon pricing of the block, at the generic emission factor and the block’s own ECP sector and fuel (code xcpb; 0 for electricity).

The block’s ECP key for xcpb: coal and gas by price sector; gasoline and diesel transport; LPG, kerosene and biomass buildings; other oil products industry.






TipPseudocode: Pigouvian components



for t in years:
    phi[t] = min(max(t - CPIntro + 1, 0) / max(PhaseInYears, 1), 1)
    w[t] = EFFinShare * (t - t0) / (EFEndYear - t0)
    vpm = air_vpm[max(t, t0 + 1)]
    for (s, f) in airpol_rows:
        mc[s, f, t] = vpm * ((1 - w[t]) * d0[s, f] + w[t] * d1[s, f]) * 1e9 / PJperKtoe / 1e6
for c in price_codes_14:
    for t in years:
        ap = weighted_average(mc[rows_of(c), t], weights=ener0) * u[c]     # table above
        cc = scc_nat[t] * ef_generic[fuel(c)] * u[c]
        tr = sum(trb[k, fuel(c)] * trg[k][t] for k in kinds(c))            # gso, die only
        pigx[c][t] = phi[t] * (ap + (cc if ClimateEffTax == 'Yes' else 0) + tr)
        xcpb[c][t] = ef_generic[fuel(c)] * (XT[c][col] * xct_p[t] + XE[c][col] * xets_p[t] - XCP0[c])
        xpre[c][t] = txo[c][t] + pcsw[c][t] + ppcw[c][t] + xcpb[c][t]
        ntxg[c][t] = fpr[c][t] + (pigx[c][t] if AddEfficientTaxes == 'Yes' else 0)
        if AddEfficientTaxes == 'Yes':
            ntxb[c][t] = min(ntxg[c][t], max(0, ntxg[c][t] - xpre[c][t] * u[c]))
        else:
            ntxb[c][t] = ntxg[c][t]
        ntxb[c][t] *= (scenario > 1)

WarningDifferences from legacy CPAT






I104 (departs, user decision). Legacy’s air-pollution unit costs are average damages; the model uses marginal damages from the module’s concentration coefficients.
I113 (replicated). The Pigouvian tax tops up existing taxes, and the climate component can be charged on top of a carbon tax (climate charged twice), as legacy (legacy rows 8782, 8805, … 9012).
I116 (replicated). Climate damage per unit is the national SCC × a generic emission factor.
I118, I119 (replicated). Road damage only for diesel; the electricity Pigouvian tax is always 0.

L195, L196 (fixed). Legacy has no phase-in in 2022-2024 and divides by 0 when the phase-in years are 0; one formula now holds in every year with \(\max(n, 1)\).

title: 2  Energy prices
text:
2.16 Average prices and price indices
Prices differ by subsector, so a single price per fuel needs weights. The model reports two kinds of averages: the average new-policy wedges of each price block, and average prices and price indices by fuel. Both are computed in the year loop, because they read fuel use. The methodology’s aggregate price is the fuel-use weighted average (section 3.2.5).

2.16.1 New policies by price block
Over the subsectors \(s \in c\) priced by block \(c\), weighted by their fuel use \(F_{s,f}\) (ktoe):
\[
\bar{p}_c = \frac{\sum_{s \in c} p_{s,f}\,F_{s,f}}{\sum_{s \in c} F_{s,f}}
\tag{2.32}\]
where \(\bar{p}_c\) is the retail price including new taxes and subsidies of the block (code rpn; \(p^0_c\) where the subsectors use none; A2.6). The block also shows:







Code
Meaning




pnq
\(\sum_{s \in c} F_{s,f}\), the weights (ktoe)


pctx, etsnew, pntx, pxcd
fuel-use weighted averages of ctxnew, ets, ntx, xcpd


pnce
\(\bar{p}_c - p^0_c\), the total new policy including VAT


pvatn
pnce − (pctx + etsnew + pntx + pxcd + pcsw + ppcw): the VAT on the new policies and wedges, and the effect of the price floor



These are weighted averages with each scenario’s own quantities, not price indices.


2.16.2 Average prices and indices by fuel
For each fuel (coal, gas, gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene, jet fuel, other oil products, biomass), for electricity and for all energy, the model sums over the 16 subsectors (electricity: the residential and industry user groups). Subscript 1 is scenario 1 in the same year; subscript 0 is the base year, whose quantities and prices are data and so equal in every scenario.



Table 2.6: Average prices and price indices by fuel










Code
Formula
Meaning




pav.sp
\(\sum_s p\,F\)
spending, own quantities


pav.q
\(\sum_s F\)
fuel use


pav.uv
\(\sum p\,F / \sum F\)
average price (unit value)


pav.spr
\(\sum_s p\,F_1\)
spending at scenario-1 quantities


pav.las
\(\sum p\,F_1 / \sum p_1 F_1\)
price index against scenario 1 (Laspeyres; scenario 1 = 1)


pav.sp0
\(\sum_s p\,F_0\)
spending at base-year quantities


pav.time
\(\sum p\,F_0 / \sum p_0 F_0\)
price index over time (base year = 1)


pav.mix
\((uv / uv_1) / las\)
mix effect: what the unit-value ratio adds to the price index


pav.leg
below
average price as legacy


pav.lidx
\(leg / leg_1\)
legacy average price against scenario 1 (pav.las for fuels without a legacy average)


pav.idx
Settings AveragePriceMethod
price index reported (MTOutputs mit.pav.idx): Legacy* = pav.lidx (default), Laspeyres = pav.las


rpe
pav.uv of all energy
average retail energy price






The unit-value ratio against scenario 1 equals the price index times the mix effect. Legacy reports the unit-value ratio as the price change (issue I31); here the two parts are separate.
\[
\frac{uv}{uv_1} = las \times mix, \qquad las = \frac{\sum_s p_s\,F_{1,s}}{\sum_s p_{1,s}\,F_{1,s}}, \qquad time = \frac{\sum_s p_s\,F_{0,s}}{\sum_s p_{0,s}\,F_{0,s}}
\tag{2.33}\]
Units. Fuels: USD/GJ × ktoe for spending, USD/GJ for the unit value. Electricity: USD/kWh and GWh. All energy: spending in USD million (fuel spending × PJ per ktoe, plus electricity spending USD/kWh × GWh), fuel use in ktoe with electricity converted (GWh × GJ per kWh / PJ per ktoe), so its unit value is in USD million per ktoe.
The legacy average (pav.leg, legacy rows 16293-16405):

Coal and gas average three sector prices with scenario-1 quantities of the same year: residential rpn (weight: scenario-1 residential subsector use, pavl.qr), industry rpn (the 8 industry subsectors, pavl.qi), and power (weight: scenario-1 power generation fuel use, pavl.qp). The power price is the pre-policy price plus the policy cost per GJ of the power type: \(pp = p^0_{pow} + G \cdot M \cdot pc / (FU \cdot \theta)\) (code pavl.pp; \(G\) generation in MWy, \(M\) million kWh per MWy, \(pc\) the new policy cost per kWh xac, \(FU\) the power fuel use). This is a Laspeyres index on three sectors; it falls back to the unit value where the weights are 0.
Oil products take the single price rpn of their .all block.
Electricity averages residential and industry with each scenario’s own consumption (= pav.uv).
Biomass, jet fuel and all energy have no legacy average: their unit value, and their reported index is the Laspeyres one.







TipPseudocode: averages (year loop, year t)



for c in PRICES:
    rows = [(s, f) for (s, f) in fuel_rows if price_block(s, f) == c]
    pnq[c] = sum(ener[s, f] for (s, f) in rows)
    wavg = lambda v: sum(v[s, f] * ener[s, f] for (s, f) in rows) / pnq[c] if pnq[c] else 0

    pvatn[c] = pnce[c] - (pctx[c] + etsnew[c] + pntx[c] + pxcd[c] + pcsw[c] + ppcw[c])
for f in PAV_FUELS:                               # coa, nga, gso, die, lpg, ker, jfu, oop, bio
    sp  = sum(atp[s, f] * ener[s, f] for s in subsectors)
    q   = sum(ener[s, f] for s in subsectors)

    sp0 = sum(atp[s, f] * ener_base_year[s, f] for s in subsectors)
    uv = sp / q;  las = spr / sp_scen1[f];  time = sp0 / sp_base_year[f]
    mix = (uv / uv_scen1[f]) / las
    leg = legacy_average(f)                       # coal, gas: res, ind, power at scenario-1 quantities
    lidx = leg / leg_scen1[f]
    idx = lidx if AveragePriceMethod.startswith('Leg') else las

title: 3  Energy demand
text:
3.1 Overview
This chapter explains how the model projects the use of each fuel in each sector of the economy, year by year. Fuel use is the quantity at the heart of the model: emissions, revenues, the GDP effect and the household effects are all fuel use multiplied by something else.
The core is one behavioural equation, the same for every sector and fuel: last year’s use grows with GDP, shrinks with autonomous efficiency gains, and responds to the after-tax price through two margins, how much the equipment is used and how efficient it is. A handful of special cases sit around it: biofuels blended into road fuels, renewables used outside the power sector, a possible shift of households from modern cooking fuels to biomass, and cooking fuel that is initially exempt from price increases.
The chapter also computes electricity demand by sector, which it hands to the power model (Chapter 4), and it closes with the energy totals by sector group and fuel and their change against the baseline.
The methodology describes this block in methodology, section 3.3. The prices that drive it are built in Chapter 2; road fuel use under the engineer model is in Chapter 5; the GDP growth that feeds the income term comes from Chapter 7.
Indices. Every equation holds for each scenario \(o\) and country \(c\), which are omitted. Sector (subsector) \(s\), fuel \(f\), sector group \(g\) and year \(t\) are shown where they matter; electricity demand uses the demand group \(d\). A value of the baseline (scenario 1) in the same year carries the superscript \(B\).
The model distinguishes 16 sectors (Excel-AI calls them subsectors) in four groups, and 9 fuels. Power generation is a fifth group whose fuel input comes from Chapter 4. The tables below give, for each sector and fuel, the keys that the fuel-use equation reads: which row of the elasticity table applies, which additional efficiency input applies, and which electricity demand group the sector belongs to.
Two more “fuels” appear outside this grid: renewables used directly in aviation and navigation (Section 3.3), and electricity, whose demand by sector is computed here but which is supplied by the power model (Section 3.7).
Within one year the block runs in a fixed order. GDP growth is known first, because the GDP effect of a policy enters one year later; electricity demand reads last year’s power price; fuel use reads this year’s after-tax prices, which were computed for all years before the year loop.

title: 3  Energy demand
text:
3.2 The fuel-use equation
Each year, fuel use in a sector is last year’s use multiplied by five growth factors. This is the constant-elasticity form of the methodology (methodology, section 3.3.3), with three additions: the shadow price of non-pricing policies acts on the efficiency margin only, an additional policy-induced efficiency gain joins the autonomous one, and the income elasticity is adjusted to the country’s income level.
In full (M3.1):
\[
\frac{F^{e}_{s,f,t}}{F^{e}_{s,f,t-1}} =
\left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha_{s,f} + \alpha^{+}_{g(s)}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U}}
\;\Psi_t\;
\left(1 + g_t\right)^{\epsilon_{Y}\, inc_t}
\left(\frac{p_{s,f,t}}{p_{s,f,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U}}
\left(\frac{p_{s,f,t} + sh_{s,f,t}}{p_{s,f,t-1} + sh_{s,f,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{F}(1 + \epsilon_{U})}
\tag{3.1}\]
where

\(F^{e}_{s,f,t}\) is fuel use by the elasticity model (ktoe; code enel); in the base year \(t_0\) it is the base-year use of the energy data (Section 3.2.6);
\(\epsilon_Y\), \(\epsilon_U\), \(\epsilon_F\) are the income, usage and efficiency elasticities of the fuel in the sector (they depend on the country, the fuel and the sector; the indices are dropped);
\(\alpha_{s,f}\) is the autonomous energy efficiency improvement (share per year) and \(\alpha^{+}_{g(s)}\) the additional policy-induced efficiency gain of the sector’s efficiency group (Section 3.2.1);
\(\Psi_t\) is the exogenous demand shock factor (Section 3.2.5);
\(g_t\) is real GDP growth after the GDP feedback and \(inc_t\) the income-level factor on the GDP elasticities (Section 3.2.2);
\(p_{s,f,t}\) is the after-tax price of the fuel in the sector (USD per GJ, real; code atp) and \(sh_{s,f,t}\) the shadow price of non-pricing policies (USD per GJ; code shp), both from Chapter 2 (Section 3.2.4).

The methodology writes the GDP term as \((Y_t / Y_{t-1})^{\epsilon_Y}\), total real GDP (not per capita). The model writes the same ratio as \(1 + g_t\).
The equation is easier to read as a product of named factors. Each is one idea:
\[
F^{e}_{s,f,t} = F^{e}_{s,f,t-1} \cdot A_{s,f} \cdot \Psi_t \cdot G_{s,f,t} \cdot U_{s,f,t} \cdot E_{s,f,t}
\tag{3.2}\]

The methodology assumes that all effects take place within the year: the elasticities are long-term elasticities applied in one step. CPAT is therefore better suited to anticipated and progressively phased policies over the medium term than to sudden shocks.

3.2.1 Autonomous and additional efficiency
Equipment becomes more efficient over time even without new policies. The autonomous energy efficiency improvement \(\alpha\) captures this; the methodology sets it between 0.5% and 1% per year depending on the fuel and sector (methodology, section 3.3.5.6).
A scenario can add a policy-induced gain \(\alpha^{+}\) for three groups of sectors:
\[
A_{s,f} = \left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha_{s,f} + \alpha^{+}_{g(s)}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U}}
\tag{3.3}\]
where

\(\alpha_{s,f}\) is the autonomous efficiency gain of the sector’s elasticity sector and the fuel’s autonomous efficiency fuel (Table 3.1, Table 3.2); gasoline and diesel take the oil value;
\(\alpha^{+}_{g(s)}\) is the scenario input of the sector’s additional efficiency group (share per year, default 0).

The exponent \(1 + \epsilon_U\) (with \(\epsilon_U < 0\)) is the rebound: more efficient equipment makes each unit of service cheaper, so part of the saving is used up by more use. The methodology puts this rebound from exogenous efficiency between 20% and 60% across fuels and sectors.


3.2.2 Income term, income-level adjustment and GDP feedback
Energy demand grows with the economy. The income term raises GDP growth to the power of the income elasticity, and the income elasticity is scaled by a factor that depends on the country’s GDP per capita:
\[
G_{s,f,t} = \left(1 + g_t\right)^{\epsilon_{Y}\, inc_t}
\tag{3.4}\]
where \(\epsilon_Y\) is the income (GDP) elasticity of the fuel in the sector, \(g_t\) real GDP growth after the feedback, and \(inc_t\) the income-level factor.
The income-level factor. The literature finds that income elasticities rise as countries leave low income, peak around lower-middle income (about USD 3,000 per capita) and then decline towards the level of developed countries (methodology, section 3.3.5.2). The model draws this reverse-U as a polynomial in log GDP per capita:
\[
x_t = \min\left(\bar{x},\ \ln y_{t-1}\right), \qquad
inc_t = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{\max\left(0,\ a x_t^4 + b x_t^3 + c x_t^2 + d x_t + e\right)}{n} & \text{if IncElAdj is Yes} \\[1ex]
1 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{3.5}\]
where

\(y_{t-1}\) is baseline real GDP per capita of the previous year (USD; in the base year, the base year’s own value), from the macro series (real GDP over population);
\(\bar{x} = 10\) caps log GDP per capita (about USD 22,000, the methodology’s “developed country” level);
\(a, \dots, e\) and \(n\) are fixed constants (table below), \(n = 0.74\) normalising the factor to the global average income elasticity of Burke and Csereklyei (2016);
IncElAdj is the scenario switch “Adjust income elasticities for GDP levels?” (default Yes*; a starred Yes counts as Yes).

The factor is a data path: it is computed from baseline GDP per capita before the year loop (code incp, then inc.ela.adj after the switch), so it is the same in every scenario. The same factor multiplies the GDP elasticities of electricity demand (Section 3.7).
The GDP feedback. \(g_t\) is not the baseline growth rate but growth after the effect of the policy’s revenue use on GDP (methodology, section 4.7). The effect is computed in Chapter 7 and enters with a lag of one year, as a change in the GDP level:
\[
\ell_t = 1 + \epsilon^{GDP}_{t-1}, \qquad 1 + g_t = \left(1 + g^{0}_t\right)\frac{\ell_t}{\ell_{t-1}}
\tag{3.6}\]
where \(g^{0}_t\) is baseline real GDP growth (IMF WEO), \(\epsilon^{GDP}_{t-1}\) last year’s GDP effect (share of GDP; 0 when endogenous GDP effects are switched off) and \(\ell_t\) the GDP level factor (\(\ell_{t_0} = 1\); code gdp.lvl). The baseline has no fiscal space of its own, so its growth is \(g^{0}_t\). Because the effect is lagged, fuel use in year \(t\) never depends on revenue in year \(t\): there is no circular reference. This is the “rebound” through GDP that Appendix E of the methodology mentions under “Include endogenous GDP effects?”.
Residential biomass. Residential biomass is treated as an inferior good by default: its income elasticity is set to 0 unless the setting BiomassNormal (“Biomass is a normal good”, read from the baseline column; default No) is Yes.


3.2.3 Price terms: usage, efficiency and rebound
A higher price reduces fuel use through two margins (methodology, section 3.3.5.3):

the usage (intensive) margin: existing equipment is used less (fewer kilometres driven), elasticity \(\epsilon_U\);
the efficiency (extensive) margin: equipment is replaced by more efficient equipment, elasticity \(\epsilon_F\).

\[
U_{s,f,t} = \left(\frac{p_{s,f,t}}{p_{s,f,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U}}, \qquad
E_{s,f,t} = \left(\frac{p_{s,f,t} + sh_{s,f,t}}{p_{s,f,t-1} + sh_{s,f,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{F}(1 + \epsilon_{U})}
\tag{3.7}\]
where \(p\) is the after-tax price and \(sh\) the shadow price, both per GJ. The after-tax price (M2.5) includes existing taxes and subsidies, the new carbon tax, the auctioned ETS cost, the new excise, the change in existing carbon pricing, the subsidy and price-control phase-outs, and VAT on all of them; it has a floor of USD 0.01 per GJ. It is built in Chapter 2.
Rebound. When the shadow price is zero the two price terms combine into one:
\[
U_{s,f,t}\,E_{s,f,t} = \left(\frac{p_{s,f,t}}{p_{s,f,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U} + \epsilon_{F} + \epsilon_{U}\epsilon_{F}}
\tag{3.8}\]
The cross term \(\epsilon_U \epsilon_F\) is positive (both elasticities are negative): it is the direct rebound, the extra use of equipment that has become cheaper to run (methodology, section 3.3.5.4). With \(\epsilon_U = \epsilon_F = -0.3\) the combined exponent is \(-0.51\) instead of \(-0.6\), so the rebound offsets about 15% of the price response (the methodology quotes 15.5%, against 26-29% in a meta-analysis of 74 studies).


3.2.4 Shadow prices of non-pricing policies
Some policies do not raise the fuel price but push towards more efficient equipment: feebates, efficiency regulations, vehicle fuel-economy standards, and the free (output-based) allocation of an ETS. The model expresses each as a shadow price per tonne of CO2, which enters the efficiency term only (Equation 3.7) and raises no revenue. A regulation does not make fuel dearer to use, so it has no usage effect; it changes which equipment is bought.
Demand reads the shadow price per GJ (M2.6):
\[
sh_{s,f,t} = \Sigma_{s,t}\; ef_{s,f}
\tag{3.9}\]
where \(ef_{s,f}\) is the calibrated CO2 emission factor (tCO2 per GJ; Chapter 6) and \(\Sigma_{s,t}\) the shadow price of the sector (USD per tCO2; code shpx; M1.4), built in Chapter 2 from three parts:
\[
\Sigma_{s,t} = \underbrace{b_{g(s),t}\, a_{s}}_{\text{feebate}} \;+\; \underbrace{reg_{s,t}}_{\text{regulation}} \;+\; \underbrace{\tilde{p}^{E}_t\, \kappa_{s,t}\, \omega_{s,t}}_{\text{ETS free allocation}}
\tag{3.10}\]
where

\(b_{g,t}\) is the feebate rate of the sector’s feebate group (USD per tCO2) and \(a_s = \mathbb{1}[\text{feebate covers } s] \times\) SPPEffAdjFeebates the share of the feebate on the efficiency margin (code ssc; ScenarioDefinition row 251, default 1);
\(reg_{s,t}\) is the regulation shadow price (below);
\(\tilde{p}^{E}_t\) is the tax-equivalent ETS price, \(\kappa_{s,t}\) the new ETS coverage and \(\omega_{s,t}\) the share allocated free (output-based) (Chapter 6).

Regulations as shadow prices. The scenario’s main policy (ScenarioSelected, ScenarioDefinition row 13) picks a row of the legacy table of main scenarios. Explicit-pricing scenarios (carbon tax, total carbon price, coal excise, road fuel tax, electricity emissions tax and excise) use the carbon price path as the carbon tax. Shadow-pricing scenarios (feebates, power supply feebates, energy efficiency regulations, power feebate, vehicle fuel economy, residential and industrial efficiency regulations, and “Baseline”) have no explicit carbon tax; the carbon price path becomes a shadow price:
\[
reg_{s,t} = \left(\tau_t - \tau^{x}_t\right) \cdot r \cdot \mathbb{1}[\text{the scenario covers } s]
\tag{3.11}\]
where \(\tau_t\) is the carbon price path (code cptraj), \(\tau^{x}_t\) the explicit carbon price (equal to \(\tau_t\) in an explicit scenario and 0 otherwise; code cpx), so the bracket is the shadow carbon price (code cp.shd); \(r\) is the efficiency adjustment of the scenario (code regadj) and the coverage comes from the scenario table (code regc).

Power demand responds to the same shadow prices through the costs of the power model (Chapter 4). The shadow price is not removed for exempt residential LPG and kerosene (Section 3.5), as legacy.


3.2.5 Exogenous demand shock
Legacy CPAT calibrates the first projection years to observed emissions with a one-off shock on energy demand. The model keeps it as a factor:
\[
\Psi_t = 1 + \text{shock}_t \cdot \text{switch}
\tag{3.12}\]
where \(\text{shock}_t\) is the country’s shock (share; code shock) and the switch is the setting “Fuel use and power demand: apply the legacy 2023-2024 shock” (Settings C19; 1 = on, the default, as legacy).
The shock values are typed calibration values of the legacy GHGs tab (rows 1202-1388, columns G and H), by country, for the first two projection years (2023 and 2024) and 0 afterwards; a country without a value gets 0. For Egypt they are −20.8% in 2023 and +9.2% in 2024. The same shock multiplies electricity demand, scaled there by EngineerModelProportionOfCovidFactor (Section 3.7).
The methodology describes the shock as a Covid adjustment of 2020 and 2021, calibrated to emissions outturns (methodology, section 3.3.4.4). The model’s base year is 2022, so the shock that remains is legacy’s 2023-2024 calibration.


3.2.6 Elasticities and base-year fuel use
Every fuel and sector pair reads its parameters from one table, the fuel | subsector table (Excel-AI sheet Inputs rows 5-148; A3.2).
Elasticities (A3.1). Legacy CPAT holds income, usage and efficiency elasticities for 8 elasticity fuels (coal, natural gas, gasoline, diesel, oil products, biomass, renewables, electricity) in 4 elasticity sectors (transport, residential, industry, services), and autonomous efficiency gains for 6 fuels (coal, gas, oil, biomass, renewables, electricity) in the same sectors. The country’s value is read from the legacy Elasticities table (column “Elasticity use”; Excel-AI sheet Inputs_ela). A fuel and sector pair takes the values of its elasticity fuel and elasticity sector (Table 3.1, Table 3.2). A blank cell reads as 0.
The methodology explains how these values were chosen (methodology, section 3.3.5): 32 base income elasticities from Burke and Csereklyei (2016), adjusted for income levels after Gertler and others (2016); price elasticities from the meta-study of Labandeira and others (2017), split into the usage and efficiency margins and raised slightly for developing countries; all checked against in-house databases and other models.
Base-year fuel use. \(F^{e}_{s,f,t_0}\) comes from one of two sources, chosen by BalancesOrConsumption (ScenarioDefinition row 234; default Balances):

Balances: the IEA energy balance flow of the sector, plus a second signed flow where there is one. Fuel transformation is the negative of own use plus heat (both flows with sign −1), so the residual between primary and final consumption becomes an additional industrial sector (methodology, section 3.3.4.5).
EnergyCons: the CPAT energy consumption table (enc.<fuel> of the sector; blank or missing is 0).

Other energy use contains principally military fuel use; it follows the same equation (methodology, section 3.3.4.6). Whether it is taxed is a matter of coverage (Chapter 2).

    for f in fuels:
        # additional efficiency group: road vehicles / residential / industrial
        alpha_add = AdditionalEfficiency[eff_group[s]]
        aef[s,f] = (1 / (1 + alpha[s,f] + alpha_add)) ** (1 + eu[s,f])
        eff_exp[s,f] = ef[s,f] * (1 + eu[s,f])

# year loop
for t in years:
    g = gdp.pos.pct[t]                     # growth after the GDP feedback (lag 1)
    GDPI = (1 + g) ** inc.ela.adj[t] - 1   # income-level factor on the elasticity
    SHOCK = 1 + shock[t] * ApplyDemandShock
    for s in sectors:
        for f in fuels:
            if t == t0:
                enel[s,f,t] = ener0[s,f]   # energy balance or EnergyCons
                continue
            usage = (atp[s,f,t] / atp[s,f,t-1]) ** eu[s,f]
            effic = ((atp[s,f,t] + shp[s,f,t])
                     / (atp[s,f,t-1] + shp[s,f,t-1])) ** eff_exp[s,f]
            # ey = 0 for residential biomass unless BiomassNormal
            enel[s,f,t] = (enel[s,f,t-1] * aef[s,f] * (1 + GDPI) ** ey[s,f]
                           * usage * effic * SHOCK)

title: 3  Energy demand
section: 3.3 Biofuels, jet fuel and self-generated renewables
text:
3.3 Biofuels, jet fuel and self-generated renewables
A few fuels do not fit the grid of 9 fuels by 16 sectors (methodology, section 3.3.4.1). Jet fuel is a fuel of its own, used in domestic aviation; it follows the fuel-use equation with the oil-products elasticities and is priced at the kerosene price. Road biomass is split into three biofuels, and aviation and navigation can use renewables directly (A3.3).
Blended biofuels. Bioethanol and biodiesel are blended into gasoline and diesel, so they follow the road use of the fossil fuel they are blended into:
\[
B^{bgs}_t = B^{bgs}_{t-1}\,\frac{F^{e}_{rod,gso,t}}{F^{e}_{rod,gso,t-1}}, \qquad
B^{bdi}_t = B^{bdi}_{t-1}\,\frac{F^{e}_{rod,die,t}}{F^{e}_{rod,die,t-1}}
\tag{3.13}\]
where \(B^{bgs}\) and \(B^{bdi}\) are road bioethanol and biodiesel (ktoe; code trbe). Where last year’s fossil use is 0 the biofuel holds its value.
Other biofuels follow the fuel-use equation with the oil | transport elasticities and autonomous efficiency, the road vehicles additional efficiency, and the road biomass price:
\[
B^{obf}_t = B^{obf}_{t-1}\,
\left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha^{oil,tra} + \alpha^{+}_{rod}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U}}
\Psi_t \left(1 + g_t\right)^{\epsilon_{Y}\,inc_t}
\left(\frac{p_{rod,bio,t}}{p_{rod,bio,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U}}
\left(\frac{p_{rod,bio,t} + sh_{rod,bio,t}}{p_{rod,bio,t-1} + sh_{rod,bio,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{F}(1+\epsilon_{U})}
\tag{3.14}\]
with \(\epsilon_Y, \epsilon_U, \epsilon_F\) of oil products in transport (code trp.bfe; efficiency factor code trbea). Road biomass is the sum of the three:
\[
F^{e}_{rod,bio,t} = B^{bgs}_t + B^{bdi}_t + B^{obf}_t
\tag{3.15}\]
The base-year biofuels are the road flows of the energy balance (bioethanol, biodiesel, other biofuels) or the EnergyCons values, following BalancesOrConsumption.
Self-generated renewables. Renewable energy used directly in domestic aviation and navigation (base year: the EnergyCons value enc.ren of the sector) follows the fuel-use equation with the renewables | transport elasticities, the road vehicles additional efficiency and, as its price, the levelised investment cost of solar power from Chapter 4 (methodology, section 3.3.4.2):
\[
R_{s,t} = R_{s,t-1}
\left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha^{ren,tra} + \alpha^{+}_{rod}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U}}
\Psi_t \left(1 + g_t\right)^{\epsilon_{Y}\,inc_t}
\left(\frac{tic^{sol}_t}{tic^{sol}_{t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U} + \epsilon_{F}(1+\epsilon_{U})},
\qquad s \in \{avi, nav\}
\tag{3.16}\]
where \(R_{s,t}\) is renewable use (ktoe; code ener with fuel ren), \(tic^{sol}_t\) the levelised investment cost of solar (USD per kWh; code trpren) and the elasticities those of renewables in transport (code trp.rne; efficiency factor code trrena). There is no shadow price on this price. Renewables count in the sector, group and grand totals, but not in any fuel total (Section 3.8).






TipPseudocode: biofuels and self-generated renewables



for t in years:
    # blended biofuels follow the fossil fuel they are blended into
    for b, fossil in (("bgs", "gso"), ("bdi", "die")):
        if t == t0:
            trbe[rod,b,t] = road_biofuel_base[b]       # balance or EnergyCons
        elif enel[rod,fossil,t-1] == 0:
            trbe[rod,b,t] = trbe[rod,b,t-1]
        else:
            growth = enel[rod,fossil,t] / enel[rod,fossil,t-1]
            trbe[rod,b,t] = trbe[rod,b,t-1] * growth

    # other biofuels: oil | transport elasticities, road biomass price
    add = AdditionalEfficiencyRoadVehicle
    trbea = (1 / (1 + aei[oil,tra] + add)) ** (1 + usg[oil,tra])
    if t == t0:
        trbe[rod,obf,t] = road_biofuel_base["obf"]
    else:
        usage = (atp[rod,bio,t] / atp[rod,bio,t-1]) ** usg[oil,tra]
        effic = ((atp[rod,bio,t] + shp[rod,bio,t])
                 / (atp[rod,bio,t-1] + shp[rod,bio,t-1])) \
                ** (eff[oil,tra] * (1 + usg[oil,tra]))
        trbe[rod,obf,t] = (trbe[rod,obf,t-1] * trbea
                           * (1 + GDPI) ** inc[oil,tra] * usage * effic * SHOCK)
    trbe[rod,bio,t] = trbe[rod,bgs,t] + trbe[rod,bdi,t] + trbe[rod,obf,t]

    # renewables in aviation and navigation: price = solar investment cost
    trpren[t] = tic[pow,sol,t]
    trrena = (1 / (1 + aei[ren,tra] + add)) ** (1 + usg[ren,tra])
    for s in ("avi", "nav"):
        if t == t0:
            ener[s,ren,t] = enc_ren[s]
            continue
        r = trpren[t] / trpren[t-1]
        price = r ** usg[ren,tra] * r ** (eff[ren,tra] * (1 + usg[ren,tra]))
        ener[s,ren,t] = (ener[s,ren,t-1] * trrena
                         * (1 + GDPI) ** inc[ren,tra] * price * SHOCK)

title: 3  Energy demand
text:
3.4 Residential leakage to biomass
When modern cooking fuels become dearer, some households may switch back to traditional biomass. This “leakage” reduces the emission savings and worsens household air pollution (methodology, section 3.3.4.3; air pollution effects in methodology, section 6.6.5).
The option is off by default. It is switched on by BiomassLeakage (“Include leakage to biomass in residential sector”, ScenarioDefinition row 325, read from the baseline column; on when it starts with “Yes”). It applies only to the country’s most-used cooking fuel, and only if that fuel is natural gas, LPG or kerosene (A3.4).
The calculation runs in five steps for each leaking fuel \(m \in \{nga, lpg, ker\}\) in the residential sector, from the first projection year (all flows are 0 in the base year).
Step 1: the new policy in the price. Only new policies cause leakage, not movements of the international price:
\[
W_{m,t} = N_{res,m,t}\left(1 + v_m\right)
\tag{3.17}\]
where \(N_{res,m,t}\) is the total new policy per GJ of the residential row (new carbon tax, ETS cost and new excise; code nce) and \(v_m\) its VAT rate. An exempt fuel (Section 3.5) has no new policy, so it does not leak.
Step 2: the share that leaks. A rise in the new policy relative to last year’s price moves a share of the fuel to biomass:
\[
\pi_{m,t} = \mathbb{1}[\text{on},\ m = m^{*}] \cdot
\min\left( \left(1 + \frac{W_{m,t} - W_{m,t-1}}{p_{res,m,t-1}}\right)^{\sigma \eta_{bio} / (\eta_m L)} - 1,\ 1 \right)
\tag{3.18}\]
where

\(m^{*}\) is the country’s most-used cooking fuel (WHO cooking data, overall sample; LPG if the country has no entry);
\(\sigma\) is the cross-price elasticity of biomass with respect to LPG (default 0.25; legacy Elasticities C131, legacy row 360);
\(\eta_m\), \(\eta_{bio}\) are the cookstove efficiencies of the fuel and of biomass (table below);
\(L\) is the substitution lag (1 year, sheet Constants; it divides the exponent);
\(p_{res,m,t-1}\) is last year’s after-tax price of the fuel.

Step 3: the change in fossil use. The share is read as a share of useful energy, so it is weighted by the stove efficiency of the fuel:
\[
d_{m,t} = -\left(F_{res,m,t-1} - X_{m,t-1}\right)\eta_m\,\pi_{m,t}
\tag{3.19}\]
where \(F_{res,m,t-1}\) is last year’s actual fuel use (which already includes earlier leakage) and \(X_{m,t-1}\) the initially exempt use (Section 3.5; 0 unless that option is on), which does not leak.
Step 4: the biomass that replaces it. Biomass supplies the same useful energy:
\[
b_{m,t} = -d_{m,t}\,\frac{\eta_m}{\eta_{bio}}, \qquad \text{so that}\quad \eta_m d_{m,t} + \eta_{bio} b_{m,t} = 0
\tag{3.20}\]
Step 5: cumulative changes. The yearly changes add up to level shifts that are added to residential fuel use:
\[
Lk_{m,t} = Lk_{m,t-1} + d_{m,t} + \left(X^{a}_{m,t} - X^{a}_{m,t-1}\right), \qquad
Lk_{bio,t} = Lk_{bio,t-1} + \sum_{m} b_{m,t}
\tag{3.21}\]
where \(X^{a}\) is the adjustment for initially exempt use (Equation 3.24; 0 unless that option is on), and \(Lk_{t_0} = 0\). The net change \(\sum_m Lk_m + Lk_{bio}\) is reported as a memo row (code lks).

How the leakage behaves:

A fall in the new policy moves fuel back from biomass (\(\pi < 0\)). The share is capped at 1.
A policy that rises and then stays flat moves fuel only in the years it rises. The shift then stays as a level shift: \(Lk\) is not grown with GDP.
With natural gas and a 10% rise in its price from new policies, the exponent is \(0.25 \times 0.20 / 0.58 \approx 0.086\), so \(\pi \approx 0.8\%\); the fossil change is \(\pi \eta_{nga} \approx 0.5\%\) of gas use, replaced by \(0.5\% \times 0.58/0.20 \approx 1.4\%\) of gas use in biomass (in ktoe).
Every product of residential fuel use follows the leakage: CO2, CH4, local pollutants, revenues, the weights of the average prices and the distribution module. \(F^{e}\) stays the elasticity model.







TipPseudocode: residential leakage to biomass



on = BiomassLeakage.startswith("Yes")
LEAK = ("nga", "lpg", "ker")
for t in years:
    for m in LEAK:
        lkt[m,t] = nce[res,m,t] * (1 + vat[res,m])    # new policy, with VAT
        if t == t0:
            lkp[m,t] = 0
            lkd[m,t] = 0
        else:
            expo = sigma * BioEff / Eff[m] / ResSubstLag
            active = 1 if (on and m == CookFuel) else 0
            rise = (lkt[m,t] - lkt[m,t-1]) / atp[res,m,t-1]
            lkp[m,t] = active * min((1 + rise) ** expo - 1, 1)
            not_exempt = ener[res,m,t-1] - lkx[m,t-1]
            lkd[m,t] = -not_exempt * Eff[m] * lkp[m,t]
        lkb[m,t] = -lkd[m,t] * Eff[m] / BioEff
    for m in LEAK:
        if t == t0:
            lkc[m,t] = 0
        else:
            lkc[m,t] = (lkc[m,t-1] + lkd[m,t]
                        + (lkxa[m,t] - lkxa[m,t-1]))  # exempt-use adjustment
    lkcb[t] = 0 if t == t0 else lkcb[t-1] + sum(lkb[m,t] for m in LEAK)
    lks[t] = sum(lkc[m,t] for m in LEAK) + lkcb[t]

title: 3  Energy demand
text:
3.5 Exempt residential cooking fuel
Two options protect households’ cooking fuel from new policies. Both act through the price or the quantity of the residential rows.
Always exempt residential LPG and kerosene. With AlwaysExemptResLPGKer (ScenarioDefinition row 268, by scenario; default No*; a starred Yes* counts as Yes) the new carbon tax, the new ETS cost and the new excise of the residential LPG and kerosene rows are 0 (exemption factor, code exf; Chapter 2). Their after-tax price then keeps only existing taxes, the change in existing carbon pricing and the subsidy phase-outs, so their demand responds only to those. The shadow price stays, and so does their place in ETS-covered emissions where the residential sector is in an ETS. Exempt fuels do not leak to biomass. Exemptions are introduced in user guide, section 1.2.4.
Initially exempt demand of the most-used cooking fuel. With ExemptMostCook = Yes (row 312), the use of the most-used cooking fuel by the bottom deciles of households is initially shielded from the price response, which is phased in later. The shielded share \(\chi\) is the spending of the bottom ExemptCookDeciles deciles (row 313, default 4) on the fuel, over the economy-wide spending on it: household survey budget share times consumption per capita times the weight of each decile (Settings C83, ExemptCookShare).
The exempt use starts as a share of base-year use and then grows with the elasticity model, but with the usage response to the price removed until the phase-in:
\[
X_{m,t_0} = \chi\,F^{e}_{res,m,t_0}, \qquad
X_{m,t} = X_{m,t-1}\;\frac{F^{e}_{res,m,t}}{F^{e}_{res,m,t-1}}\;\left(\frac{p_{res,m,t}}{p_{res,m,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_U(\phi_t - 1)}
\tag{3.22}\]
where \(m\) is the most-used cooking fuel (\(\chi = 0\) for the other fuels), \(\epsilon_U\) its residential usage elasticity, and \(\phi_t\) the phase-in of the usage response:
\[
\phi_t = \begin{cases}
\min\left(\max\left(\dfrac{t + 1 - T^{pha}}{N^{pha}},\ 0\right),\ 1\right) & \text{if ExemptPhaseout} \\[1ex]
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{3.23}\]
with \(T^{pha}\) = YearPha (row 50, default 2027), \(N^{pha}\) = ExemptPhaseoutPeriod (row 51, default 5 years) and ExemptPhaseout (row 49, default FALSE). Where last year’s use or price is 0, the ratio is taken as 1.
\(F^{e}\) already contains the usage term \((p_t/p_{t-1})^{\epsilon_U}\); the last factor multiplies it by \((p_t/p_{t-1})^{-\epsilon_U(1-\phi_t)}\), which takes out the share \(1 - \phi_t\) of it. Before the phase-in the exempt use keeps only the income, efficiency and shock terms; once \(\phi_t = 1\) it responds like the rest.
The difference with the share of the elasticity model is added to residential fuel use through the leakage rows (Equation 3.21):
\[
X^{a}_{m,t} = X_{m,t} - \chi\,F^{e}_{res,m,t}, \qquad X^{a}_{m,t_0} = 0
\tag{3.24}\]
So residential use of the cooking fuel is \((1-\chi)F^{e} + X\) plus the leakage, and the leakage is computed on the use that is not exempt.

    else:

        share = ExemptCookShare if m == CookFuel else 0
        if t == t0:
            lkx[m,t] = share * enel[res,m,t]
            lkxa[m,t] = 0
            continue
        lkxe = ratio(enel[res,m,t], enel[res,m,t-1])   # 1 if last year is 0
        lkxr = ratio(atp[res,m,t], atp[res,m,t-1])     # 1 if last year is 0
        lkx[m,t] = lkx[m,t-1] * lkxe * lkxr ** (eu[res,m] * (lkxp[t] - 1))
        lkxa[m,t] = lkx[m,t] - share * enel[res,m,t]   # enters lkc, so ener

title: 3  Energy demand
section: 3.6 Fuel use used by the rest of the model
text:
3.6 Fuel use used by the rest of the model
The elasticity model \(F^{e}\) is not always the fuel use that the rest of the model reads. Two things can replace or adjust it: the road engineer model, and the residential adjustments above. The result is the fuel use \(F\) (code ener) used everywhere else (M3.2):
\[
F_{s,f,t} = \begin{cases}
F^{T}_{f,t} & s = \text{road},\ f \in \{gso, die, lpg, nga, bio\},\ \text{TrModel} = \text{Engineer} \\
F^{e}_{s,f,t} + Lk_{s,f,t} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{3.25}\]
where

\(F^{T}_{f,t}\) is road fuel use from the engineer road model, calibrated to the energy balance in the base year (Chapter 5); it covers gasoline, diesel, LPG, natural gas and biofuels;
\(F^{e}\) is the elasticity model (Equation 3.1), with road biomass from Equation 3.15;
\(Lk_{s,f,t}\) is the cumulative residential leakage and exempt-use adjustment (Equation 3.21) for residential natural gas, LPG, kerosene and biomass, and 0 for every other pair.

TrModel (ScenarioDefinition row 338) is Elasticity by default; then road fuel use stays the elasticity model’s and the engineer model’s results go only to the transport co-benefits.
Everything downstream reads \(F\): CO2 and other emissions (Chapter 6), revenues and the GDP effect (Chapter 7), the price averages and indices (Chapter 2) and the distribution module (Chapter 8).

title: 3  Energy demand
text:
3.7 Electricity demand
Electricity demand by sector follows the same logic as fuel use, with its own elasticities by demand group. It is computed at the start of the year, before the power model, which turns it into the generation required (Chapter 4). The methodology describes it in methodology, section 3.4.2.3 (M4.1).
Sector policies (carbon tax, ETS, feebates, fuel price reform) act on electricity demand only through the electricity price, which carries the policy cost of power generation. The demand price is a blend of last year’s end-user prices, so demand never depends on this year’s power price:
\[
\bar{p}_{d,t} = w_d\,p^{res}_{t-1} + \left(1 - w_d\right) p^{ind}_{t-1}
\tag{3.26}\]
where \(p^{res}\) and \(p^{ind}\) are the residential and industrial end-user electricity prices (USD per kWh, real; Chapter 4) and \(w_d\) the weight of the residential price in demand group \(d\). In the base year the demand price is the price of the year before (data).
The demand multiple of each group combines the same terms as fuel use:
\[
M_{d,t} = \left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha_d + \alpha^{+}_{pow}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U,d}}
\left(1 + g_t\right)^{\epsilon_{Y,d}\,inc_t}
\left(\frac{\bar{p}_{d,t}}{\bar{p}_{d,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U,d} + \epsilon_{F,d} + \epsilon_{U,d}\epsilon_{F,d}}
\left(1 + \text{shock}_t \cdot \text{switch} \cdot \kappa^{cov}\right)
\tag{3.27}\]
where

\(\alpha_d\), \(\epsilon_{Y,d}\), \(\epsilon_{U,d}\), \(\epsilon_{F,d}\) are the electricity elasticities and autonomous efficiency gain of the group (electricity row of the elasticity table, in the group’s elasticity sector);
\(\alpha^{+}_{pow}\) is AdditionalEfficiencyPower (ScenarioDefinition row 242, by scenario, default 0);
\(\kappa^{cov}\) is EngineerModelProportionOfCovidFactor, the share of the shock passed on to power demand (ScenarioDefinition row 372, default 1);
there is no shadow price term: the shadow prices reach power through its own costs (Chapter 4).

Demand of each sector is last year’s demand times its group’s multiple:
\[
E_{s,t} = \begin{cases}
E^{T}_{t} & s = \text{road and TrModel} = \text{Engineer} \\
E_{s,t-1}\,M_{d(s),t} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad E_{s,t_0} = \text{data}
\tag{3.28}\]
where \(E_{s,t}\) is electricity demand (ktoe; code dem), \(E^{T}\) road electricity from the engineer road model (Chapter 5) and \(d(s)\) the demand group of the sector (Table 3.1). Demand covers 15 sectors (fuel transformation has none). The base-year demand comes from the energy balance.

title: 3  Energy demand
section: 3.8 Energy totals and changes against the baseline
text:
3.8 Energy totals and changes against the baseline
The last step adds fuel use up by sector group and by fuel, adds the fuels burnt in power plants, and compares every total with the baseline of the same year (M3.3).
By sector. The total of a sector is the sum over its fuels, plus renewables in aviation and navigation:
\[
F_{s,t} = \sum_{f} F_{s,f,t} + R_{s,t}\,\mathbb{1}[s \in \{avi, nav\}], \qquad
F_{g,t} = \sum_{s \in g} F_{s,t}
\tag{3.29}\]
for the sector groups \(g\) transport, buildings, industry and other energy use (Table 3.1).
Power. The power group is the fuel input of power generation, coal, gas, oil and biomass (code pet; Chapter 4):
\[
F_{pow,t} = \sum_{k \in \{coa,\, nga,\, oop,\, bio\}} F^{pow}_{k,t}
\tag{3.30}\]
Nuclear, wind, solar, hydro and other renewables have no fuel input in this total.
By fuel and in total.
\[
F_{f,t} = \sum_{s} F_{s,f,t} + F^{pow}_{f,t}, \qquad
F_t = \sum_{s} F_{s,t} + F_{pow,t}
\tag{3.31}\]
where \(F^{pow}_{f,t}\) is the generation fuel use of the type that burns fuel \(f\) (0 for the other fuels). Renewables in aviation and navigation are in \(F_t\) but in no fuel total. A check row confirms that the totals agree:
\[
\left|\sum_{s} F_{s,t} + F_{pow,t} - F_t\right| + \left|\sum_{f} F_{f,t} + R_{avi,t} + R_{nav,t} - F_t\right| = 0
\tag{3.32}\]
Change against the baseline. Each total \(x\) (the 9 fuel totals, the 4 sector groups, power and the grand total) is compared with the baseline value of the same year:
\[
\Delta F_{x,t} = F_{x,t} - F^{B}_{x,t}, \qquad
\%\Delta F_{x,t} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\Delta F_{x,t}}{F_{x,t} - \Delta F_{x,t}} & F_{x,t} - \Delta F_{x,t} \ne 0 \\[1ex] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{3.33}\]
where \(F^{B}_{x,t}\) is scenario 1’s value in the same year (codes echg and epct). In the baseline itself the change is 0. The grand total also has its baseline value and percentage change as rows (ener.ref, ener.pct \(= F_t / F^{B}_t - 1\)).
Electricity totals. Electricity demand (memo) is summed by sector group and in total: \(E_{g,t} = \sum_{s \in g} E_{s,t}\), \(E_t = \sum_g E_{g,t}\) (code eldem).






TipPseudocode: totals and change against the baseline



GROUPS = ("tra", "bld", "ind", "oen")
for t in years:
    for s in sectors:
        ren = ener[s,ren,t] if s in ("avi", "nav") else 0
        ener[s,all,t] = sum(ener[s,f,t] for f in fuels) + ren
    for g in GROUPS:
        ener[g,all,t] = sum(ener[s,all,t] for s in sectors if group[s] == g)
    ener[pow,all,t] = pet[t]          # coal, gas, oil, biomass burnt in power
    for f in fuels:
        burnt = pe[pow,f,t] if f in power_types else 0
        ener[all,f,t] = sum(ener[s,f,t] for s in sectors) + burnt
    total = sum(ener[s,all,t] for s in sectors) + ener[pow,all,t]
    ener[all,all,t] = total
    by_sector = sum(ener[s,all,t] for s in sectors) + ener[pow,all,t]
    by_fuel = (sum(ener[all,f,t] for f in fuels)
               + ener[avi,ren,t] + ener[nav,ren,t])
    ener.chk[t] = abs(by_sector - total) + abs(by_fuel - total)
    ener.ref[t] = baseline.ener[all,all,t]
    ener.pct[t] = total / ener.ref[t] - 1
    rows = ([(all,f) for f in fuels] + [(g,all) for g in GROUPS + ("pow",)]
            + [(all,all)])
    for x in rows:
        echg[x,t] = ener[x,t] - baseline.ener[x,t]
        level = ener[x,t] - echg[x,t]
        epct[x,t] = 0 if level == 0 else echg[x,t] / level
    for g in GROUPS:
        eldem[g,t] = sum(eldem[s,t] for s in sectors if group[s] == g)
    eldem[all,t] = sum(eldem[g,t] for g in GROUPS)

title: 4  Power
text:
4.1 The power block at a glance
The power block is CPAT’s techno-economic (“engineer”) power model. Every year it works out how much electricity the economy needs, which plants generate it, which plants retire, what is built to replace them, what it all costs and what electricity users pay.
It is the largest block of the model and the one where most of the sector’s policy effects arise: a carbon price changes the cost of each generation type, which changes dispatch and investment, which changes the generation mix, emissions, the cost of supply and, a year later, electricity prices and demand.
The methodology describes the power models in section 3.4: power prices and generation costs in 3.4.1, the engineer model in 3.4.2, and the data in 3.4.4. The methodology also has an elasticity-based power model (3.4.3) and, for it, the “old” generation costs of Appendix C. Excel-AI and CPAT Python implement the engineer model only; the elasticity model is not part of this book. (The methodology’s corrections of 2026-10-31 to these two parts, DOC5 and DOC15, therefore have no counterpart here; the corrections that concern the engineer model are linked in the sections below: corrections.)
The chapter follows the order of the calculation:

4.1.2 Notation
The chapter uses the notation of the methodology where it has a symbol, and the symbol of the equation list (Appendix A) otherwise.

Indices. Generation type \(f\); user group \(g \in \{\text{res}, \text{ind}\}\) (residential, industry); demand group \(d \in \{\text{tra}, \text{res}, \text{ind}, \text{srv}\}\) (transport, residential, industry, services); subsector \(s\); year \(t\). Every equation holds for each scenario \(o\) and country \(c\); these two indices are omitted. A value of the baseline in the same year carries the superscript \(B\).
Years. \(t_0\) is the base year (first year of calculations, 2022), \(L\) the last historical price year (2024 for the current data), \(T = 2041\) the last model year.
Units. Generation and capacity in MW (generation as MWy, i.e. average MW over the year); demand in ktoe; costs in real US dollars of the results year (2026) per kWh (USD/kWh); capital costs in USD/kW; money flows in USD million.
Constants. \(H = 8{,}760\) hours per year; \(\theta_e = 0.0036\) GJ per kWh; 8.76 million kWh per MWy (MWyMkWh); \(\theta_g = 11.63\) GWh per ktoe (KtoeGWh); 0.041868 PJ per ktoe.
Minimum cost. \(c_{min}\) = MinPostSubsidyPowerPrice (default 0.01 USD/kWh) is the floor on costs that enter a ratio (dispatch and investment logits) and on end-user prices.

The CPAT variable code of each quantity is given in code font (cap, tic, …): it is the row code of Excel-AI and the variable of CPAT Python.


4.1.3 Inputs by scenario
Every power input of the scenario sheet is read in the scenario’s own column. This covers capacity-factor and efficiency bounds, WACC options, discounted lifetimes, investment permissions and start years, scale-up and retirement rates, the early-retirement factor, the capex decline scenario, storage, PPAs, renewable subsidies, rebates and excises. The sub-table A0 (Inputs of the scenario) applies them to the power data of the country.
Scenario 1 is the baseline of every scenario. A technical input (logit constants, WACC, capacity-factor bounds, storage, cost decline) changed in a policy scenario therefore changes that scenario only, and its difference from scenario 1 mixes the input change with the policy. Technical inputs are not usually changed across scenarios.
Not read, because the model has no such feature: CostBreakdownYear (the cost breakdown is computed for every year instead), ElasticityModel, PowGenCostsOldNew, UseElasticityModelPowerDemandInEngineerModel. The final deficit to gas (Investment) is a global setting, not a scenario input.

Built later: PPAs, deficit to gas, renewable subsidies, rebate, electricity excise, every power input by scenario, manual capacity and investment, the coal implicit cost, the cost memos.
Planned retirement is available for every generation type; legacy offers it for coal only (LD26).
One formula per quantity. Legacy’s duplicates and partial tables are merged (S1-S3 in Generation costs): the price chain of one scenario has about 330 rows in legacy (A5-G4, J1-J3) and about 140 in the model.

title: 4  Power
section: 4.2 Order of the calculation within a year and across years
text:
4.2 Order of the calculation within a year and across years
The power block runs once per year, inside the year loop, after the GDP level of the year and before fuel use. A few rows that depend only on prices and policies are computed for all years before the loop. Everything else is computed year by year, and the chain is free of circular references because two links are lagged by one year.
The methodology summarises the algorithm in section 3.4.2.1.





flowchart TD
  H["H demand, required generation"] --> I["K1, I capacity of the year, dispatch"]
  I --> J["J storage: VRE share, storage cost"]
  J --> E["B, C, E costs: fixed, levelised, average"]
  E --> K["K retirement, early coal, capacity needed"]
  E -. "next year" .-> G["G prices"]
  K --> L["L investment"]
  L -. "next year: capacity" .-> I
  G -. "next year" .-> H






Solid arrows run within year \(t\); dotted arrows carry a value of year \(t\) into year \(t+1\): investment becomes capacity, the average generation cost becomes the supply cost of next year’s prices, and the prices drive next year’s demand.
Within year \(t\) the order is:

Demand (H). Electricity demand of year \(t\) from last year’s demand, this year’s GDP growth and the change in last year’s electricity prices. Required generation follows.
Capacity (K1). Capacity of year \(t\) = capacity of \(t-1\) less retirement of \(t-1\) plus investment of \(t-1\). Capacity bought in year \(t\) is available in \(t+1\).
Dispatch (I). Generation by type from capacity, required generation and the variable costs of year \(t\).
Storage (J). The VRE share of generation sets the marginal storage cost of year \(t\).
Costs (B, C, E). Fixed costs of the existing stock (vintages) and of new plants; the average generation cost and the average policy cost per kWh.
Prices (G). End-user prices of year \(t\) use the average generation cost of \(t-1\).
Retirement (K). Retirement of year \(t\), including early coal retirement, which compares the coal variable cost with the wind and solar investment costs of year \(t\).
Investment (L). Investment of year \(t\) fills the gap between expected requirement and capacity after retirement, allocated by a logit over the levelised costs of year \(t\). Its share in the stock, \(\Phi\), feeds the vintage averages of \(t+1\).
Revenues (M). Power revenues of year \(t\).

The levelised variable cost of year \(t\) averages the variable cost from \(t\) to the end of the horizon. Variable costs depend only on prices and policies, not on the generation mix, so it is computed before the year loop, backwards from the last year.
The table lists every link of the block with the rest of the model and how the loop is broken.










#
From
To
What flows
How the loop is broken

One way

Dispatch uses current variable costs, which do not depend on the average cost; prices use last year’s average cost (I5)


I4

Lagged one year: the price in \(t\) uses the cost of \(t-1\)

Uses the current VRE share from dispatch

I9
