Data years. A year is a data year when Transport1 has it (2022-2025). In data years the model takes the data (ownership, stocks, EV shares, fuel economy, distance) wherever legacy has IF(ISNUMBER(data), data, model); from 2026 it projects. A blank Transport1 cell counts as no data.
Base-year split of road fuel. Transport1 gives, for each fuel, the share used by each vehicle type in the first data year. Light vehicles take the rest (A3.5):
\[
Q_{k,f} = sh_{k,f}\, F^{bal}_{f,t_0}, \qquad L_{k,f} = Q_{k,f}\, \lambda_f / 10^{9}, \qquad sh_{lgt,f} = 1 - \sum_{k \ne lgt} sh_{k,f}
\tag{5.4}\]
where

\(sh_{k,f}\) is the share of fuel \(f\) used by vehicle type \(k\) (passenger, 2-3 wheeler, bus, freight), trshf;
\(F^{bal}_{f,t_0}\) is base-year road use of the fuel in the energy balance (ktoe), trp.eb;
\(\lambda_f\) is liters per ktoe (natural gas counted in liters of gasoline equivalent, as legacy), trp.lpk;
\(Q_{k,f}\) and \(L_{k,f}\) are the base-year fuel use of the type in ktoe and billion liters, trp.bsh.

Gasoline is split between passenger vehicles, 2-3 wheelers and light vehicles; diesel, LPG and gas between passenger, bus, freight and light vehicles.
Purchase taxes from the data. VAT on vehicles is the general VAT rate of the customs data year (VAT_WEO, from the domestic price data); freight vehicles pay no VAT, as legacy. Import duties on ICEVs and BEVs are those of the customs data year (2024), import shares those of the import data year (2022); 2-3 wheelers use the passenger import share. Bus electricity in the base year is the passenger EV stock share of 2024 times base-year bus fuel.

5.3.3 Data-year quantities
In the data years the model turns the Transport1 data into the quantities it needs. Passenger cars and light vehicles are blended by the passenger share of their ownership,
\[
\sigma = \frac{O^{data}_{pas}}{O^{data}_{pas} + O^{data}_{lgt}}, \qquad x_{mix} = \sigma\, x_{pas} + (1 - \sigma)\, x_{lgt}
\tag{5.6}\]
which gives the blended fuel economy (LPG and CNG light vehicles scaled by \(fe_{pas,f}/fe_{pas,gso}\)), BEV fuel economy, distance, and EV shares of the stock and of purchases (trsps, trfem, trfem2, trfebm, trvkm, trevom, trevpm). From them:

PHEV distance share \(\phi = fe_{gso}/fe_{phv}\), the share of PHEV distance on gasoline; PHEV share of distance = (EV − BEV stock share) × \(\phi\) × \(\sigma\).
Distance by fuel = fuel economy × base-year fuel (billion liters, Equation 5.4), held from the base year; the vehicle shares by fuel are this distance split × (1 − EV stock share). The base-year split is used in every data year.
BEV distance: ICEV distance × \(\min\!\big(cap, (c^{BEV}/c^{ICE})^{\epsilon_U}\big)\), the cost-per-km ratio of a BEV to a gasoline car (prices before new policies; last year’s residential power price) raised to the usage elasticity, capped (trbvu).
Freight distance per vehicle in the base year = diesel freight distance / (diesel vehicle share × freight ownership × population); in later data years it moves with the passenger distance ratio (trvkfd).
Stocks by class and powertrain = ownership × (1 − BEV stock share) for ICEVs, the rest for BEVs (trstd).
Ownership years of a passenger vehicle \(= u\,L_{pas} + (1-u)\,n\) (trowny), with \(u\) the used share (data, then held).

The freight share of ownership is freight ownership over passenger and light ownership in data years; after the last data year it falls with income towards its target, capped at the last-data-year value \(\nu\):
\[
\phi^{fre}_t = \min\!\left(\nu,\ \max\!\left(\phi^{*},\ \nu - (\nu - \phi^{*})\,\frac{y_t}{y^{*}}\right)\right)
\tag{5.7}\]
where \(\phi^{*} = 0.0236\) is the target share and \(y^{*} = 87{,}398\) USD the income at which it is reached.

title: 5  Road transport
text:
5.4 Vehicle ownership and its calibration
Ownership is the backbone of the model: how many vehicles per thousand people a country wants at its income. It follows an S-shaped Gompertz curve in GDP per capita, scaled so that it passes through the observed ownership, and the fleet moves only part of the way towards it each year (M5.1, A3.6).
The Gompertz target for passenger and light vehicles:
\[
O^{*}_{pas,t} = \overline{S}\,(1 - \phi^{fre}_t)\; e^{\,a\, e^{\,b\, y_t/1000}}\; J_{pas}
\tag{5.8}\]
where

\(\overline{S}\) is the ownership saturation point (vehicles per 1,000 people, Transport1, held after the data years), trsat;
\(\phi^{fre}_t\) is the freight share of ownership (Equation 5.7);
\(a = -5.897\) and \(b = -0.23\) per 1,000 USD are the Gompertz constants;
\(J_{pas}\) is the calibration factor (Equation 5.9), trjjp.

Freight uses the same curve with \(\overline{S}\,\phi^{fre}_t\) in place of \(\overline{S}\,(1-\phi^{fre}_t)\) and its own \(J_{fre}\).
Calibration to observed ownership. In each data year the model compares actual ownership with the curve; the factor of the last data year is held for all later years:
\[
J_{pas} = \frac{O^{data}_{pas,T}}{\overline{S}\,(1 - \phi^{fre}_{T})\, e^{\,a\, e^{\,b\, y_{T}/1000}}}, \qquad T = \text{last data year (2025)}
\tag{5.9}\]
Freight’s \(J_{fre}\) is the same ratio with the freight curve. The factor works both ways: a country below the curve stays below it. For Egypt, ownership was 55 per 1,000 in 2025 against a Gompertz level of 152, so \(J = 0.36\).
Partial adjustment and limits. Desired ownership moves a fraction \(\mu\) of the way to the target, and actual ownership may grow or fall only within limits:
\[
\tilde{O}_{k,t} = \mu\, O^{*}_{k,t} + (1 - \mu)\, O_{k,t-1}
\tag{5.10}\]
\[
O_{k,t} = \begin{cases} S^{data}_{k,ICE,t} + S^{data}_{k,BEV,t} & \text{data year} \\ \max\!\Big(O_{k,t-1}(1 - d_k),\ \min\big(O_{k,t-1}(1 + g_k),\ \tilde{O}_{k,t}\big)\Big) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{5.11}\]
where \(\mu = 0.09\) (own_adj), \(g_k = 7.5\%\) the maximum annual growth and \(d_k = 10\%\) the maximum annual decline (TrOwnDecline for passenger and freight, own_max_decline for 2-3 wheelers). This is the only partial-adjustment equation of the model.
2-3 wheelers follow a hump in income instead of a Gompertz curve, without partial adjustment (\(\mu = 1\)). With \(H = 7{,}000\) USD the income of the peak and \(\kappa = 0.737\) a scale factor:
\[
J^{cyc} = O^{data}_{cyc,T}\left(1 + \kappa\Big(1 - \frac{y_T}{H}\Big)\right), \qquad O^{*}_{cyc,t} = \frac{2\, J^{cyc}}{y_t/H + H/y_t} = \frac{2\,J^{cyc}\,H\,y_t}{y_t^2 + H^2}
\tag{5.12}\]
\(J^{cyc}\) is the peak level, set from the last data year \(T\) and held. The target then enters Equation 5.11 with the 2-3 wheeler limits.






TipPseudocode: ownership



for t in years:
    if data_year(t):
        J_pas = own_data[pas, t] / (sat * (1 - fsh[t]) * exp(a * exp(b_pas * gpc[t] / 1000)))
        J_fre = own_data[fre, t] / (sat * fsh[t] * exp(a * exp(b_fre * gpc[t] / 1000)))
        J_cyc = own_data[cyc, t] * (1 + scale * (1 - gpc[t] / peak))
    # (held after the last data year)
    target[pas] = sat * (1 - fsh[t]) * exp(a * exp(b_pas * gpc[t] / 1000)) * J_pas_prev
    target[fre] = sat * fsh[t] * exp(a * exp(b_fre * gpc[t] / 1000)) * J_fre_prev
    target[cyc] = 2 * J_cyc_prev / (gpc[t] / peak + peak / gpc[t])
    for k in ["pas", "fre", "cyc"]:
        if stock_data[k, t] > 0:
            own[k, t] = stock_data[k, ICE, t] + stock_data[k, BEV, t]
        else:
            adj = 1 if k == "cyc" else own_adj[k]
            desired = adj * target[k] + (1 - adj) * own[k, t-1]
            own[k, t] = max(own[k, t-1] * (1 - decline[k]),
                            min(own[k, t-1] * (1 + max_growth[k]), desired))

title: 5  Road transport
section: 5.5 The stock: retirements, purchases and the closing stock
text:
5.5 The stock: retirements, purchases and the closing stock
Each year some vehicles are scrapped and new ones are bought to reach the ownership of Equation 5.11. The stock is followed separately for new and used passenger vehicles, freight vehicles and 2-3 wheelers, each split into ICEVs and BEVs (A3.6).
Opening stock. In a data year it is the data (passenger: × the new or used share); otherwise last year’s closing stock:
\[
S^{o}_{k,v,t} = \begin{cases} S^{data}_{k,v,t}\, w_k & \text{data year} \\ S^{cl}_{k,v,t-1} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{5.13}\]
where \(v\) is ICE or BEV and \(w_{pas} = 1 - u_t\), \(w_{pau} = u_t\), \(w_{fre} = w_{cyc} = 1\).
Retirement is the average opening stock of the last years over the life, at most the stock itself:
\[
R_{k,v,t} = \min\!\left(\frac{1}{L_k}\cdot\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=0}^{m-1} S^{o}_{k,v,t-j},\ \ S^{o}_{k,v,t}\right), \qquad m = \min(L_k,\ t - t_0 + 1)
\tag{5.14}\]
with lives \(L_{pas} = n = 7\) (a new passenger vehicle is resold after seven years), \(L_{pau} = 20 - 7 = 13\), \(L_{fre} = 10\) and \(L_{cyc} = 7\). The stock after retirement is \(S^{a} = S^{o} - R\).
Purchases fill the gap between ownership and the stock that remains; passenger purchases are split between new and used vehicles by the used share:
\[
P_{k,t} = O_{k,t} - \sum_{v} S^{a}_{k,v,t}, \qquad P_{pas,t}^{new} = (1 - u_t)\, P_{pas,t}, \qquad P_{pau,t} = u_t\, P_{pas,t}
\tag{5.15}\]
The purchases of each powertrain are the class purchases × its share from the choice of Section 5.10.
Closing stock. In data years a balancing item makes the closing stock equal the data; afterwards it is zero:
\[
S^{cl}_{k,v,t} = S^{a}_{k,v,t} + s_{k,v,t}\, P_{k,t} + \Delta_{k,v,t}, \qquad \Delta_{k,v,t} = \begin{cases} S^{data}_{k,v,t}\, w_k - S^{a}_{k,v,t} - s_{k,v,t}\, P_{k,t} & \text{data year} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{5.16}\]
where \(s_{k,v,t}\) is the purchase share of the powertrain. The BEV stock in million vehicles, \(\sum_k S^{o}_{k,BEV}\,N/1000\), drives the charging stations of Section 5.6; the EV share of the opening passenger stock drives the charging mark-up.






TipPseudocode: the stock



for t in years:
    for k in ["pas", "pau", "fre", "cyc"]:
        for v in ["ice", "bev"]:
            if stock_data[k, v, t] > 0:
                opening[k, v, t] = stock_data[k, v, t] * share_of_class[k]
            else:
                opening[k, v, t] = closing[k, v, t-1]
            m = min(life[k], t - base_year + 1)
            retired[k, v, t] = min(mean(opening[k, v, t-m+1 : t+1]) / life[k], opening[k, v, t])
            after[k, v, t] = opening[k, v, t] - retired[k, v, t]
    # ... ownership (previous section) and choice (below) ...
    buy[pas] = own[pas, t] - sum(after[pas|pau, :, t]);  buy_new = (1 - used_share) * buy[pas]
    buy_used = buy[pas] - buy_new;  buy[fre] = own[fre, t] - sum(after[fre, :, t]);  ...
    for k, v:
        purchases[k, v, t] = share[k, v, t] * buy[k]
        plug = stock_data[k, v, t] * share_of_class[k] - after[k, v, t] - purchases[k, v, t] if data else 0
        closing[k, v, t] = after[k, v, t] + purchases[k, v, t] + plug

title: 5  Road transport
section: 5.6 Charging, the charging mark-up and range anxiety
text:
5.6 Charging, the charging mark-up and range anxiety
Electric vehicles face two costs that petrol cars do not: a mark-up for public charging, and range anxiety, the money-equivalent of the fear of running out of charge. Both fall as electric vehicles spread and charging stations are built.
Charging-station subsidy (policy scenarios only): zero before its start year, linear to the target level, then constant:
\[
\varsigma_t = \pi_t \cdot \begin{cases} 0 & t < t^{cs}_{0} \\ \varsigma_0 + (\varsigma_1 - \varsigma_0)\min\!\left(1,\ \dfrac{t - t^{cs}_0}{\max(1,\ t^{cs}_1 - t^{cs}_0)}\right) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{5.17}\]
where \(\pi_t\) is 1 in a policy scenario (scenario number above 1) and 0 in the baseline, \(t^{cs}_0, \varsigma_0\) the start year and level, \(t^{cs}_1, \varsigma_1\) the target year and level (TrCsStartYear, TrCsStartLevel, TrCsTargetYear, TrCsTargetLevel). The cost per charging port after the subsidy is \(C_t = C^{port}_t(1-\varsigma_t)\).
Charging stations are the data in data years, then grow with the BEV stock and fall with their cost:
\[
H_t = H_{t-1}\left(\frac{V^{BEV}_t}{V^{BEV}_{t-1}}\right)^{0.3}\left(\frac{C_t}{C_{t-1}}\right)^{-0.67}
\tag{5.18}\]
where \(V^{BEV}\) is the BEV stock (million vehicles).
Charging mark-up on the electricity price falls with the EV share of the passenger stock \(e_t\):
\[
mku_t = \max\!\left(0.02,\ 0.3\,\frac{0.5 - e_t}{1 - 0.5}\right)\times 0.2
\tag{5.19}\]
(minimum and maximum mark-up in USD per kWh, the EV share where the minimum is reached, the share of public charging). The EV electricity price is last year’s end-user price plus the mark-up, \(p^{EV}_{u,t} = p^{T}_{u,t-1} + mku_t\), for residential (\(u = res\): passenger vehicles, 2-3 wheelers, PHEVs) and industrial users (\(u = ind\): freight). Using last year’s price avoids a circular reference with the power model.
Range anxiety (USD per vehicle, by class) keeps its start value for the first three years, then falls with the growth of charging stations:
\[
RA_{k,t} = \begin{cases} RA^{0}_k & t - t_0 + 1 \le 3 \\ RA_{k,t-1} & RA_{k,t-1} < 0 \\ \max\!\left(0,\ RA_{k,t-1}\,(1 - \delta_k)\left(\dfrac{H_t}{H_{t-1}}\right)^{-0.5}\right) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{5.20}\]
where \(\delta_k\) is an annual decline (default 0) and \(RA^0_k\) the start value from Transport3.
The start value is fitted. \(RA^0_k\) is the value that makes the model’s EV share of purchases in the fit year (2025, scenario 1) equal the observed share:
\[
r_k(RA^0_k) = s^{EV}_{k}(2025;\ RA^0_k) - s^{EV,data}_{k}(2025) = 0
\tag{5.21}\]
The root is found offline by a goal seek on this model and stored by country (negative values allowed, issue I145); countries without a fitted value use the legacy Transport3 value, and countries without either the Transport3 average. The fit is reported in the rows “EV sales share calculated − actual” of the data years (Section 5.14). For the data edition Public01 the fitted values (Egypt, the only country fitted so far) are 64,064 USD (passenger), 469,574 USD (freight) and 1,027 USD (2-3 wheeler). Legacy also allowed a Dashboard source of 10,000 USD for every class (ra_source, ra_dash); the model uses the per-country values.

title: 5  Road transport
section: 5.7 Fuel economy of new vehicles and the feebate
text:
5.7 Fuel economy of new vehicles and the feebate
New vehicles become more efficient over time, and faster when fuel is dear. A vehicle feebate (a fee on high-emission vehicles and a rebate on low-emission ones) acts as if it raised the fuel price (A3.8). The methodology describes this efficiency margin of the price response in section 3.3.5.3.
The feebate rate (USD per tCO2) is the scenario’s vehicle feebate from its introduction year, plus the road regulation shadow price; it applies in policy scenarios only:
\[
\beta_{k,t} = \pi_t\left(\mathbb{1}[t \ge t^{fb}_k]\,\beta^{0}_k + reg_{rod,t}\right)
\tag{5.22}\]
where \(\beta^0_k\) is TrFbRate<k>, \(t^{fb}_k\) is TrFbYear<k> and \(reg_{rod,t}\) the road regulation shadow price (Chapter 1). The carbon price is not added: it is in the fuel price already.
Feebate per liter is the rate × the fossil CO2 per liter of the fuel:
\[
fb_{k,f,t} = \beta_{k,t}\, \varepsilon_f\, \theta_f
\tag{5.23}\]
where \(\varepsilon_f\) is the CO2 emission factor (tCO2 per liter) and \(\theta_f\) the fossil share of road gasoline and diesel in the base year (base-year fossil use / (fossil + bioethanol or biodiesel); 1 for LPG and gas).
New fuel economy is the data × (1 + gap) in data years, then responds to the price incl. the feebate and gains an autonomous efficiency improvement:
\[
fe^{new}_{k,f,t} = \begin{cases} fe^{data}_{k,f,t}\,(1 + \gamma_k) & \text{data year} \\ fe^{new}_{k,f,t-1}\left(\dfrac{p_{f,t} + fb_{k,f,t}}{p_{f,t-1} + fb_{k,f,t-1}}\right)^{|\epsilon_{F}|}(1 + \alpha) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{5.24}\]
where

\(\gamma_k = 0.05\) is how much better new vehicles are than the stock average (fe_gap);
\(\epsilon_F\) is the road efficiency elasticity (passenger and 2-3 wheeler: gasoline’s for every fuel; freight: diesel’s);
\(\alpha\) is the autonomous efficiency gain of road oil;
\(p_{f,t}\) is the fuel price (freight: net of VAT; PHEV: the PHEV price, its ratio taken on the average passenger price).

The average new ICEV fuel economy and CO2 intensity weight the fuels by last year’s stock shares (data years: the vehicle shares); CO2 intensity of a fuel is \(\varepsilon_f \cdot 10^6 / fe\) (gCO2 per km). Used vehicles carry the past: their fuel economy is the average new fuel economy of the last \(\min(n, t - t_0 + 1)\) years, their CO2 intensity and their BEV fuel economy those of new vehicles \(n - 1\) years earlier.

        fb_rate[k, t] = ((TrFbRate[k] if t >= TrFbYear[k] else 0) + reg[rod, t]) * is_policy_scenario
        for f in fuels[k]:
            fb_l[k, f, t] = fb_rate[k, t] * ef[f] * fossil_share[f]
            if data_year(t):
                fe_new[k, f, t] = fe_data[k, f, t] * (1 + fe_gap[k])
            else:
                ratio = (price[f, t] + fb_l[k, f, t]) / (price[f, t-1] + fb_l[k, f, t-1])
                fe_new[k, f, t] = fe_new[k, f, t-1] * ratio ** abs(ela_eff[k]) * (1 + aeei)

        weights = vehicle_share_data if data_year(t) else stock_share[k, :, t-1]
        fe_new_avg[k, t] = weighted_average(fe_new[k, :, t], weights)
    m = min(own_years, t - base_year + 1)
    fe_used[t] = mean(fe_new_avg[pas, t-m+1 : t+1])
    intensity_used[t] = intensity_avg[pas, t-m+1];  fe_used_bev[t] = fe_new_bev[pas, t-m+1]

title: 5  Road transport
5  Road transport
text:
5.9 Total cost of ownership
The choice between an ICEV and a BEV is made on the total cost of ownership per km: what the vehicle costs to buy, insure, maintain and fuel over the years it is owned, discounted, divided by the discounted distance it is driven (A3.7).

5.9.1 Discounted distance and purchase price
Discounted distance over the ownership period is the present value of the yearly distance:
\[
K_{k,v,t} = v_{k,v,t}\,\frac{(1 + r_t)^{N_k} - 1}{r_t\,(1 + r_t)^{N_k}}
\tag{5.27}\]
with \(N_{pas} = 7\), \(N_{pau} = 13\), \(N_{fre} = 10\), \(N_{cyc} = 7\) and \(r_t\) the consumer discount rate (Equation 5.5).
Purchase price after policies. For an ICEV and a BEV of class \(k\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
P^{ICE}_{k,t} &= P^{0,ICE}_{k,t}\,(1 + du^{ICE}_k\, m_k)(1 + adv^{ICE}_{k,t})(1 + vat_k) + FB^{ICE}_{k,t} \\
P^{BEV}_{k,t} &= P^{0,BEV}_{k,t}\,(1 + du^{BEV}_{k,t}\, m_k)(1 + vat^{BEV}_{k,t})(1 + adv^{BEV}_{k,t}) + FB^{BEV}_{k,t} + sub_{k,t}
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.28}\]
where

\(P^{0}\) is the vehicle price before taxes (Transport2), USD;
\(du_k\) the import duty and \(m_k\) the share of imports (customs and import data years);
\(adv\) the ad-valorem purchase tax: the baseline rate, or the policy rate from TrAdvYear<k> in policy scenarios (TrAdvIceBase, TrAdvBevBase, TrAdvIcePol, TrAdvBevPol);
\(vat_k\) the VAT on vehicles (0 for freight); for BEVs the policy rate (baseline × TrVatPolFactor) applies from TrVatYear<k>, and the policy BEV duty (baseline × TrCustPolFactor) from TrCustYear<k>;
\(FB\) the vehicle feebate (Equation 5.29);
\(sub_{k,t}\) the EV purchase subsidy (negative), Equation 5.30.

The vehicle feebate charges the CO2 intensity above a pivot, at the feebate rate, over the discounted distance:
\[
FB^{v}_{k,t} = \left(I^{v}_{k,t} - I^{piv}_{k,t}\right)\frac{\beta_{k,t}}{10^6}\, K_{k,v,t}
\tag{5.29}\]
where \(I^{v}\) is the CO2 intensity of the vehicle (gCO2 per km; BEVs 0; used ICEVs the used intensity) and \(I^{piv}\) the pivot. Below the pivot the feebate is a rebate. The pivot is blank in the first two years, then either

Average: last year’s sales-weighted intensity extrapolated by its own trend, \(I^{piv}_t = \bar{I}_{t}\,\bar{I}_{t}/\bar{I}_{t-1}\), where \(\bar{I}_t\) is the intensity of last year’s sales (new and used, weighted by their ICE shares); or
Manual: TrFbPivot<k> in the feebate year, then lower by TrFbPivotChg<k> gCO2 per km each year, at least 0 (0 before the feebate year).

The EV subsidy (policy scenarios only) is \(-\)TrSubAmount<k> in its year, then changes by TrSubChg<k> a year, never positive:
\[
sub_{k,t} = \pi_t \cdot \begin{cases} -A_k & t = t^{sub}_k \\ \min(0,\ sub_{k,t-1} - \Delta_k) & t > t^{sub}_k \\ 0 & t < t^{sub}_k \end{cases}
\tag{5.30}\]


5.9.2 Cost components
The TCO of a new vehicle adds five parts. With \(P\) the price after policies, \(d = 0.30\) the first-year depreciation, \(L\) the useful life, \(n\) the ownership period and \(r\) the discount rate:
\[
\begin{aligned}
D^{1} &= d\,P && \text{first-year depreciation} \\
D^{ann} &= \frac{P - dP}{L - 1}\cdot\frac{1 - (1 + r)^{-(L-1)}}{r} && \text{depreciation annuity of the rest} \\
SV &= \min\!\left(0,\ -P\,\frac{(L - n)/L\,(1 - d)}{(1 + r)^{n}}\right) && \text{salvage value (passenger only)} \\
IM &= \frac{P\,\iota}{r}\left(1 - (1 + r)^{-(n+1)}\right)\theta + m^{v}\,K && \text{insurance and maintenance} \\
FU &= \left(\frac{p}{fe^{new}} + \tau^{km}\right)K && \text{fuel or electricity and distance tax}
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.31}\]
where \(\iota = 1.5\%\) is the insurance rate, \(\theta = 0.5\) the insurance factor, \(m^{v}\) the maintenance cost per km (ICEV or EV), \(p\) the average ICE fuel price over the fuel mix and \(fe^{new}\) the average new fuel economy (BEVs: the EV electricity price and new BEV fuel economy). Then
\[
TCO^{v}_{k,t} = D^1 + D^{ann} + SV + IM + FU + \mathbb{1}[v = BEV]\,RA_{k,t}, \qquad c^{v}_{k,t} = \frac{TCO^{v}_{k,t}}{K_{k,v,t}}
\tag{5.32}\]
Used passenger vehicles are bought at their resale price after taxes, \(P^{res} = P^{0}\left(1 - \big(d + \frac{n - 1}{L - 1}(1 - d)\big)\right) \times\) (the same tax factors) + the feebate (BEV: + the subsidy). Their TCO has no first-year depreciation and no salvage value: the annuity is over the used ownership period less one year, \(13 - 1 = 12\) years, for ICEVs and BEVs alike; insurance runs over 13 years; fuel uses the used fuel economy. A used BEV carries range anxiety scaled by its price, \(RA^{used} = RA\,P^{used}/P^{new}\).
Freight vehicles and 2-3 wheelers have no salvage term; freight pays no VAT and charges at the industrial EV price, 2-3 wheelers at the residential one.
Per-fuel ICE TCO (for the fuel split of Section 5.10) uses the cost per km of each fuel and shares the feebate by intensity: \(TCO_f = K\,c^{km}_f + (D^1 + D^{ann} + SV) + IM + FB\,(I_f/\bar{I})\).
Plug-in hybrids take the BEV’s capital cost (no PHEV price exists in the data): BEV depreciation and salvage, insurance on the BEV price, ICEV maintenance over the ICEV distance, and the PHEV fuel cost; they carry no range anxiety, since they refuel with gasoline.

    r = disc[t]
    K_ice = v_new_avg * ((1 + r) ** own_years - 1) / (r * (1 + r) ** own_years)
    K_bev = v_new_bev * ((1 + r) ** own_years - 1) / (r * (1 + r) ** own_years)
    fb_ice = (intensity_avg[t] - pivot[t]) * fb_rate[t] / 1e6 * K_ice      # blank in the base year
    fb_bev = (0 - pivot[t]) * fb_rate[t] / 1e6 * K_bev
    P_ice = price0_ice[t] * (1 + duty_ice * imp) * (1 + adv_ice[t]) * (1 + vat) + fb_ice
    P_bev = price0_bev[t] * (1 + cust_bev[t]) * (1 + vat_bev[t]) * (1 + adv_bev[t]) + subsidy[t] + fb_bev
    for v, P, K, maint, fuel_km in [("ice", P_ice, K_ice, maint_ice, p_avg / fe_new_avg + dtax),
                                    ("bev", P_bev, K_bev, maint_ev, pev[res] / fe_new_bev + dtax)]:
        dep1 = dep * P
        ann = (P - dep1) / (life - 1) / r * (1 - (1 + r) ** -(life - 1))
        salv = min(0, -P * ((life - own_years) / life * (1 - dep)) / (1 + r) ** own_years)
        ins_m = P * ins / r * (1 - (1 + r) ** -(own_years + 1)) * ins_factor + maint * K
        tco[v] = dep1 + ann + salv + ins_m + fuel_km * K + (ra[pas, t] if v == "bev" else 0)
        tco_km[v] = tco[v] / K

title: 5  Road transport
section: 5.10 Choice: the EV share and the ICE fuel split
text:
5.10 Choice: the EV share and the ICE fuel split
Buyers choose between an ICEV and a BEV by their TCO per km. The model uses a binary logit, as the power model does for dispatch and investment (methodology section 3.4.2.4.1); among ICEVs, the fuel mix shifts with the relative TCO of each fuel (M5.2, A3.7).
EV share of purchases. For each class (new passenger, used passenger, freight, 2-3 wheelers):
\[
s^{ICE}_{k,t} = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\left(-k_k\,\dfrac{c^{BEV}_{k,t} - c^{ICE}_{k,t}}{\bar{c}_{k,t}}\right)}, \qquad s^{BEV}_{k,t} = 1 - s^{ICE}_{k,t}, \qquad \bar{c}_{k,t} = s^{ICE}_{k,t-1}\,c^{ICE}_{k,t} + (1 - s^{ICE}_{k,t-1})\,c^{BEV}_{k,t}
\tag{5.33}\]
where \(k_k\) is the logit parameter (3 passenger, 2 freight, 4 2-3 wheelers) and \(\bar{c}\) the average TCO per km weighted by last year’s ICE share (base year: 1 − the data EV share). This is the two-option form of the equation list’s multinomial logit. In data years the actual shares replace the logit. The passenger EV share of purchases is \(u\,s^{BEV}_{pau} + (1 - u)\,s^{BEV}_{pas}\), the actual share where there is one.
ICE fuel split of passenger purchases. In data years the shares are the base-year distance split scaled to the ICE total; the PHEV share is (EV − BEV purchase share) × the passenger share \(\sigma\), at least 0. Afterwards each fuel’s share moves with its own TCO change and the TCO change of the other fuels:
\[
\tilde{s}_{f,t} = \tilde{s}_{f,t-1}\left(\frac{TCO_{f,t}}{TCO_{f,t-1}}\right)^{-1.265}\left(\frac{\sum_{g \ne f}\tilde{s}_{g,t-1}\,TCO_{g,t}/TCO_{g,t-1}}{\sum_{g \ne f}\tilde{s}_{g,t-1}}\right)^{0.5725}
\tag{5.34}\]
over \(f, g \in\) {gasoline, diesel, LPG, CNG, PHEV}. If no other fuel has a share the share is held. The shares are then scaled to the ICE part of purchases, \(s_{f,t} = \tilde{s}_{f,t} / \sum_g \tilde{s}_{g,t}\,(1 - s^{EV}_t)\).
Stock shares turn over slowly: each year the ownership period’s share of the stock is replaced,
\[
s^{stock}_{f,t} = s^{stock}_{f,t-1}\,\frac{Y - 1}{Y} + \frac{s_{f,t}}{Y}
\tag{5.35}\]
with \(Y\) the ownership years (\(u\,L_{pas} + (1-u)\,n\); 13.57 for Egypt) for passenger vehicles and \(L_{fre} = 10\) for freight; data years take the data. Divided by their sum plus the EV stock share, they give the vehicles by fuel (million) = passenger stock × share × population / 1,000.
Freight follows the same steps with diesel, LPG and LNG, scaled to \(1 - s^{BEV}_{fre}\). 2-3 wheelers have only gasoline ICEVs.






TipPseudocode: EV choice and ICE fuel split



for t in years:
    for k in ["pas", "pau", "fre", "cyc"]:
        avg = ice_share[k, t-1] * tco_km[k, ice] + (1 - ice_share[k, t-1]) * tco_km[k, bev]
        logit_ice = 1 / (1 + exp(-k_par[k] * (tco_km[k, bev] - tco_km[k, ice]) / avg))
        ice_share[k, t] = 1 - ev_share_data[k, t] if data_year(t) else logit_ice
    for f in ["gso", "die", "lpg", "nga", "phv"]:
        if data_year(t):
            s[f, t] = data_split[f, t]
        else:
            ratio = tco_f[f, t] / tco_f[f, t-1]
            others = [g for g in fuels if g != f]
            cross = sum(s[g, t-1] * tco_f[g, t] / tco_f[g, t-1] for g in others) / sum(s[g, t-1] for g in others)
            s[f, t] = s[f, t-1] * ratio ** own_price_el * cross ** cross_price_el
    for f: s_new[f, t] = s[f, t] if data_year(t) else s[f, t] / sum(s[:, t]) * (1 - ev_share[pas, t])
    for f: s_stock[f, t] = data if data_year(t) else s_stock[f, t-1] * (Y - 1) / Y + s_new[f, t] / Y

title: 5  Road transport
section: 5.11 Stock fuel economy, distance driven and fuel use
text:
5.11 Stock fuel economy, distance driven and fuel use
Fuel use is vehicles × distance per vehicle / fuel economy of the stock (M5.3, A3.8). Each factor is projected separately.
Stock fuel economy turns over with the purchases: the data in data years, then
\[
fe^{stock}_{k,f,t} = \tau_k\, fe^{new}_{k,f,t} + (1 - \tau_k)\, fe^{stock}_{k,f,t-1}
\tag{5.36}\]
with the turnover share \(\tau_{pas} = 1/\big(u\,n + (1-u)\,L_{pas}\big)\) (7 years used, 20 new), \(\tau_{fre} = 1/10\), \(\tau_{cyc} = 1/7\). The opening value is last year’s closing value. The BEV stock fuel economy turns over in the same way, with the share of this year’s BEV purchases in the closing BEV stock and the new BEV fuel economy (passenger: new and used BEVs weighted by their purchases).
Distance per vehicle is the data in data years (times the calibration factor of Equation 5.40), then responds to the cost per km of the stock and to income:
\[
v_{k,f,t} = v_{k,f,t-1}\left(\frac{c^{stock}_{k,f,t}}{c^{stock}_{k,f,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_U}\left(\frac{y_t}{y_{t-1}}\right)^{\eta_k}, \qquad c^{stock}_{k,f,t} = \frac{p_{f,t}}{fe^{stock,o}_{k,f,t}} + \tau^{km}_{k,t}
\tag{5.37}\]
where \(fe^{stock,o}\) is the opening stock fuel economy, \(\epsilon_U\) the usage elasticity and \(\eta_k\) the income elasticity of distance (2-3 wheelers: −0.4, so they are driven less as income rises). The base distance is the Transport1 average distance (passenger and light blended; freight from the fuel shares, Section 5.3.3; BEVs with their uplift).
Distance driven and fuel use:
\[
B_{k,f,t} = \frac{V_{k,f,t}\, v_{k,f,t}}{1000}, \qquad F_{k,f,t} = \frac{B_{k,f,t}}{fe^{stock}_{k,f,t}}
\tag{5.38}\]
where \(V\) is vehicles (million), \(B\) billion km and \(F\) billion liters (BEVs: billion kWh). Here \(fe\) is km per liter, so the equation list’s \(F = \sum VKT \cdot FE\) (M5.3) reads with \(FE = 1/fe\). PHEV distance is split: gasoline use \(B_{phv}/fe_{phv}\) is added to gasoline, electricity use is \(B_{phv}(1 - \phi)/fe^{BEV}\). CO2 by class is fuel use × the emission factor.

title: 5  Road transport
text:
5.12 Calibration to the energy balance
The bottom-up fleet (Transport1 ownership × distance / fuel economy) rarely adds up to the road fuel use of the energy balance. Two calibration steps close the gap in the base year; their factors are then held (A3.8, A3.9).
Step 1: distance factors by class. The bottom-up base-year fuel use, grossed up for buses, is compared with the energy balance fuel by fuel:
\[
Q^{bu}_{f} = \frac{F^{0}_{f,t_0}\, 10^9 / \lambda_f}{1 - b_f}, \qquad q_f = \frac{F^{bal}_{f,t_0}}{Q^{bu}_f}
\tag{5.39}\]
where \(F^{0}_{f,t_0}\) is uncalibrated fuel use (billion liters: gasoline = passenger + 2-3 wheelers; diesel, LPG and gas = passenger + freight), \(b_f\) the bus share of the fuel (gasoline 0), and \(q_f = 1\) when either is zero. The distance factor of a class is the fuel-use-weighted average of the \(q_f\):
\[
\kappa_{pas} = \frac{\sum_f F^{0}_{pas,f}\, q_f}{\sum_f F^{0}_{pas,f}}, \qquad \kappa_{fre} = \frac{\sum_f F^{0}_{fre,f}\, q_f}{\sum_f F^{0}_{fre,f}}, \qquad \kappa_{cyc} = q_{gso}
\tag{5.40}\]
The factors multiply the data distance of each class in Equation 5.37 (BEVs too) and are held after the base year.
Step 2: a residual factor by fuel. After buses (Section 5.13) the calibrated total still differs from the energy balance, because a class factor averages over fuels. A second factor by fuel closes it:
\[
\gamma_f = \frac{F^{bal}_{f,t_0}}{F_{f,t_0}\,10^9/\lambda_f}, \qquad F^{T}_{f,t} = F_{f,t}\,\frac{10^9}{\lambda_f}\,\gamma_f
\tag{5.41}\]
where \(F_{f,t}\) is road use of the fuel (billion liters: gasoline = passenger + 2-3 wheelers; diesel, LPG and gas = passenger + freight + buses) and \(F^{T}_{f,t}\) the result in ktoe. In the base year \(F^{T}\) equals the energy balance. Electricity has a factor only if recon_ele = Yes (default No, factor 1):
\[
E^{T}_t = E_t\,\frac{1000}{\omega}\,\gamma_{e}
\tag{5.42}\]
with \(E_t\) road electricity (billion kWh: buses, 2-3 wheelers, freight, passenger), \(\omega\) GWh per ktoe.
The factors are large where the data explain little of road fuel use: for Egypt, passenger distance × 2.67 (freight 1.70, 2-3 wheelers 3.30), then gasoline × 1.23 (diesel 0.86, gas 1.14). The workbook reports them.






TipPseudocode: calibration



if t == base_year:
    for f in ["gso", "die", "lpg", "nga"]:
        liters = fuel0[pas, gso] + fuel0[cyc, gso] if f == "gso" else fuel0[pas, f] + fuel0[fre, f]
        bottom_up[f] = liters / liters_per_ktoe[f] * 1e9 / (1 - bus_share[f])
        q[f] = 1 if bottom_up[f] == 0 or eb[f] == 0 else eb[f] / bottom_up[f]
    dist_factor[pas] = sum(fuel0[pas, f] * q[f]) / sum(fuel0[pas, f])
    dist_factor[fre] = sum(fuel0[fre, f] * q[f]) / sum(fuel0[fre, f])
    dist_factor[cyc] = q["gso"]
    # ... calibrated fuel use and buses ...
    for f: cf2[f] = 1 if road_liters[f] == 0 or eb[f] == 0 else eb[f] / (road_liters[f] / liters_per_ktoe[f] * 1e9)
    cf2[ecy] = 1 if recon_ele == "No" or elec == 0 or eb[ecy] == 0 else eb[ecy] / (elec / gwh_per_ktoe * 1000)
# held after the base year
trkt[f, t] = road_liters[f, t] / liters_per_ktoe[f] * 1e9 * cf2[f]
trkte[t] = elec[t] * 1000 / gwh_per_ktoe * cf2[ecy]

title: 5  Road transport
text:
5.13 Buses
Buses are not modelled as a fleet. Their base-year fuel use (from the Transport1 fuel shares) moves with passenger energy use:
\[
F_{bus,f,t} = F_{bus,f,t_0}\,\frac{\sum_g F^{kt}_{pas,g,t}}{U_{t_0}}, \qquad E_{bus,t} = \Big(\sum_f F^{kt}_{bus,f,t_0} + E^{kt}_{bus,t_0}\Big)\frac{E^{kt}_{pas,t}}{U_{t_0}}
\tag{5.43}\]
where

\(F_{bus,f,t_0}\) is base-year bus use of diesel, LPG and gas (billion liters);
\(F^{kt}_{pas,g,t}\) is passenger fuel use in ktoe and \(E^{kt}_{pas,t}\) passenger electricity in ktoe;
\(U_{t_0}\) is base-year passenger fuel and electricity use (ktoe, held);
\(E^{kt}_{bus,t_0}\) is base-year bus electricity: the passenger EV stock share of 2024 × base-year bus fuel.

Bus electricity is converted to billion kWh. All base-year bus energy electrifies with passenger electricity, as legacy.

5.14 Results and links to the rest of the model
The engineer model delivers road fuel and electricity use in ktoe, and a set of fleet indicators (A3.9).
Road biofuels follow the engineer gasoline and diesel: bioethanol and other biofuels with gasoline, biodiesel with diesel, as legacy:
\[
F^{T}_{bio,t} = \big(F^{bal}_{bgs,t_0} + F^{bal}_{obf,t_0}\big)\frac{F^{T}_{gso,t}}{F^{bal}_{gso,t_0}} + F^{bal}_{bdi,t_0}\,\frac{F^{T}_{die,t}}{F^{bal}_{die,t_0}}
\tag{5.44}\]
(base-year value held where base-year gasoline or diesel is zero). Base-year biofuels come from Balances or EnergyCons (BalancesOrConsumption). Under the elasticity model road biofuels follow the elasticity gasoline and diesel instead (Chapter 3).

title: 5  Road transport
text:
5.15 Caveats

The engineer model is off by default. It is a calibration that has not been reviewed for every country; results are the elasticity model’s unless a scenario sets TrModel = Engineer.
CPAT Python runs it either way, equal to Excel-AI (test_road_engineer.py).
Calibration factors are large where Transport1 explains only part of road fuel use (for Egypt 30-60%: passenger distance × 2.67, then gasoline × 1.23). Review the data before using the engineer results.
Range anxiety is fitted to one year (2025) of observed EV sales in scenario 1; it is the main lever on the EV share and absorbs whatever the TCO misses.
Freight distance in the TCO is the Transport1 average (Egypt 48,630 km), floored at 50,000 km, which binds in every projection year; fuel use uses the distance derived from fuel shares (Egypt 8,091 km × 1.70). Kept as legacy (open question B14, Section 5.16.5).
Data years of inputs are kept as legacy: VAT on vehicles and customs duties of 2024, import shares of 2022, bus electricity from the 2024 EV share.
The ownership decline limit of 10% a year is a placeholder.
Not built: mode shift, and the road externalities of legacy sheet Transport driven by the engineer model’s distance and fuel economy (the co-benefits module works from fuel use instead).
Parameters are legacy values; the methodology note proposes others (Section 5.3.2).

Reading the effects.

B3 (two-sided ownership calibration) dominates. Egypt’s ownership was 55 per 1,000 in 2025 against a Gompertz level of 152, so the calibration factor is 0.36 instead of legacy’s floor of 1. Passenger ownership reaches 82 per 1,000 in 2041 instead of 173, and road fuel use is a third lower by 2035.
B20 is the largest choice-side fix. Legacy front-loads used ICEV depreciation, which raises used ICEV costs and the EV share; the fix lowers the passenger EV sales share by about 10 points in 2035.
B4 has no effect for Egypt, because ownership still rises after B3.
Fixes with no effect for Egypt (B1, B7, B10, B21, B22) act through policies or fuels that are zero in both Egypt runs: distance tax, EV subsidies, charging subsidy, LPG and LNG trucks. The carbon tax does not enter the legacy feebate because the road feebate coverage (row 2404) is 0. They matter for other countries and scenarios.

5.16.6 Corrections to the survey of legacy






WarningDifferences from legacy CPAT: corrections to the survey






Transport1 holds 220 countries (880 rows of 4 years), not 221; Transport3 has stored values for 194 countries.
B4: the 2026 jump (P4787 = 59.25 against O = 55.12) is the 7.5% growth cap binding (55.12 × 1.075), not a closing-stock mismatch.
B2 also hits 2-3 wheelers (4501 = 4487). For freight it has no effect on the TCO distance because the 50,000 km minimum binds; the effect shows only through 2-3 wheelers and BEV freight from 2038.
B6 also mixes units in bus electricity (5318 adds billion liters of diesel, LPG and gas to billion kWh).
B3: with the data to 2025, actual/expected is 55.1/152.1 = 0.36 (the survey’s 57.8/138.9 is the 2024 column used by legacy).
Not in the survey: B19 (new BEV maintenance at the ICEV rate), B20 (used ICEV and BEV depreciation periods differ), B21 (freight distance output omits LPG and LNG), B22 (gas fuel-economy weights use LPG freight; the EV fallback tests diesel); the BEV freight feebate (4637) uses ICEV discounted km (same values in legacy; fixed as M16); vehicle shares 2078-2081 use the 2022 distance split in every data year; the Transport3 calibration does not hold in this file (open question 3).
Dashboard labels: the charging-station subsidy cells G95:G98 are labelled one row off (start level labelled “start year”, target level “start level”, start year “target year”, target year “target level”); the model reads them by meaning.

5.17 Implementation in Excel-AI and CPAT Python
The engineer model is section 5b of the Excel-AI Mitigation sheet and the block road of CPAT Python. The boxes below hold the implementation notes; the user guides are the Excel-AI tab and the CPAT Python blocks.

Section 5b sits directly after section 5 (Transport), headed “5b. Road transport: engineer model and outputs to the transport co-benefits module”, with the summary row trsum (road fuel and electricity use of the engineer model, ktoe) visible when the section is rolled up. When it was built it held 855 rows with year values or parameters, 75 label rows (a label row names the D:G parameters above every run of rows of one variable that has D:G values; the ScenarioDefinition rows share one) and 19 heading rows. Formula rules. Every calculated row has one formula per row for the base year, 2023-2040 and 2041; 2041 calls a named LAMBDA (light beige), 2023-2040 hold its body with the arguments substituted (at most 100 characters). Rows whose base year is data or a held base-year value have their own base-year formula (95 rows); base-year values that a formula reads from the previous column (the code column) are guarded by IF or N(). Held values (calibration factors, base-year distance split, last-data-year values) carry forward from the previous column, so no cell reads a later column. References are relative in the row (column-relative copy across years and scenario groups).

NoteIn Excel-AI and CPAT Python: switch wiring






Section 5: the elasticity fuel use is the variable enel. ener = ROADSWITCH($D, tr.sw, result rows, enel); D = Inputs column trpos (gasoline 1, diesel 2, LPG 3, gas 4, biofuels 6; 0 elsewhere). With Engineer, road gasoline, diesel, LPG, gas and biofuels of section 5 are those of section 5b in every year (base year: the calibrated value = the energy balance); CO2, revenues, CH4, air pollutants and the totals follow.
Section 3 H: dem = DEMROAD($F, tr.sw, road electricity, previous, multiple); F = Inputs_power column tr (1 for road). From 2023 road electricity demand is the engineer value when switched on (base year: the data).
Biofuels: road biofuels = base year × engine use / base-year use (Equation 5.44).
No circular reference: last year’s power price (base year: the same year’s), last year’s GDP growth, the GDP level after the feedback (which uses last year’s effect); fuel prices do not depend on fuel use.
CPAT Python: the switch is wired as in Excel-AI (fuel_use._use, power.step); the road block runs early in the year loop (after the GDP level and population) and feeds fuel use, power demand, the transport externalities (externalities.transport) and welfare.










NoteIn Excel-AI and CPAT Python: deviations from the reference engine

title: 6  Emissions and emissions trading
text:
6.1 Overview
This chapter turns the fuel use of Chapter 3, Chapter 4 and Chapter 5 into emissions. It covers carbon dioxide from fuel combustion, the other greenhouse gases of the national inventory, methane by source with the methane fee, the comparison with the country’s NDC, and the local air pollutants. It closes with the new emissions trading system (ETS): how its cap becomes a permit price, and how that price enters fuel prices and revenue.
Emissions matter twice in the model. They are an output (the GHG path of each scenario, the change against the baseline, the gap to the NDC) and they feed back: CO2 emission factors convert every carbon price into a price per unit of fuel (Chapter 2), and covered emissions set the ETS price. The carbon pricing indicators (coverage of the carbon tax and the ETS, effective carbon rates, revenue per tonne) are described with the revenues in Chapter 7.
The methodology describes emissions in methodology, section 3.5, the local pollutants in methodology, section 6.4 and the ETS price in methodology, section 3.2.4 and Appendix C.

title: 6  Emissions and emissions trading
text:
6.1.1 Order of calculation
The ETS price is set before the year loop, with the other policies: it depends only on inputs and on stored baseline emissions, never on the fuel use of the year. Inside each year, the emission blocks run after fuel use and power, in this order.





flowchart LR
  P["Policies (all years):<br/>ETS cap and price,<br/>methane fee"] --> F["Year t: power,<br/>fuel use"]
  F --> C["CO2 by sector, fuel,<br/>ETS sector; ETS check"]
  C --> G["Methane by source,<br/>GHG inventory categories"]
  G --> A["Local air<br/>pollutants"]
  A --> K["Kaya identity"]
  K --> N["After the last year:<br/>NDC comparison"]






The CO2 of each subsector and fuel is computed inside the fuel-use block (Chapter 3), and the CO2 of each generation type inside the power block (Chapter 4); this chapter gives the equation once and builds the totals. The NDC rows run after the year loop because they read the baseline in the NDC target year.


6.1.2 Notation and units
Every equation holds for each scenario \(o\) and country \(c\); these indices are omitted. A value of the baseline (scenario 1) in the same year carries the superscript \(B\); the previous year carries \(t-1\). Other indices:







Index
Set




\(s\)
subsector (16; Chapter 3), or a coverage sector \(e\) (power and the 16 subsectors, 17 in all)


\(f\)
fuel (8, plus jet fuel for CO2), or generation type \(k\) (9; Chapter 4)


\(u\)
UNFCCC inventory category: energy, industrial processes (IPPU), agriculture, LULUCF, waste, other


\(p\)
gas: CO2, CH4, N2O, F-gases; or local pollutant: PM2.5, NOx, SO2, VOC, BC, OC, CO


\(j\)
methane source: oil and gas, downstream gas, coal mining, biomass, livestock, rice, waste


\(t\)
year, from the base year \(t_0\) to 2041; \(Y\) is the last year of the country’s GHG inventory



Units: CO2 in Mt; other greenhouse gases in Mt CO2e with the IPCC AR6 GWP100 (fossil methane 29.8, non-fossil methane 27.2); methane by source in kt CH4; local pollutants in kt; fuel use in ktoe. \(\theta\) is PJ per ktoe (0.041868), so fuel use (ktoe) \(\times\ \theta\ \times\) a factor in t CO2 per GJ gives Mt CO2. For Egypt \(Y\) = 2024.

title: 6  Emissions and emissions trading
text:
6.2 Energy CO2
Energy CO2 is fuel use times an emission factor, for every subsector, fuel and generation type. The factors are those of the country, scaled once so that the model’s base year matches the national inventory. The methodology describes this in methodology, sections 3.5.3 and 3.5.4.1.

6.2.1 Emission factors
Each fuel and EF sector has one CO2 factor. The EF sectors are power, road, residential and industry; every subsector reads one of them:



EF sector
Subsectors




power
power generation (by generation type)


road
road, rail, domestic aviation, domestic navigation


residential
residential, food & forestry, services


industry
the eight industrial subsectors and other energy use



The factor is looked up in the IIASA (GAINS) table of the country, else of its World Bank region, else of the world:
\[
ef^{0}_{s,f} = \begin{cases}
ef^{IIASA}_{c \to r \to w}(f', s') / 1000 & \text{fossil fuels} \\
ef^{IEA}_{jet} & f = \text{jet fuel, in every sector} \\
0 & f = \text{biomass}
\end{cases}
\tag{6.1}\]
where

\(ef^{0}_{s,f}\) is the CO2 factor before calibration, t CO2 per GJ;
\(ef^{IIASA}_{c \to r \to w}\) is the factor of sheet EF_GHG in kg CO2 per GJ, for the country \(c\), else its World Bank region \(r\), else the world \(w\) (0 if none), divided by 1000 kg per t;
\((f', s')\) is the fuel and EF sector the row reads: the row’s own, except for the substitutions below;
\(ef^{IEA}_{jet}\) = 0.0715 t CO2 per GJ (IEA, 19.5 tC per TJ \(\times\) 44/12), used for jet fuel in every sector and in domestic aviation.

Some fuel and sector pairs have no factor of their own. They read another, as the methodology’s table of missing factors:



Fuel and sector
Factor used




coal in road
coal in power


LPG in power
LPG in industry


LPG in road
LPG in residential


kerosene in power and in road
kerosene in residential


other oil products in road
diesel in road


biomass, every sector
0



The factors of this table are the model’s data step (A7.1). The local-pollutant and combustion-methane factors follow a different chain, described in Section 6.7.1.


6.2.2 Calibration to the GHG inventory
The IIASA factors include some process and fugitive emissions, and fuel-use data differ between sources. The model therefore scales every CO2 factor by one number, so that modelled base-year CO2 equals the inventory. This is legacy CPAT’s rule (issue I32, replicated by user decision).
\[
\chi = \frac{CO2^{inv}_{t_0 - 1}}{CO2^{B,raw}_{t_0}}, \qquad ef_{s,f} = \chi\, ef^{0}_{s,f}, \qquad ef_k = \chi\, ef^{0}_k
\tag{6.2}\]
where

\(\chi\) (EFCalib) is the calibration factor, 1 when the switch is off;
\(CO2^{inv}_{t_0 - 1}\) is the inventory energy CO2 of the year before the base year (Mt);
\(CO2^{B,raw}_{t_0}\) is scenario-1 energy CO2 of the base year with the uncalibrated factors: the base-year energy balance times \(ef^{0}\) (Mt);
\(ef_{s,f}\), \(ef_k\) are the calibrated factors of subsectors and generation types.

The switch is on by default (Yes*), as legacy, whose two switches EFsAdjustmentAnnexI and EFsAdjustmentNonAnnexI are both Yes*. The model has one switch for all countries.
Why the baseline value is data. A live formula for \(CO2^{B,raw}\) would be circular: the factors feed the carbon prices, which feed fuel use. The uncalibrated scenario-1 CO2 is therefore stored as data, keyed by country, and refreshed by the build, like the ETS baseline (Section 6.9.2). This is exact: scenario-1 fuel use does not depend on the factors (there is no new carbon price in the baseline, and existing carbon pricing changes only after the historical years), so the calibrated baseline is the uncalibrated one times \(\chi\). Another country finds no stored rows until the build has been run for it.
What follows from \(\chi\). Everything downstream uses the calibrated factors: CO2 by subsector, fuel and generation type; the carbon tax, the ETS cost and existing carbon pricing per unit of fuel and their revenue; the ETS baseline; energy CO2 in the GHG totals. Scenario-1 fuel use and prices do not change. In policy scenarios, carbon prices per unit of fuel change by the factor (7% lower for Egypt), so fuel use, revenue and the GDP effect change too.


6.2.3 CO2 by subsector, fuel and coverage sector
With the factors in hand, CO2 is fuel use times the factor (M7.1):
\[
em_{s,f,CO_2} = \theta\, F_{s,f}\, ef_{s,f}, \qquad em_{k,CO_2} = \theta\, PE_k\, ef_k
\tag{6.3}\]
where

\(em_{s,f,CO_2}\) is the CO2 of subsector \(s\) and fuel \(f\) (Mt), co2;
\(F_{s,f}\) is fuel use (ktoe), ener (Chapter 3);
\(PE_k\) is the fuel input of generation type \(k\) (ktoe), pe (Chapter 4), and \(ef_k\) its factor.

The totals sum over fuels, subsectors and generation types:
\[
em_{CO_2} = \sum_{s}\sum_{f} em_{s,f,CO_2} + \sum_{k} em_{k,CO_2}
\tag{6.4}\]
The block also reports CO2 by sector group (transport, buildings, industry, other energy use, power), by fuel (power fuels included), the baseline value of the same year (co2.ref), the change against it (co2.pct, co2.chg) and a check that the totals by group and by fuel both equal the total (co2.chk = 0). CO2 by coverage sector (co2.sec) feeds the ETS check of Section 6.9.2:
\[
em_{e} = \sum_{f} em_{e,f,CO_2} \ (e \ne \text{power}), \qquad em_{pow} = \sum_k em_{k,CO_2}
\tag{6.5}\]






TipPseudocode: energy CO2



# data step, once per country
for (f, s) in co2_ef_rows:                      # fuel x EF sector (pow, rod, res, ind)
    if f == "jfu":   ef0[f, s] = EFJetIEA        # 0.0715 tCO2/GJ
    elif f == "bio": ef0[f, s] = 0
    else:            ef0[f, s] = pick(country, region, world, source_fuel(f, s), source_sector(f, s)) / 1000
EFCalib = inv_energy_co2[base_year - 1] / stored_raw_co2_s1[base_year] if calibrate else 1
ef = EFCalib * ef0

for t in years:
    for s in subsectors:
        for f in fuels:
            co2[s, f][t] = ener[s, f][t] * PJ_PER_KTOE * ef[f, ef_sector(s)]
    for k in gen_types:
        co2["pow", k][t] = pe[k][t] * PJ_PER_KTOE * ef[k]
    co2_total[t] = sum(co2[s, f][t] for s, f) + sum(co2["pow", k][t] for k)
    co2_sec[e][t] = sum over fuels of co2[e, f][t]    # power: sum over types
    co2_ref[t] = co2_total_baseline[t]
    co2_pct[t] = co2_total[t] / co2_ref[t] - 1
    co2_chk[t] = |co2_total - sum by group| + |co2_total - sum by fuel|    # 0

section: 6.3 Methane by source and the methane fee
text:
6.3 Methane by source and the methane fee
Methane is the second greenhouse gas of most inventories and the one a methane fee targets. The model splits the inventory’s methane between seven sources, projects each with its own activity, lets the fee abate it along the source’s cost curve, and collects the fee revenue. The methodology describes this in methodology, section 3.5.4.2 (energy methane) and sections 3.5.5.2 and 3.5.5.3.1 (agriculture and waste).

6.3.2 The methane fee
The fee is a price per tonne of CO2-equivalent methane. It follows a linear path that keeps its slope after the target year, applies only in policy scenarios, and can add the carbon price (M1.8):
\[
MF_t = \Lambda(t;\, T^{m}_0, T^{m}_1, x^{m}_0, x^{m}_1)\ \mathbb{1}[o \ne B] \;+\; NCT_t\ \mathbb{1}[\texttt{CTforMethane} = \text{Yes}]
\tag{6.6}\]
where

\(MF_t\) is the methane fee (USD per t CO2e, real), mfee;
\(\Lambda\) is the linear policy path of Chapter 1, from MPLevelStart in MPIntro to MPLevelTarget in MPOutro, continued linearly after MPOutro (as legacy);
\(\mathbb{1}[o \ne B]\) is 1 in policy scenarios (scenario number above 1, legacy row 2238);
\(NCT_t\) is the carbon price (USD per t CO2), added when CTforMethane = Yes. This part has no scenario condition, as legacy row 2239.



6.3.3 Allocation of inventory methane to sources
The inventory reports methane by category, not by source. The model splits the methane of the last inventory year \(Y\) between the sources of each category. For the four energy sources, each source’s input share is capped by ten times its share of energy activity, and the capped weights are normalised:
\[
w_j = \min\!\left(\mu\,\frac{X^{0}_j}{\sum_{i \in \text{fossil}} X^{0}_i},\ sh_j\right), \qquad
\pi_j = \frac{w_j}{\sum_{i \in \text{fossil}} w_i} \quad (j \in \text{fossil})
\tag{6.7}\]
where

\(sh_j\) is the country’s input share of source \(j\) (CH4Inputs: oil row per_upstream_og, per_downstream_g, per_biomass; coal row per_upstream_c), 0 if missing;
\(X^{0}_j\) is the base-year activity of the source (data): oil plus gas production and coal production from Balances; gas and biomass use from the energy-consumption data of the first year (every column but electricity);
\(\mu\) = 10 (MethShareCap, legacy row 899);
\(\pi_j\) is the share of energy methane allocated to source \(j\).

Livestock and rice take their input shares of agricultural methane (\(\pi_j = sh_j\), rows per_livestock, per_rice); waste takes all waste methane (\(\pi_{wst} = 1\)). The base emissions of each source, in kt CH4, are then
\[
M_{j,0} = M^{inv}_{u(j),Y}\ \pi_j\ \frac{1000}{GWP_j}
\tag{6.8}\]
where

\(M^{inv}_{u(j),Y}\) is the inventory methane of the source’s category (energy, agriculture or waste) in year \(Y\), Mt CO2e (ghg.invb);
\(GWP_j\) is 29.8 for the fossil sources and 27.2 for livestock, rice and waste.

The shares and base emissions are data of the country: they are the same in every scenario, so the calibration is to the observed inventory.


6.3.4 Activity
Each source has an activity that moves its emissions. Downstream gas and biomass follow the scenario’s total use of the fuel (power included), so fuel switching changes their methane. Livestock, rice and waste follow an index driven by income and population:
\[
X_j(t) = X_j(t-1)\,(1 + g^{pc}_t)^{\epsilon^{Y}_{u(j)}}\,(1 + n_t)^{\epsilon^{N}_{u(j)}}, \qquad X_j(t_0) = 1 \qquad (j \in \{\text{liv}, \text{ric}, \text{wst}\})
\tag{6.9}\]
where

\(g^{pc}_t\) is GDP per capita growth and \(n_t\) population growth (Equation 6.24);
\(\epsilon^{Y}\), \(\epsilon^{N}\) are the income and population elasticities of the category: agriculture 0.15 and 0.9, waste 0 and 1 (Section 6.5).

The two extraction sources follow fuel production, \(X_{og} = Prd_{oil} + Prd_{gas}\) and \(X_{cm} = Prd_{coal}\), described next.

Fuel production for supply methane
The model has no production model for fossil fuels. Production follows world demand of the global demand scenario, and responds to the producer price change that the methane fee causes, as legacy rows 6132-6149 (issue I66). First, the fee per ktoe produced, after abatement:
\[
fk_j(t) = MF_t\, GWP_j\, \iota_j \cdot 1000 \cdot \frac{M_{j,0}}{X^{0}_j}\,(1 - a_j(t)), \qquad fk_j(t_0) = 0 \qquad (j \in \{\text{og}, \text{cm}\})
\tag{6.10}\]
where \(\iota_j\) is 1 if the fee applies to the source (fossil fuel production switch), else 0, and \(a_j\) the abatement share of Equation 6.13. \(fk_j\) is in USD per ktoe. Its change raises the producer price index:
\[
\Pi_f(t) = 1 + \frac{fk_{j(f)}(t) - fk_{j(f)}(t-1)}{p^{int}_f(t)\ \gamma_f}\ \phi^{pass}, \qquad \Pi_f(t_0) = 1
\tag{6.11}\]
where

\(j(f)\) is the oil-and-gas source for oil and gas, coal mining for coal;
\(p^{int}_f\) is the international price of the fuel in its own unit (oil per barrel, gas per MMBtu, coal per tonne; Chapter 2);
\(\gamma_f\) is price units per ktoe: 41,868 GJ per ktoe divided by 6.1408 GJ per barrel, 1.055056 GJ per MMBtu or 29.3076 GJ per tonne;
\(\phi^{pass}\) is the pass-through (Manual inputs J194, default 0, so \(\Pi_f = 1\) by default).

Production holds the base-year value in the base year and the next, then grows with the price response and with world demand of the year before:
\[
Prd_f(t) = \begin{cases}
Prd^{0}_f & t \le t_0 + 1 \\
Prd_f(t-1)\ \Pi_f(t)^{\varepsilon_f}\ \dfrac{WD_f(t-1)}{WD_f(t-2)} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{6.12}\]
where

\(Prd^{0}_f\) is base-year production of oil products, coal and gas (Balances, ktoe);
\(\varepsilon_f\) is the price elasticity of production (Manual inputs J190:J192);
\(WD_f\) is world production of the fuel in the IEA scenario GlobalEnergyDemand of scenario 1 (Stated Policies, Announced Pledges, Sustainable Development, Net Zero), Mtoe. As legacy, the third and fourth options both read the Net Zero row.

The source shares use base-year production as their activity, so the shares do not depend on this projection (no loop).



6.3.5 Abatement and emissions
The fee abates methane along a power-function cost curve of the source (A7.3):
\[
a_j(t) = \min\!\Big(1,\ \max\!\big(0,\ A_j\,(MF_t\, GWP_j\, \iota_j)^{B_j}\big)\Big)
\tag{6.13}\]
where

\(a_j\) is the abatement share (ch4.abt);
\(MF_t\,GWP_j\) is the fee per tonne of CH4 (USD);
\(A_j\), \(B_j\) are the curve coefficients of CH4Inputs (avg_pow_a, avg_pow_b) for the country and the source’s curve row; where the country value is 0 or missing, the CH4Inputs average (AVG) is used, as legacy (issue I152);
\(\iota_j\) is the fee switch of the source (Section 6.3.1).

Methane intensity also declines on its own, from the last inventory year:
\[
I_j(t) = (1 - \delta_j)^{\max(0,\ t - Y)}
\tag{6.14}\]
where \(I_j\) is the intensity index (ch4.int) and \(\delta_j\) the source’s rate of autonomous technological improvement (Manual inputs J185:J188; oil and gas also for downstream gas and biomass, issue I141). The emissions of each source combine base emissions, activity, intensity and abatement:
\[
M_j(t) = M_{j,0}\ \frac{X_j(t)}{X^{0}_j}\ I_j(t)\ \big(1 - a_j(t)\big)
\tag{6.15}\]
where \(M_j(t)\) is the methane of source \(j\) in kt CH4 (ch4.em), 0 if \(X^{0}_j = 0\). For livestock, rice and waste \(X^{0}_j = 1\). Fuel-supply methane is \(M^{sup}(t) = \sum_{j \in \text{fossil}} M_j(t)\).


6.3.6 Flaring and the fee revenue
Part of the abated oil-and-gas methane is flared: it burns to CO2 and is reported as energy CO2.
\[
CO2^{flr}_t = r_{fl}\ \phi_{fl}\ M_{og,0}\ \frac{X_{og}(t)}{X^{0}_{og}}\ a_{og}(t)\ /\ 1000
\tag{6.16}\]
where \(CO2^{flr}\) is in Mt (ghg.flr), \(r_{fl}\) = 44/16 = 2.75 t CO2 per t CH4 and \(\phi_{fl}\) the flared share (CH4Inputs oil row per_flare). The fee raises revenue on the methane that remains:
\[
R^{mf}_t = MF_t \sum_j M_j(t)\, GWP_j\, \iota_j\ \frac{1000}{10^{6}}
\tag{6.17}\]
where \(R^{mf}\) is in USD million (ch4.rev), part of total revenue (Chapter 7).






TipPseudocode: methane by source and the methane fee



# data step, once per country
for j in SOURCES:                                  # og, dg, cm, bm, liv, ric, wst
    A[j], B[j] = curve(country, j) or curve("AVG", j)          # 0 or missing: the average
    gwp[j] = GWPCH4F if j in FOSSIL else GWPCH4NF
    fee_on[j] = 1 if fee_switch[j] == "Yes" else 0
act0 = {og: prod0[oil] + prod0[gas], cm: prod0[coal], dg: cons0[gas], bm: cons0[bio], liv: 1, ric: 1, wst: 1}
for j in FOSSIL:
    w[j] = min(MethShareCap * act0[j] / sum(act0[i] for i in FOSSIL), share_input[j])
for j in SOURCES:
    pi[j] = w[j] / sum(w[i] for i in FOSSIL) if j in FOSSIL else (1 if j == wst else share_input[j])
    em0[j] = inv[Y][category(j), "ch4"] * pi[j] * 1000 / gwp[j]          # kt CH4

for t in years:
    mfee[t] = path(t, MPIntro, MPOutro, MPLevelStart, MPLevelTarget, continue_linear=True) * (scenario > 1) \
              + (cptraj[t] if CTforMethane == "Yes" else 0)
    for j in SOURCES:
        abt[j][t] = min(1, max(0, A[j] * (mfee[t] * gwp[j] * fee_on[j]) ** B[j]))
    for j in (og, cm):
        fk[j][t] = 0 if t == t0 else mfee[t] * gwp[j] * fee_on[j] * 1000 * em0[j] / act0[j] * (1 - abt[j][t])
    for f in (oil, gas, coal):
        pidx[f][t] = 1 if t == t0 else 1 + (fk[j(f)][t] - fk[j(f)][t-1]) / (gp_int[f][t] * units_per_ktoe[f]) * pass_through
        prd[f][t] = prod0[f] if t <= t0 + 1 else prd[f][t-1] * pidx[f][t] ** elast[f] * wd[f][t-1] / wd[f][t-2]
    act = {og: prd[oil][t] + prd[gas][t], cm: prd[coal][t], dg: ener["all", gas][t], bm: ener["all", bio][t]}
    for j in (liv, ric, wst):
        act[j] = 1 if t == t0 else act_prev[j] * (1 + gdppc_g[t]) ** el_inc[cat(j)] * (1 + pop_g[t]) ** el_pop[cat(j)]
    for j in SOURCES:
        intensity[j][t] = (1 - decline[j]) ** max(0, t - Y)
        ch4_em[j][t] = em0[j] * act[j] / act0[j] * intensity[j][t] * (1 - abt[j][t]) if act0[j] else 0
    ch4_sup[t] = sum(ch4_em[j][t] for j in FOSSIL)
    flr[t] = FlareCO2perCH4 * flared_share * em0[og] * act[og] / act0[og] * abt[og][t] / 1000     # Mt CO2
    ch4_rev[t] = mfee[t] * sum(ch4_em[j][t] * gwp[j] * fee_on[j] for j) * 1000 / 1e6           # USD m

The memo rows ch4.emf and ch4.revf (the same sum with the stored scenario-1 activity for downstream gas and biomass, sheet BaselineCO2 rows dg, bm, check ch4bs.chk = 0 in scenario 1) are kept but no longer used. See Chapter 7.










WarningDifferences from legacy CPAT






L18, fixed. Legacy holds non-energy methane constant and does not apply the abatement. Here livestock, rice and waste grow with income and population and the fee abates them (LD43).
L19, fixed. Legacy counts the flaring CO2 as methane. Here it is energy CO2 (LD44).
L20, fixed. Legacy’s population growth path differs from UN WPP; the model uses UN WPP.

L135, fixed. Legacy applies the autonomous intensity decline to the energy sources only. Here livestock, rice and waste decline too. Legacy keeps the index at 1 up to 2023 and declines from 2024; the model declines from the last inventory year (I141).
I152, as legacy. Where the country’s curve coefficient is 0 or missing, the average curve is used (legacy Mitigation L6084:M6084).

title: 6  Emissions and emissions trading
section: 6.4 Energy GHGs: combustion methane, N2O and F-gases
text:
6.4 Energy GHGs: combustion methane, N2O and F-gases
The energy category of the inventory holds CO2, methane, N2O and F-gases. CO2 comes from Section 6.2 plus flaring. Methane combines combustion and fuel supply and is scaled to the inventory. N2O and F-gases follow simple rules. The methodology describes these in methodology, sections 3.5.4.2 and 3.5.4.3.

6.4.1 Combustion methane
Every fuel burnt emits some methane. The factor moves on a straight line from its base-year value towards its final value in EFEndYear, and the line continues after that year, as legacy:
\[
w_t = \omega\ \frac{t - t_0}{T^{EF} - t_0}
\tag{6.18}\]
\[
CH4_{s,f}(t) = F_{s,f}(t)\ \frac{e^{0}_{s,f} + (e^{1}_{s,f} - e^{0}_{s,f})\, w_t}{1000}, \qquad CH4_k(t) = PE_k(t)\ \frac{e^{0}_{k} + (e^{1}_{k} - e^{0}_{k})\, w_t}{1000}
\tag{6.19}\]
where

\(w_t\) is the weight of the final factor, 0 in the base year;
\(\omega\) (EFFinShare) follows the factor selection EFSel: Constant 0, Variable 1, Average 0.5;
\(T^{EF}\) = 2039 (EFEndYear, the legacy column of the final factor; later years extrapolate the line);
\(e^{0}\), \(e^{1}\) are the GAINS CH4 factors of the base year and the final year, t per ktoe, looked up as for the local pollutants (Section 6.7.1);
\(CH4_{s,f}\), \(CH4_k\) are in kt CH4 (ch4); power uses the fuel input of the coal, gas, oil and biomass types.

The combustion methane of all subsectors and power is \(CH4^{c}(t)\) (ch4.c), also reported by sector group.


6.4.2 Energy methane, calibrated to the inventory
Combustion plus supply methane, in CO2e, is scaled by one factor so that it equals the inventory in the last inventory year:
\[
k_{CH_4} = \frac{M^{inv}_{enr,Y}}{\big(CH4^{c,B}_{Y} + M^{sup,B}_{Y}\big)\, GWP_F / 1000}
\tag{6.20}\]
\[
E_{enr,CH_4}(t) = k_{CH_4}\ \big(CH4^{c}(t) + M^{sup}(t)\big)\ \frac{GWP_F}{1000}
\tag{6.21}\]
where

\(k_{CH_4}\) is the calibration factor (ghg.k);
\(M^{inv}_{enr,Y}\) is the inventory energy methane in year \(Y\) (Mt CO2e);
\(CH4^{c,B}_{Y}\), \(M^{sup,B}_{Y}\) are the scenario-1 combustion and supply methane of year \(Y\) (kt), stored as data (sheet BaselineCO2 rows ch4c, ch4sup, refreshed by the build), so that the factor, used in every year, reads no later model year (no circular reference);
\(GWP_F\) = 29.8, the fossil GWP;
\(E_{enr,CH_4}\) is energy methane in Mt CO2e.

Energy methane thus equals the inventory in \(Y\) and then moves with fuel use, supply activity and abatement.


6.4.3 Energy CO2, N2O and F-gases
\[
E_{enr,CO_2}(t) = em_{CO_2}(t) + CO2^{flr}_t
\tag{6.22}\]
Energy CO2 is always the model’s (fuel combustion, power included, plus flaring), also in inventory years. Energy N2O and F-gases take the inventory while it has the year; after it, N2O moves with energy CO2 and F-gases are held:
\[
E_{enr,N_2O}(t) = E_{enr,N_2O}(t-1)\ \frac{em_{CO_2}(t)}{em_{CO_2}(t-1)}, \qquad E_{enr,F}(t) = E_{enr,F}(t-1)
\tag{6.23}\]
(the ratio is 1 if last year’s CO2 is 0).






TipPseudocode: energy GHGs



for t in years:
    w = EFFinShare * (t - t0) / (EFEndYear - t0)              # continues after EFEndYear
    for s, f: ch4[s, f][t] = ener[s, f][t] * (ef0_ch4[s, f] + (ef1_ch4[s, f] - ef0_ch4[s, f]) * w) / 1000
    for k in (coal, gas, oil, bio): ch4["pow", k][t] = pe[k][t] * (e0[k] + (e1[k] - e0[k]) * w) / 1000
    ch4_c[t] = sum(ch4[s, f][t]) + sum(ch4["pow", k][t])
    k_ch4 = inv[Y]["enr", "ch4"] / ((stored_ch4c_s1[Y] + stored_ch4sup_s1[Y]) * GWPCH4F / 1000)
    ghg["enr", "co2"][t] = co2_total[t] + flr[t]
    ghg["enr", "ch4"][t] = k_ch4 * (ch4_c[t] + ch4_sup[t]) * GWPCH4F / 1000
    if t in inventory:
        ghg["enr", "n2o"][t], ghg["enr", "fga"][t] = inv[t]["enr", "n2o"], inv[t]["enr", "fga"]
    else:
        ghg["enr", "n2o"][t] = ghg["enr", "n2o"][t-1] * (co2_total[t] / co2_total[t-1] if co2_total[t-1] else 1)
        ghg["enr", "fga"][t] = ghg["enr", "fga"][t-1]








NoteIn Excel-AI and CPAT Python






Excel-AI: combustion CH4 rows ch4 of sections 5-8 (LAMBDA NONCO2, weight EFWEIGHT) and of section 14 (power); ch4.c, ghg.k, ghg (energy rows) in section 14; stored values on sheet BaselineCO2; factors on sheet Inputs_nc (table by legacy EF code).
CPAT Python: fuel_use.py (combustion CH4 of subsectors), emissions.py, ghg() (power CH4, ch4.c, ghg.k, energy rows; EQ-A7.2). The factor reads Excel-AI’s stored scenario-1 values.










WarningDifferences from legacy CPAT






I34. Legacy 465 has the CH4 factor lookups but leaves the factors blank, so its combustion methane is zero. The model fills them from GAINS (country, else World Bank region, else world).
Factor path (LD47, I98). As legacy: linear from the base year to the final factor in 2039, continued after it. Only the base and final GAINS values are used: the yearly legacy paths are proprietary.
Methodology. The methodology calibrates energy methane on 2019 and sets energy F-gases to zero after 2018. The model calibrates on the last inventory year and holds the inventory’s last F-gas value.










NoteCheck: energy methane for Egypt






Combustion methane exceeds inventory energy methane, so \(k_{CH_4}\) is about 0.25 for Egypt.
Open issue I91. Egypt’s inventory breaks after 2021: energy CH4 is 21.9 Mt CO2e in 2021 and 1.9-2.0 in 2022-2024, while the fugitive-emissions memo alone is 20.3 in 2023. Calibrating to 2024, as legacy, may understate energy methane by about 19 Mt CO2e.
Oil, gas and coal production have no production model: they follow world demand from the base year.

title: 6  Emissions and emissions trading
text:
6.5 Other inventory categories
The non-energy categories take the inventory while it has the year. After that, each grows with its own driver: industrial energy CO2 for industrial processes, income and population for agriculture, waste and other, an exogenous decline for LULUCF. The methodology describes these in methodology, section 3.5.5 (A7.2, M7.2).

6.5.1 Drivers
\[
n_t = \frac{pop_t}{pop_{t-1}} - 1, \qquad g^{pc}_t = \frac{1 + g_t}{1 + n_t} - 1, \qquad
\psi_t = \begin{cases} em_{CO_2}(t) / em^{B}_{CO_2}(t) & \texttt{AdditionMitigationPoliciesNonEnergy} = \text{Yes} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{6.24}\]
where

\(pop_t\) is UN WPP population (thousands), \(n_t\) its growth (pop.g);
\(g_t\) is real GDP growth after the GDP feedback (Chapter 7), \(g^{pc}_t\) GDP per capita growth (gdppc.g);
\(\psi_t\) is the mitigation effort in non-energy sectors (ghg.m): the scenario’s energy CO2 over the baseline’s, if the scenario’s switch is on. This option, in effect, extends the carbon price’s effect to non-energy GHGs.

The growth factor of a category is
\[
d_{u,t} = (1 + g^{pc}_t)^{\epsilon^{Y}_u}\,(1 + n_t)^{\epsilon^{N}_u}\ \frac{\psi_t}{\psi_{t-1}}, \qquad d_{u,t_0} = 1
\tag{6.25}\]
with the elasticities of sheet Manual inputs K325:M327, at the legacy addresses (a text entry such as “na” counts as 0):








Category \(u\)
Income elasticity \(\epsilon^{Y}\) (row 327)
Population elasticity \(\epsilon^{N}\) (row 326)




Agriculture
0.15
0.9


Waste
0 (“na”)
1


Other
0 (“na”)
1



These values reproduce the cached results of the legacy run exactly. Legacy Mitigation uses the same values; it never reads the manual cells, whose formula is broken (#REF!).


6.5.2 Projection by category and gas
Each category \(u\) and gas \(p\) takes the inventory value while the inventory has the year:
\[
E_{u,p}(t) = \begin{cases} \text{inventory}_{u,p,t} & t \le Y \\ \text{projection of the table below} & t > Y \end{cases}
\tag{6.26}\]
(energy CO2 and energy methane excepted: they are always modelled, Section 6.4).







Category and gas
Projection after the inventory




Industrial processes, all gases
\(E(t-1)\,(1 + \Delta_t)\) with \(\Delta_t\) the growth of industrial energy CO2 (ghg.gi), if IndustrialProcessEmissionsScaleEner = Yes; else held


Agriculture CO2, N2O, F-gases
\(E(t-1)\, d_{agr,t}\)


Agriculture CH4
livestock and rice methane: \((M_{liv} + M_{ric})\, GWP_{NF} / 1000\)


Waste CO2, N2O, F-gases
\(E(t-1)\, d_{wst,t}\)


Waste CH4
waste methane: \(M_{wst}\, GWP_{NF} / 1000\)


Other, all gases
\(E(t-1)\, d_{oth,t}\)


LULUCF CO2
Equation 6.27


LULUCF CH4, N2O, F-gases
held



The industrial growth may be negative: process emissions decline with industrial CO2, as legacy rows 7553 and 7566-7569.
LULUCF CO2 declines by a share of the last inventory value while it is a source, and is held while it is a sink:
\[
E_{lucf,CO_2}(t) = \begin{cases}
E_{lucf,CO_2}(t-1) & E_{lucf,CO_2}(t-1) < 0 \\
E_{lucf,CO_2}(t-1)\ \dfrac{\psi_t}{\psi_{t-1}} - \delta_{lu}\, \big|E^{inv}_{lucf,CO_2,Y}\big| & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{6.27}\]
where \(\delta_{lu}\) is LULUCFAnnualEmissionsDecline (ScenarioDefinition, share per year of the last inventory value; the methodology’s default is 2.5%) and \(E^{inv}_{lucf,CO_2,Y}\) the inventory value of year \(Y\).


6.5.3 Totals
\[
GHG_t = \sum_{u \ne \text{LULUCF}} \sum_{p} E_{u,p}(t), \qquad GHG^{inc}_t = GHG_t + \sum_p E_{lucf,p}(t)
\tag{6.28}\]
The block reports totals by gas and by category, GHG emissions excluding (ghg) and including LULUCF (ghg.inc), the baseline value (ghg.ref) and the change against it (ghg.pct, ghg.chg).






TipPseudocode: other inventory categories



for t in years:
    pop_g[t] = pop[t] / pop[t-1] - 1
    gdppc_g[t] = (1 + gdp_growth[t]) / (1 + pop_g[t]) - 1
    m[t] = co2_total[t] / co2_ref[t] if AdditionMitigationPoliciesNonEnergy == "Yes" and co2_ref[t] > 0 else 1
    gi[t] = 0 if t == t0 else co2["ind"][t] / co2["ind"][t-1] - 1      # 0 if last year's is 0
    for u in (agr, wst, oth):
        dr[u][t] = 1 if t == t0 else (1 + gdppc_g[t]) ** el_inc[u] * (1 + pop_g[t]) ** el_pop[u] * m[t] / m[t-1]
    for u in (ipr, agr, lucf, wst, oth):
        for p in (co2, ch4, n2o, fga):
            if t in inventory: ghg[u, p][t] = inv[t][u, p]; continue
            prev = ghg[u, p][t-1]
            if u == ipr:   ghg[u, p][t] = prev * (1 + (gi[t] if IndustrialProcessEmissionsScaleEner == "Yes" else 0))
            elif (u, p) == (agr, ch4): ghg[u, p][t] = (ch4_em[liv][t] + ch4_em[ric][t]) * GWPCH4NF / 1000
            elif (u, p) == (wst, ch4): ghg[u, p][t] = ch4_em[wst][t] * GWPCH4NF / 1000
            elif (u, p) == (lucf, co2):
                ghg[u, p][t] = prev if prev < 0 else prev / m[t-1] * m[t] - abs(inv[Y][lucf, co2]) * LULUCFAnnualEmissionsDecline
            elif u == lucf: ghg[u, p][t] = prev
            else:          ghg[u, p][t] = prev * dr[u][t]
    ghg_total[t] = sum(ghg[u, p][t] for u != lucf, p)
    ghg_inc[t] = ghg_total[t] + sum(ghg[lucf, p][t] for p)

ScenarioDefinition AdditionMitigationPoliciesNonEnergy, IndustrialProcessEmissionsScaleEner, LULUCFAnnualEmissionsDecline; elasticities Manual inputs K325:M327 (names GhgElCat, GhgElPop, GhgElInc).
CPAT Python: cpat_model/mitigation/ghg_data.py, inventory(), population(), nonenergy_elasticities(); emissions.py, ghg() (EQ-M7.2, EQ-A7.2).










WarningDifferences from legacy CPAT and the methodology






Industrial processes. The model lets process emissions decline with industrial CO2 in every year (as legacy rows 7553, 7566-7569). The methodology floors the growth at 0 in its first projection year only.
LULUCF. The model holds sinks (negative values) and holds LULUCF CH4, N2O and F-gases. The methodology also subtracts the annual decline from sinks, scales CH4 and N2O by the effort and grows N2O and F-gases with population.
Population (L20). UN WPP population, not legacy’s growth path.
Validation. When the block was introduced, every earlier output was unchanged (the methane fee is 0 in the shipped scenarios). The check recomputes every GHG and combustion-methane row in Python from the data files (scenarios 1 and 2, every year). Sheet LegacyDiff lists the remaining differences.

title: 6  Emissions and emissions trading
text:
6.6 NDC comparison
The NDC rows translate the country’s nationally determined contribution into a target for GHG emissions including LULUCF and measure how far each scenario goes towards it. They compare only: there is no goal seek on the NDC (user decision). The methodology describes the NDC types in methodology, section 3.5.6, with worked examples in Appendix D (A7.4).

6.6.1 Data and choices








Sheet
Content
Source




NDCs
NDC table by country and round (latest, second, first): type, target years, reference year, unconditional and conditional values, LULUCF and gas coverage; key ISO | round
Legacy NDCs rows 48-242 (latest), 250-444 (second), 451-644 (first), columns C-P


GHGHist
Historical GHGs excluding and including LULUCF, CO2 excluding LULUCF, energy CO2, by year; key group | year
Legacy GHGs rows 954-1189



Three choices, read from scenario 1 as legacy:







Input
Options




NDCs
First round, Second round, else the latest (Latest*)


NDCTargetYear
Main* = the first target year; otherwise the second, where given


Conditionality
Unconditional, Conditional, else the average of the two



The target year is at most 2035 (NDCYrCap): later targets are compared in that year. A country without an NDC row is Unquantifiable.


6.6.2 Target level
The target is first built on the NDC’s own basis (gases CO2 or GHGs; LULUCF included or excluded), against the modelled BAU \(B_{ty}\): scenario 1 on that basis in the target year \(ty\). With \(x\) the target value as given (a reduction is negative; Fixed targets in Mt CO2e), the level \(\ell\) is:







Type
Target level \(\ell\)




BAU
\(B_{ty}\,(1 + x)\)


Fixed
\(x\)


Historical
\(H\,(1 + x)\), with \(H\) the emissions of the reference year


Intensity
\(H\ \dfrac{GDP_{ty}}{GDP_{ref}}\ (1 + x)\), real GDP of WEO


Unquantifiable
\(B_{ty}\)



\(H\) is scenario 1 when the reference year is modelled (from the base year), else the GHGs inventory (2021-2024, rows ndc.hc, ndc.hv), else GHGHist. The reduction against the BAU and the target in GHGs including LULUCF are
\[
r = 1 - \frac{\ell}{B_{ty}}, \qquad L^{NDC} = \min\!\big(B^{inc}_{ty},\ B^{inc}_{ty}\,(1 - r)\big)
\tag{6.29}\]
where

\(r\) is computed for the unconditional (\(u\)) and conditional (\(c\)) values; \(r_a\) is their average (the one given if only one; 0 if none); \(r_{sel}\) is the Conditionality choice (\(r_a\) if the chosen one is not given);
\(B^{inc}_{ty}\) is scenario-1 GHGs including LULUCF in the target year;
\(L^{NDC}\) is the target (ndc.lvl), for \(u\), \(c\) and \(sel\), as legacy rows 18494-18496.



6.6.3 Progress against the NDC
For every scenario and year:
\[
red_t = 1 - \frac{GHG^{inc}_t}{GHG^{inc,B}_t}, \qquad gap_t = \frac{red_t}{r_{sel}}, \qquad over_t = GHG^{inc}_t - L^{NDC}_{sel}
\tag{6.30}\]
where

\(red_t\) is the reduction of GHGs including LULUCF against scenario 1 (ndc.red);
\(gap_t\) is the share of the NDC reduction achieved (ndc.gap, legacy “Gap to NDC”; 1 if no reduction is required);
\(over_t\) is the excess over the chosen target (ndc.over); in the target year it is the legacy goal-seek difference (G18501).

The rows also give the target against base-year GHGs including LULUCF (ndc.idx).






TipPseudocode: NDC comparison (after the year loop)



row = ndc_table[country, round(NDCs)]                       # None: Unquantifiable
alt = NDCTargetYear != "Main*" and row.ty2 > 0
ty = min(NDCYrCap, row.ty2 if alt else row.ty1)
basis = ghg_co2 (+ lulucf_co2 if LULUCF included) if gases == "CO2" else (ghg_inc if LULUCF included else ghg)
B_ty, Binc_ty = basis_s1[ty], ghg_inc_s1[ty]
H = basis_s1[ref] if ref modelled else inventory[ref] if ref in 2021..2024 else ghghist[ref]
for v in (u, c):
    f = 1 + x[v]                                            # N/A if not given
    level[v] = {BAU: B_ty*f, Fixed: f-1, Historical: H*f, Intensity: H*gdp[ty]/gdp[ref]*f, Unq: B_ty}[type]
    r[v] = 1 - level[v] / B_ty
r[a] = mean of the given r[u], r[c] (0 if none)
r[sel] = r[Conditionality] if given else r[a]
for v in (u, c, sel): target[v] = min(Binc_ty, Binc_ty * (1 - r[v]))
for t in years:
    red[t] = 1 - ghg_inc[t] / ghg_inc_s1[t]
    gap[t] = red[t] / r[sel] if r[sel] > 0 else 1
    over[t] = ghg_inc[t] - target[sel]
