title: 6  Emissions and emissions trading
text:
6.7 Local air pollutants
The model computes seven local air pollutants from the fuel use of every subsector and of power generation: fine particulate matter (PM2.5), nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulphur dioxide (SO2), volatile organic compounds (VOC), black carbon (BC), organic carbon (OC) and carbon monoxide (CO). They are not part of the GHG totals; a memo converts them to CO2 equivalents. They are also grouped into the sectors of the air-pollution module, which reads them. The methodology describes the emissions in methodology, sections 6.4.2 and 6.4.3 (A7.6).
Units: emissions in kt; factors in t per ktoe; forcing in Mt CO2e (GWP100).

6.7.1 Data and factor lookup








Sheet
Content
Source




EF_NonCO2
Combustion factors by country or World Bank region, GAINS subsector, fuel and pollutant, base year and final, kt per PJ
Legacy sheet EF_PM (GAINS, all countries and regions); also used for combustion CH4


GWP_AP
GWP100 of the pollutants by GAINS region
Legacy GWP table of the pollutant forcing


Countries (column O)
GAINS region of every country (Egypt: afr)
Legacy Countries tab



The factors are those of legacy 465 (Mitigation rows 1052-1663), in a table by legacy EF code. Each factor is chosen in three steps:

EF subsector. Road, rail, aviation (jet fuel), residential, services, construction, other manufacturing, food & forestry and other energy keep their own code. Mining & chemicals, iron & steel, other metals, machinery, cement and fuel transformation take manufacturing (mnf, legacy rows 6388-6395). Navigation, which legacy leaves out (bug L22), takes its own GAINS code nav.
Country, region, world. The factor of the country (egy.mit.ef.<sub>.<fuel>.<pollutant>), else of its World Bank region (CtryReg, Egypt mea), else of the world (wld, absent from the data), else 0. The kt per PJ values are converted to t per ktoe (factor 41.868).
Other energy (oen) takes, for each fuel and pollutant, the maximum factor across the other legacy subsectors (power included), as the legacy note says (issue I147).

Only the fuel and subsector pairs of the legacy table have factors: power (coal, gas, oil, biomass); road (gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene, gas); rail (diesel); aviation (jet fuel); residential (no gasoline or diesel). A pair or pollutant with no factor in the chain gives 0, as legacy: for example power biomass, road kerosene, residential oil, construction coal, gas, oil and biomass, services and other manufacturing coal, organic carbon and SO2 of LPG. None of these pairs burns fuel in Egypt.


6.7.2 Emissions and totals
The factor path is that of combustion methane (Equation 6.18). Emissions are fuel use times the weighted factor, summed over fuels:
\[
AP_{p,s}(t) = \sum_f F_{s,f}(t)\ \frac{(1 - w_t)\, e^{0}_{p,s,f} + w_t\, e^{1}_{p,s,f}}{1000}, \qquad
AP_{p,pow}(t) = \sum_k PE_k(t)\ \frac{(1 - w_t)\, e^{0}_{p,k} + w_t\, e^{1}_{p,k}}{1000}
\tag{6.31}\]
where

\(AP_{p,s}\) is the emission of pollutant \(p\) by subsector \(s\) (kt), ap;
\(e^{0}\), \(e^{1}\) are the base-year and final factors (t per ktoe);
fuel use is the modelled one, so prices, policies and scenarios carry through.

Transport, buildings and industry sum their subsectors, navigation included. A pollutant’s total is all subsectors plus power: \(AP_p = \sum_s AP_{p,s} + AP_{p,pow}\).
The forcing memo converts the emissions with the GWP100 of the country’s GAINS region:
\[
F^{ap}_p = AP_p\ GWP_{p,r} / 1000, \qquad F^{ap} = \sum_{p \in \{BC, OC, NOx, SO2, VOC, CO\}} F^{ap}_p
\tag{6.32}\]
in Mt CO2e (apf). Cooling pollutants (OC, SO2, NOx) have a negative GWP, so the net forcing can be negative. Energy GHGs including the forcing are \(E_{enr} + F^{ap}\) (ghg.enrp, legacy “Total GHGs and PM”, rows 18310 and 18321).


6.7.3 Sectors of the air-pollution module
The air-pollution module reads the emissions grouped in seven sectors, which add up to each pollutant’s total:







Module sector
Content

ground level road

ground level other
residential, services, construction


other
rail, aviation, navigation, industry without construction, other energy use


food & forestry
food & forestry



In each sector, primary organic matter and the rest of PM2.5 are derived:
\[
POM = 1.3\ OC, \qquad PM^{oth} = \max(0,\ PM2.5 - BC - POM)
\tag{6.33}\]
The table follows the layout of the legacy input table (Mitigation rows 15859-15961): one block per module sector and one for all sectors; in each, ten pollutants in legacy order: NOx, SO2, BC, POM, other PM2.5, VOC, CH4, CO, PM2.5, OC; codes aps.<pollutant>.<sector>, in kt (legacy: tonnes). The module reads these rows directly. Methane in the table, as legacy (issue I34):

This methane is not calibrated: it is not scaled by \(k_{CH_4}\).
Food & forestry is also split into food and forestry/agriculture, as legacy (LD53): the food share of each fuel is info_food over the four info_ flows of the processed Balances (legacy rows 501-504, 1666-1673). Rows apfd (food fuel use) and ap.<pollutant>.fod, .fag are memo rows, not in the totals. The share is 0 for Egypt. The module also reads power and residential fuel use (apen) and energy CO2 (apco2).

section: 6.8 Changes against the baseline, grid intensity and the Kaya identity
text:
6.8 Changes against the baseline, grid intensity and the Kaya identity
A few result rows summarise the emissions of each scenario: the change against scenario 1, the carbon intensity of the grid and a Kaya decomposition of CO2.

6.8.1 CO2 and GHG change
\[
\Delta em_{CO_2,x}(t) = em_{CO_2,x}(t) - em^{B}_{CO_2,x}(t), \qquad \Delta E_{x}(t) = E_{x}(t) - E^{B}_{x}(t)
\tag{6.34}\]
cchg is the change of CO2 from fuel combustion by fuel and by sector group, power included (Mt CO2). gchg is the change of GHGs by inventory category (energy, industrial processes, agriculture, LULUCF, waste, other) and by gas (Mt CO2e). Legacy’s “GHG by broad sector” (rows 18229-18243) is the inventory categories, so no allocation of CH4 and N2O to sectors is needed.


6.8.2 Grid emission intensity
\[
EI^{grid}_t = \frac{em_{pow,CO_2}(t) \cdot 10^{6}}{G^{tot}_t \cdot H}
\tag{6.35}\]
where \(EI^{grid}\) is in t CO2 per MWh (co2.grid, 0 if there is no generation), \(G^{tot}\) total generation in MW years (Chapter 4) and \(H\) = 8760 hours per year. Egypt: 0.41 in 2022 (legacy 0.38) and 0.33 in 2030.


6.8.3 Kaya identity
The Kaya identity splits CO2 into population, income, energy intensity and carbon intensity:
\[
CO2 = POP \times \frac{GDP}{POP} \times \frac{TPES}{GDP} \times \frac{CO2}{TPES}
\tag{6.36}\]








Row
Content
Unit




kaya.pop
Population
million


kaya.gpc
GDP per capita: baseline real GDP (the header row, in every scenario) / population
thousand USD


kaya.tpes
Total primary energy supply
ktoe


kaya.ei
Energy intensity: TPES / GDP
ktoe per USD bn


kaya.ci
Carbon intensity: total CO2 including industrial processes (ghg CO2) \(\times\) 1000 / TPES
kt CO2 per ktoe



Total primary energy supply is the fuel use of all sectors (fuels burnt in power plants and biomass included) plus primary electricity, the energy input of nuclear, wind, solar, hydro and other renewables:
\[
TPES_t = \sum_{s,f} F_{s,f}(t) + \sum_{k \in \{nuc, wnd, sol, hyd, orn\}} PE_k(t)
\tag{6.37}\]
The input of a primary type is its generation divided by its efficiency (physical energy content method: nuclear at 38%, renewables at about 1). Each factor is also indexed to the base year of the scenario (kidx: population, GDP, GDP per capita, energy intensity, carbon intensity, CO2). The check kidx.chk, the product of the four factors, equals the CO2 index exactly. Ratios use SAFEDIV (0 when the divisor is 0).

title: 6  Emissions and emissions trading
text:
6.9 The new emissions trading system
A new ETS caps the CO2 of the sectors it covers. The model does not solve for the market price inside the year loop. It sets a permit price from the cap with a closed-form estimate, lets that price act on fuel use like a carbon tax (for the auctioned part) or like a feebate (for the part allocated free), and then reports how close covered emissions come to the cap, with the price that would close the gap. The methodology treats the new ETS price with the carbon prices in methodology, section 3.2.4 and its goal seek in section 3.9.3.5; the user guide in section 1.3.2.4.2.





flowchart LR
  I["Cap, coverage,<br/>benchmarks, volatility"] --> E["Fast estimate<br/>(or override)"]
  E --> P["Permit price p,<br/>tax-equivalent p·V"]
  P --> W["Auctioned part:<br/>price wedge"]
  P --> S["Free part:<br/>shadow price"]
  W --> U["Fuel use, CO2"]
  S --> U
  U --> K["Covered vs cap,<br/>next price"]
  K -. "goal seek" .-> E







6.9.1 Inputs

The sector groups of the ETS benchmarks are power, transport (road, rail, aviation, navigation), residential (residential, food & forestry, services) and industry (the industrial subsectors and other energy use). The semi-elasticity groups are the same, except that food & forestry and services use the industry value. Egypt’s semi-elasticities, per USD per t CO2: power −0.00279, transport −0.00283, residential −0.00386, industry −0.00549.


6.9.2 Coverage, benchmarks and the cap
The ETS is on from its start year, and a sector counts once it is covered and the ETS is on (M1.3):
\[
on_t = \mathbb{1}[\texttt{NewETS} = \text{Yes and } t \ge T^{E}_0], \qquad \kappa_{e,t} = on_t\ \mathbb{1}[\text{sector } e \text{ covered}]
\tag{6.38}\]
The benchmark is the share of a sector’s emission intensity allocated free. It runs linearly from the start to the target year and is flat after; the output-based (OBR) share of a sector is its group’s benchmark, bounded to 0-1:
\[
b_{G,t} = \bar\Lambda\big(t;\, T^{E}_0, T^{E}_1,\, 1 - \alpha_0,\, 1 - \alpha_1\big), \qquad \omega_{e,t} = \min\!\big(1, \max(0, b_{G(e),t})\big)
\tag{6.39}\]
where

\(b_{G,t}\) is the benchmark of group \(G\) (etsb), 0 before the start year;
\(\bar\Lambda\) is the linear path held flat after the target year (Chapter 1);
\(\alpha_0\), \(\alpha_1\) are the auctioned proportions at the start and target year, the same for every group, as legacy (issue I21). The default is \(\alpha = 0\): nothing auctioned, benchmark 1, as legacy;
\(\omega_{e,t}\) is the OBR share (obr); the auctioned share is \(1 - \omega_{e,t}\).

The cap is a change against baseline covered emissions:
\[
bce_t = \sum_e CO2^{B}_{e,t}\ \kappa_{e,t}, \qquad chg_t = \bar\Lambda\big(t;\, T^{E}_0, T^{E}_1, chg_0, chg_1\big)
\tag{6.40}\]
\[
cap_t = \begin{cases}
on_t\ cap_{t-1} & t > T^{E}_1 \text{ and } \texttt{ETSCapCont} = \text{Constant} \\
on_t\ bce_t\,(1 + chg_t) & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{6.41}\]
where

\(CO2^{B}_{e,t}\) is the stored scenario-1 CO2 of ETS sector \(e\) (bco2, Mt), \(bce_t\) baseline covered emissions (ets.bce);
\(chg_t\) is the cap change (ets.chg, negative for a cut), held at \(chg_1\) after the target year, so that “any other” continuation keeps the relative change;
\(cap_t\) is the cap (ets.cap, Mt).



6.9.3 Fast price estimate and the permit price
Price volatility makes an ETS less effective than a tax at the same price. The model expresses this as a volatility adjustment, the tax-equivalent value of one dollar of permit price:
\[
V = \frac{1 + risk \cdot imp}{1 + vol \cdot imp}
\tag{6.42}\]
where \(V\) is ets.vadj, \(risk\) the carbon tax policy risk and \(vol\), \(imp\) the values of the labels above. At Medium: \((1 + 0.2 \times 0.5)/(1 + 0.42 \times 0.5) = 1/1.1\).
The covered semi-elasticity weights each covered sector’s semi-elasticity by its baseline emissions and discounts the free part by the effectiveness of output-based allocation:
\[
\bar\sigma_t = \frac{\sum_e CO2^{B}_{e,t}\ \kappa_{e,t}\ \sigma_e\ \big(1 - (1 - \vartheta)\,\omega_{e,t}\big)}{bce_t}
\tag{6.43}\]
where \(\bar\sigma_t\) is ets.se (0 if \(bce_t = 0\)), \(\sigma_e\) the semi-elasticity of the sector’s group (per USD per t CO2) and \(\vartheta\) = 0.5 the effectiveness of output-based allocation (auctioned allowances count fully).
If emissions respond to the price as \(\ln(\text{covered}/bce) = \bar\sigma\, V\, p\), the price that meets the cap is (A1.1):
\[
\hat p^{E}_t = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{\ln(cap_t / bce_t)}{\bar\sigma_t\ V} & on_t = 1,\ 0 < cap_t < bce_t,\ \bar\sigma_t < 0,\ V > 0 \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{6.44}\]
The permit price used is the override row if the switch is on, else the fast estimate:
\[
p^{E}_t = on_t \times \begin{cases}
ovr_t \ (\text{blank: the carbon price path } NCT_t) & \texttt{ETSPriceOverride} = \text{Yes} \\
\hat p^{E}_t & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{6.45}\]
\[
\tilde p^{E}_t = p^{E}_t\, V, \qquad \rho = 1 / V
\tag{6.46}\]
where \(\tilde p^{E}\) is the tax-equivalent price (ets.pe) and \(\rho\) the revenue factor (ets.rf), the permit price per dollar of tax-equivalent price. All prices are USD per t CO2, real.


6.9.4 Effect on fuel use and revenue
The ETS replaces the carbon tax in covered sectors: the new carbon tax applies only where \(\kappa_{e,t} = 0\) (Chapter 2). The tax-equivalent price splits by the OBR share (M1.3, M1.4):
\[
A_{e,t} = \tilde p^{E}_t\ \kappa_{e,t}\ (1 - \omega_{e,t}), \qquad
\Sigma_{e,t} = \big(b^{fb}_{G(e),t} + reg_{e,t}\big)\, a\ \mathbb{1}[\text{feebate covers } e] + \tilde p^{E}_t\ \kappa_{e,t}\ \omega_{e,t}
\tag{6.47}\]
where

\(A_{e,t}\) is the price wedge, the auctioned part (etr, USD per t CO2). Times the CO2 factor of each fuel, it enters the after-tax fuel price, so usage and efficiency both respond, as for a carbon tax (Chapter 2, Chapter 3);
\(\Sigma_{e,t}\) is the shadow price (shpx): the ETS part, the free (OBR) share, is added to the feebate and regulation shadow price. It acts only on the efficiency margin of fuel use, as feebates do, and raises no revenue.

New-policy revenue includes the price wedge times the revenue factor \(\rho\): the permit price on the auctioned part of covered emissions. In power, the new-policy revenue deducts \(em_{k,CO_2}\, A_{pow}\, (1 - \rho)\). VAT on new policies is levied on the tax-equivalent ETS cost. The revenue equations are in Chapter 7.


6.9.5 Meeting the cap
The fast estimate uses one semi-elasticity, so the full model, where the response comes from prices and elasticities by fuel and subsector, does not hit the cap exactly. After CO2 is known, the model reports covered emissions, the gap and a proposed price for the next iteration:
\[
cov_t = \sum_e em_{e,t}\ \kappa_{e,t}, \qquad gap_t = \frac{cov_t}{cap_t} - 1
\tag{6.48}\]
\[
lr_t = \frac{\ln(cap_t / bce_t)}{\ln(cov_t / bce_t)}, \qquad
p^{next}_t = \begin{cases} \hat p^{E}_t & p^{E}_t \le 0 \text{ or } lr_t = 0 \\ p^{E}_t\ lr_t^{\,\beta} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{6.49}\]
where

\(cov_t\) is covered CO2 (co2.ets), \(em_{e,t}\) the CO2 of ETS sector \(e\) (Equation 6.5);
\(gap_t\) is co2.gap (0 if there is no cap), 0 when the cap is met;
\(lr_t\) is the log ratio (ets.lr), 0 if \(cap_t \le 0\), \(cap_t \ge bce_t\) or \(cov_t \ge bce_t\) (the cap does not bind);
\(\beta\) = 0.5 is the convergence exponent (Settings C15), as legacy’s PricesAdjustedByErrorFactor;
\(p^{next}_t\) is the proposed price (ets.next).

To meet the cap, the proposed prices are fed back into the override row (with the override switch on) and the model is run again. The goal seek automates this with legacy’s damped log-space step:

start from the fast estimate, or from the override row if it holds prices (setting ETSStartFreshContinue: StartFresh always starts from the fast estimate);
step \(p \leftarrow p\,(p^{next}/p)^{\alpha}\) (a linear step if a price is 0);
mix with the previous iterate (weight 0.3) from the second iteration;
smooth lightly: 5% weight on a centred 3-year moving average;
negative or invalid values keep the current price;
halve \(\alpha\) when the worst error grows (minimum 0.0625), multiply it by 1.2 when the error more than halves (maximum 1);
stop when the worst yearly \(|cov_t/cap_t - 1|\) over the ETS years is below the maximum error, or after the maximum number of iterations.

TipPseudocode: the new ETS



# policies, all years (before the year loop)
for t in years:
    on[t] = NewETS == "Yes" and t >= ETSIntro
    for e in ets_sectors: etsc[e][t] = 1 if on[t] and etscov[e] else 0
    for G in (pow, tra, res, ind):
        etsb[G][t] = 0 if t < ETSIntro else lin(min(t, ETSOutro), ETSIntro, ETSOutro, 1 - ETSAuctStart, 1 - ETSAuctTarget)
    for e in ets_sectors: obr[e][t] = min(1, max(0, etsb[group(e)][t]))
vadj = (1 + ETSCTRisk * imp[ETSVolImpact]) / (1 + vol[ETSVolatility] * imp[ETSVolImpact])
for t in years:
    bce[t] = sum(bco2[e][t] * etsc[e][t] for e)                   # stored scenario-1 CO2
    chg[t] = lin(min(t, ETSOutro), ETSIntro, ETSOutro, ETSChangeRelStart, ETSChangeRelTarget)
    if not on[t]: cap[t] = 0
    elif t > ETSOutro and ETSCapCont == "Constant": cap[t] = cap[t-1]
    else: cap[t] = bce[t] * (1 + chg[t])
    se[t] = sum(bco2[e][t] * etsc[e][t] * semi[e] * (1 - (1 - OBREff) * obr[e][t]) for e) / bce[t] if bce[t] > 0 else 0
    est[t] = log(cap[t] / bce[t]) / (se[t] * vadj) if on[t] and 0 < cap[t] < bce[t] and se[t] < 0 and vadj > 0 else 0
    p[t] = 0 if not on[t] else ((ovr[t] if ovr[t] != blank else cptraj[t]) if ETSPriceOverride == "Yes" else est[t])
    pe[t], rf = p[t] * vadj, 1 / vadj
    for e in ets_sectors:
        etr[e][t]  = pe[t] * etsc[e][t] * (1 - obr[e][t])                       # price wedge
        shpx[e][t] = fb[group(e)][t] * ssc[e] + reg[e][t] + pe[t] * etsc[e][t] * obr[e][t]

# year loop, after CO2
for t in years:
    covered[t] = sum(co2_sec[e][t] * etsc[e][t] for e)
    gap[t] = covered[t] / cap[t] - 1 if cap[t] > 0 else 0
    lr[t] = 0 if cap[t] <= 0 or cap[t] >= bce[t] or covered[t] >= bce[t] else log(cap[t]/bce[t]) / log(covered[t]/bce[t])
    next_p[t] = est[t] if p[t] <= 0 or lr[t] == 0 else p[t] * lr[t] ** ETSNextPriceExponent

6.9.6 Limits

Power is covered like any other sector: the power model gives its emissions, and the ETS cost enters its generation cost (Chapter 4).
Benchmarks are relative to current emission intensity, and output is proxied by fuel use. Free allocation therefore moves with emissions, and the OBR share equals the benchmark. Benchmarks by sector are not built yet: every group takes the scenario’s auctioned proportion.
The volatility adjustment scales behaviour (the tax-equivalent price), not the permit price.
No banking, borrowing, price floors or ceilings, and no CBAM process emissions (the legacy CBAM block is placed but not read; industrial process CO2 of the inventory is separate and untaxed).

NoteDesign note: benchmarks instead of one auction share





This note records the design proposed for the model’s ETS. Today the model uses legacy’s one auctioned share per scenario (LD7); the benchmark-based design below is the intended extension. Everything after the split stays as in the legacy split.

Inputs per subsector: the covered flag and a benchmark path \(b(t)\), a share of the subsector’s base-year emission intensity (for example 0.9: free allocation at 90% of base-year intensity; a declining path tightens it).
Shares. Free allocation \(FA = b \times\) base-year intensity \(\times\) output, with output proxied by baseline fuel use (the model has no output variable). OBR share \(s = \min(FA / \text{covered emissions}, 1)\); auctioned share \(a = 1 - s\). To first order \(s \approx b\) (intensity unchanged). Using actual covered emissions would be circular through fuel use, so the recommendation is scenario-1 (baseline) covered emissions (option A of the cap design note); \(s\) is then a data-driven input.
Then as legacy. Effectiveness \(e = a + 0.5\, s\) per subsector; the auctioned part \(p \times a\) is a price wedge (revenue = \(p \times\) (covered emissions − FA)); the OBR part \(p \times s\) joins the sector shadow price (the feebate channel); the fast estimate \(p\) = (reduction left for the ETS) / \((\varepsilon\, e)\), with \(\varepsilon\) and \(e\) weighted by covered baseline emissions.
Override. An offline goal seek (a Python script with the same damped log-space step) writes a row of prices to paste. No VBA and no circular reference.

Without benchmarks the ETS is fully effective (permit price = carbon price path \(\times\) coverage, as effective as a carbon tax, per an earlier user decision), and the auction share only affects revenue. With benchmarks, the OBR part moves from the price wedge to the shadow price, so emissions fall less for the same \(p\), and revenue falls. A benchmark of 0 (full auctioning) reproduces the fully effective case exactly.
Open points.

The fast estimate uses legacy’s sector semi-elasticities. The model could derive them from its own elasticities (a one-off calibration run) to keep them consistent.
Legacy’s linear split (\(p \times a\)) against a log form (legacy’s own TBC note).
Legacy’s relative price 1.1 (auctioned ETS against tax) and the risk-premium inputs (rows 1811-1813) are not used by the legacy fast estimate as cached; the model uses them through \(V\) (LD8).
The CBAM sector semi-elasticity (−0.001) is not modelled.

title: 7  Revenues, GDP and welfare
text:
7.1 Header and summary rows
This chapter follows the money. Once the model knows how much of each fuel is used and how much electricity is generated in a year, it can say what the government collects and what it pays out, how spending that revenue moves GDP, how the energy import bill changes, how heavily carbon is priced in effect, and what the policy is worth to society once climate damages, air pollution, road externalities and efficiency costs are counted.
The blocks of the chapter, in the order the model computes them within a year:
The GDP effect of a year acts on GDP only in the following year. That one-year lag is the only link from year \(t\) to year \(t+1\) in this chapter, and it is what keeps the model free of circular references (Section 7.3.7).
Notation. Every equation holds for each scenario \(o\) and country \(c\); these indices are omitted. The year \(t\) is shown only where an equation reaches into another year. A superscript \(B\) marks the value of the baseline (scenario 1) in the same year, and \(\Delta x = x - x^{B}\). Subsector \(s\), sector group \(g\) (transport, buildings, industry, other energy use, power) and fuel \(f\) follow Chapter 1. Equation ids in brackets, such as (M6.1), point to the equation list.
A handful of macro rows sit at the top of every scenario: they give the GDP against which revenues, trade and welfare are scaled. Every section of the model also ends with a summary row, so the results can be read at a glance.

title: 7  Revenues, GDP and welfare
text:
7.2 Revenues
Revenue is computed fuel by fuel and subsector by subsector: fuel use times a tax, subsidy or policy rate per GJ. The model keeps three separate lines (existing taxes, existing subsidies, new policies), adds the power sector, subsidy reforms, producer subsidies and the methane fee, and then rearranges the same money by fuel and by policy instrument. The methodology describes this in section 3.6, Fiscal revenues.
All revenue rows are in USD million, real. A negative number is a fiscal cost (a subsidy).

7.2.1 Revenue of each fuel and subsector
For each subsector \(s\) and fuel \(f\), the price block of the fuel (Chapter 2) gives the components of the retail price per GJ. Revenue multiplies them by fuel use.
Existing taxes include excise and other taxes, the VAT payment, and the change in existing carbon pricing against the year embedded in the price data, with VAT on that change (M6.2):
\[
revExi_{s,f} = \theta\,F_{s,f}\left(txo^{+}_{c} + vat_{c} + \Delta xcp_{s,f}\,(1 + v_{s,f})\right)
\tag{7.2}\]
Existing consumer subsidies are the negative part of the existing taxes:
\[
cs_{s,f} = \theta\,F_{s,f}\,txo^{-}_{c}
\tag{7.3}\]
New policies are the new carbon tax, the new excise (fuel price reform, and Pigouvian taxes where they are switched on), the ETS cost on the auctioned part, and VAT on all of them (M6.1):
\[
rev^{new}_{s,f} = \theta\,F_{s,f}\left(nct_{s,f} + nexc_{s,f} + \rho\,nets_{s,f} + v_{s,f}\,nce_{s,f}\right)
\tag{7.4}\]
Subsidy reform removes consumer subsidies and price controls as separate policy lines; its revenue includes VAT:
\[
rev^{sr}_{s,f} = \theta\,F_{s,f}\,(csw_{s,f} + pcw_{s,f})\,(1 + v_{s,f})
\tag{7.5}\]
where

\(c = c(s,f)\) is the price fuel of the pair (its price position in the price blocks);
\(txo^{+}_{c}\), \(txo^{-}_{c}\) are the positive part (taxes, etx) and negative part (subsidies, esub) of excise and other taxes, USD/GJ;
\(vat_{c}\) is the VAT payment on the price before new policies (vat), USD/GJ;
\(\Delta xcp_{s,f}\) is the change in existing carbon pricing against the price data (xcpd), USD/GJ;
\(v_{s,f}\) is the VAT rate of the pair (Inputs), share;
\(nct\), \(nexc\), \(nets\) are the new carbon tax (ctxnew), new excise (ntx) and ETS cost (ets), USD/GJ, and \(nce\) their total (nce);
\(\rho\) is the ETS revenue factor, the auctioned share (ets.rf); feebates are revenue-neutral and raise nothing;
\(csw\), \(pcw\) are the consumer subsidy reform wedge and the price-control phase-out wedge of the subsector (csw, pcw; Chapter 2), USD/GJ.

Two splits of the same money are kept per pair for the report by instrument (Section 7.2.5): the new excise and the VAT.
\[
rev^{exc}_{s,f} = \theta\,F_{s,f}\,nexc_{s,f}, \qquad
rev^{vat}_{s,f} = \theta\,F_{s,f}\left(vat_{c} + (\Delta xcp_{s,f} + nce_{s,f} + csw_{s,f} + pcw_{s,f})\,v_{s,f}\right)
\tag{7.6}\]
A memo row gives the level of existing carbon pricing, \(rev^{xcp}_{s,f} = \theta\,F_{s,f}\,xcp_{s,f}\) (rxcp). Only its change against the price data is revenue (inside Equation 7.2); the part embedded in the price data is already in the excise.

for t in years:
    for s in subsectors:
        for f in fuels:
            c = price_fuel[f, s]; q = ener[f, s, t] * PJ_PER_KTOE
            v = vat_rate[f, s]
            rtx[f, s, t]  = q * (etx[c, t] + vat[c, t] + xcpd[f, s, t] * (1 + v))
            rsub[f, s, t] = q * esub[c, t]                               # negative
            rnew[f, s, t] = q * (ctxnew[f, s, t] + ntx[f, s, t]
                                 + ets[f, s, t] * ets_rf[t] + nce[f, s, t] * v)
            rsr[f, s, t]  = q * (csw[f, s, t] + pcw[f, s, t]) * (1 + v)
            rex[f, s, t]  = q * ntx[f, s, t]
            wedge = xcpd[f, s, t] + nce[f, s, t] + csw[f, s, t] + pcw[f, s, t]
            rvt[f, s, t]  = q * (vat[c, t] + wedge * v)
            rxcp[f, s, t] = q * xcp[f, s, t]                             # memo




7.2.2 Power-sector revenues
The power sector raises revenue in two places: on the fuels burnt in power plants, and on the electricity sold to users. Both are computed in the power block (Chapter 4) and summed here (A6.1).
By generation type \(k\) (coal, gas, oil, nuclear, wind, solar, hydro, other renewables, biomass):
\[
\begin{aligned}
rev^{tx}_{k}  &= \delta_k\,\theta\,PE_k\,(txo^{+} + vat)_{c(k)} && \text{existing fuel taxes }(\texttt{prtx})\\
rev^{sub}_{k} &= \delta_k\,\theta\,PE_k\,txo^{-}_{c(k)} && \text{existing fuel subsidies }(\texttt{prsub})\\
rev^{xc}_{k}  &= xc_k\,H\,G_k && \text{change in existing carbon pricing }(\texttt{prxc})\\
rev^{new}_{k} &= pc_k\,H\,G_k - CO2_k\,A_{pow}\,(1 - \rho) && \text{new policies }(\texttt{prnew})\\
rev^{rns}_{k} &= rns_k\,H\,G_k && \text{renewable subsidies }(\texttt{prrns}\text{, negative})
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.7}\]
where

\(\delta_k\) is 1 for a type that burns a fuel (coal, gas, oil, biomass), else 0;
\(PE_k\) is the fuel use of type \(k\) (pe), ktoe, and \(c(k)\) its price fuel;
\(G_k\) is generation (gen_mwy), MW-years, and \(H\) converts MW-years to million kWh (MWyMkWh, 8.76);
\(xc_k\), \(pc_k\) are the existing carbon cost and the new policy cost per kWh of the type (xck, xac), USD/kWh;
\(CO2_k\) is the CO2 of the type, MtCO2, and \(A_{pow}\) the ETS cost rate of power (etr), USD/tCO2: the free part of the ETS, \(1-\rho\), is not revenue, so the ETS counts at the permit price on the auctioned part only;
\(rns_k\) is the renewable subsidy per kWh (rns), USD/kWh.

A memo row gives the level of existing carbon pricing of each type, prxl = \(CO2_k\) times the existing carbon tax and ETS prices of the price data year.
By electricity user group \(u\) (residential, industry):
\[
\begin{aligned}
rev^{vat}_{u}  &= pp_u\,\frac{v_u}{1+v_u}\,cons_u && \text{VAT on electricity }(\texttt{rvat})\\
rev^{nvat}_{u} &= \left(\overline{pc}\,\pi\,(1 - rb) + x_u\right) v_u\,cons_u && \text{VAT on the policy cost passed through }(\texttt{rnvat})\\
rev^{reb}_{u}  &= -\,rb\,\overline{pc}\,\pi\,cons_u && \text{rebate of the carbon cost }(\texttt{rreb}\text{, negative})\\
rev^{x}_{u}    &= x_u\,cons_u && \text{electricity excise }(\texttt{rpex})\\
rev^{gap}_{u}  &= gap_u\,cons_u && \text{electricity subsidy gap }(\texttt{rgap}\text{, negative})
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.8}\]
where \(pp_u\) is the electricity price before policies (rppre), \(\overline{pc}\) the average policy cost of generation (ccpav), \(\pi\) the pass-through of the power-sector price change (PowerSectorPriceChangePassOn), \(rb\) the rebate switch (rbs), \(x_u\) the electricity excise (pex), \(gap_u\) the subsidy gap (sgap), all per kWh, \(v_u\) the VAT rate and \(cons_u\) consumption in million kWh. The excise splits into the excise of the scenario “Electricity excise” (rexs = exs times total consumption) and the manual excise (rexm, the rest).
The power sector’s lines of the three revenue totals are then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
rev^{tx}_{pow}  &= \textstyle\sum_k (rev^{tx}_{k} + rev^{xc}_{k}) + \sum_u rev^{vat}_{u}\\
rev^{sub}_{pow} &= \textstyle\sum_k (rev^{sub}_{k} + rev^{rns}_{k}) + \sum_u rev^{gap}_{u}\\
rev^{new}_{pow} &= \textstyle\sum_k rev^{new}_{k} + \sum_u (rev^{nvat}_{u} + rev^{reb}_{u} + rev^{x}_{u})
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.9}\]
Subsidy reform raises nothing in power (rsr.pow = 0).


7.2.3 Producer subsidies and the methane fee
Producer subsidies are a fiscal cost outside the fuel and subsector pairs. For each fuel group \(f\) (coal, gas, oil, biomass, electricity), the subsidy before any phase-out is scaled by the phase-out factor:
\[
rev^{psu} = -\sum_{f} pros_f\,psf_f, \qquad psf_f = 1 - \psi_f\,(1 - pof)
\tag{7.10}\]
where

\(pros_f\) is the producer subsidy before the phase-out (pros), USD million: price data (USD bn nominal) times the CPI factor up to the last price year, then held;
\(\psi_f\) is the inclusion switch of the fuel and \(pof\) the phase-out factor of producer subsidies (Chapter 2);
\(psf_f\) is the share that remains (psf).

The phase-out also lowers the supply cost and so the prices (Chapter 2); this row is its fiscal line (rpsu).
The methane fee raises \(rev^{mf}\) (rmf = ch4.rev): methane emissions of the sources the fee covers, times their global warming potential, times the fee. It is computed with the methane block (Chapter 6). It is not a fuel revenue, so it appears in the totals and in the report by instrument, not in the report by fuel.


7.2.4 Totals
The totals add the pairs over subsectors and fuels and add the power line. Net revenue from existing taxes and subsidies, and total revenue (M6.3):
\[
rev^{net} = \sum_{s,f} (revExi_{s,f} + cs_{s,f}) + rev^{tx}_{pow} + rev^{sub}_{pow}
\tag{7.11}\]
\[
rev = rev^{net} + rev^{new} + rev^{sr} + rev^{psu} + rev^{mf}
\tag{7.12}\]
\[
\Delta rev = rev - rev^{B}
\tag{7.13}\]
where \(rev^{new} = \sum_{s,f} rev^{new}_{s,f} + rev^{new}_{pow}\) and \(rev^{sr} = \sum_{s,f} rev^{sr}_{s,f}\). The lines rtx, rsub, rnew, rxcp and rsr are also summed by sector group (transport, buildings, industry, other energy use) and given for power.

7.2.5 Fiscal reports
The fiscal reports (block 12d) rearrange the same revenue three ways: by fuel, by policy instrument, and against GDP. Each report has a check row that must be 0, because it splits the totals exactly.
Revenue by fuel, net of subsidies. For each final-use fuel, the existing taxes, subsidies, new policies and subsidy reform over all subsectors. Electricity collects its VAT, subsidy gap, VAT on the policy cost, rebates, excise and renewable subsidies. Fuels burnt in power plants have their own rows:
\[
rfu_{f} = \sum_{s} \left(revExi_{s,f} + cs_{s,f} + rev^{new}_{s,f} + rev^{sr}_{s,f}\right), \qquad
rfu_{ecy} = \sum_u \left(rev^{vat}_u + rev^{nvat}_u + rev^{reb}_u + rev^{x}_u + rev^{gap}_u\right) + \sum_k rev^{rns}_k
\tag{7.14}\]
\[
rfg_{k} = rev^{tx}_{k} + rev^{xc}_{k} + rev^{sub}_{k} + rev^{new}_{k}, \qquad k \in \{\text{coal, gas, oil, biomass}\}
\tag{7.15}\]
The check rfu.chk = \(\left|\sum_f rfu_f + rfu_{ecy} + \sum_k rfg_k - rev^{net} - rev^{new} - rev^{sr}\right|\) is 0. The methane fee and producer subsidies are not fuel revenues and are not in these rows.
Total revenue by policy instrument (block 12e, A6.2). The same total, split by the instrument that raises it:

title: 7  Revenues, GDP and welfare
text:
7.3 GDP effects
The policies change what the government collects. The model assumes that the extra revenue is spent, in shares the user chooses, on tax cuts, investment, current spending or transfers. Fiscal multipliers translate each use into a change in GDP over the following years. The higher energy taxes themselves weigh on GDP too, at the excise multiplier. The resulting change in the GDP level then feeds back into GDP growth, which drives fuel use, power demand and the non-energy GHG drivers.
The methodology describes the multipliers in chapter 4 and the feedback in section 4.7, GDP feedback in CPAT. The model follows legacy CPAT section 17, with legacy bug L24 fixed.

7.3.2 Fiscal multipliers
A multiplier says by how many percent GDP responds, in the year of a fiscal change and in each later year, to a change of a fiscal instrument by 1% of GDP. The model holds one multiplier per instrument \(i\) and lag \(k = 0, \dots, 19\) (A8.1):
\[
m_{i}(k) = \bar{m}_{G,i}\big(\min(k, k^{last})\big) + \sigma\,s_{G,i}\big(\min(k, k^{last})\big)
\tag{7.18}\]
where

\(G\) is the multiplier group (fis.grp): global, the country’s income group (HIC, UMIC, LMIC, LIC), the country’s estimated table, or the manual table;
\(\bar{m}_{G,i}(k)\) is the multiplier of the group at lag \(k\): for global and income groups, the median of the World Bank’s MFMod (methodology 4.3, 4.4);
\(s_{G,i}(k)\) is the standard deviation of the income group, and \(\sigma\) is 0 for Base, −1 for Low, +1 for High;
\(k^{last}\) is the last lag with data (11): lags 12-19 hold the lag-11 value, as in legacy.

7.3.3 Fiscal space
The fiscal space is the revenue the scenario gains over the baseline, as a share of baseline GDP. It is total revenue: existing taxes net of subsidies (power included), new policies, subsidy reform, producer subsidies and the methane fee (M8.1):
\[
rev^{fis} = rev^{net} + rev^{new} + rev^{sr} + rev^{psu} + rev^{mf}
\tag{7.19}\]
\[
fs_t = \frac{rev^{fis}_t - rev^{fis,B}_t}{Y^{0}_t\,M}
\tag{7.20}\]
where \(rev^{fis}\) is in USD million (fis.rev; equal to \(rev\) of Equation 7.12), \(rev^{fis,B}\) is that of scenario 1 in the same year (fis.ref), and \(fs\) is the fiscal space (fis.sp), share of GDP.
Lower fuel use also lowers the cost of existing subsidies (base erosion, Equation 7.16), and that counts. The methane fee counts on the scenario’s own methane activity. In the baseline, \(fs = 0\), so scenario 1 has no GDP effect.


7.3.4 Fiscal impulse
The impulse of a year is the new revenue gain of that year: the change in the gain in USD, over this year’s GDP. It is 0 before the start year of the GDP calculations:
\[
imp_t =
\begin{cases}
0 & t < t^{GDP}\\[2pt]
fs_{t} & t = t_0 \ge t^{GDP}\\[2pt]
fs_t - fs_{t-1}\,\dfrac{Y^{0}_{t-1}}{Y^{0}_t} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{7.21}\]
where \(t^{GDP}\) is GDPStartYear, \(t_0\) the base year and \(imp_t\) the impulse (fis.imp), share of GDP.
The revenue uses take the impulse only from the year the carbon price starts, as legacy does (it sets the revenue-use shares to 0 before then):
\[
imp^{p}_t = \begin{cases} 0 & t < T^{ct}_0\\ imp_t & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
\tag{7.22}\]
where \(T^{ct}_0\) is the carbon pricing start year (CPIntro) and \(imp^{p}\) is fis.impp. Earlier impulses still act through the excise drag.
Each impulse starts a cohort that acts for 20 years. The rows fis.lag.l1 … fis.lag.l19 (and fis.lagp.l1 … fis.lagp.l19 for \(imp^{p}\)) hold the impulses of the 19 earlier years: each is the previous year’s value of the row above it, and 0 in the base year.


7.3.5 GDP effect of each use
The effect of each use is its share times the sum, over the 20 lags, of the impulse of that cohort times the multiplier at that lag. The impulse of year \(t\) counts at lag 0 in year \(t\) (M8.2):
\[
eff_{exc,t} = -\sum_{k=0}^{19} imp_{t-k}\; m_{exc}(k)
\tag{7.23}\]
\[
eff_{i,t} = \frac{sh_i}{100}\sum_{k=0}^{19} imp^{p}_{t-k}\; m_{i}(k), \qquad i \in \{pit, cit, capt, gnfs, trns\}
\tag{7.24}\]
\[
\varepsilon_t = \mathbb{1}[\text{GDPEndogenous} = \text{Yes}]\;\Big(eff_{exc,t} + \sum_{i} eff_{i,t}\Big)
\tag{7.25}\]
where

\(sh_i\) is the revenue share of use \(i\), percent;
\(eff_{i,t}\) is the GDP effect of use \(i\) (fis.eff.<i>), share of GDP;
\(\varepsilon_t\) is the GDP effect (gdp.eff): the change of the GDP level against the baseline, as a share of GDP; 0 if endogenous GDP effects are off.

The revenue itself counts as an energy tax increase: share −1 at the excise multipliers.


7.3.6 GDP level and growth: the feedback
The GDP effect of year \(t\) raises the level of real GDP from year \(t+1\) (M8.3):
\[
lvl_t = \begin{cases} 1 & t = t_0 \\ 1 + \varepsilon_{t-1} & t > t_0 \end{cases}
\tag{7.26}\]
\[
Y_t = Y^{0}_t\; lvl_t
\tag{7.27}\]
\[
1 + g_t = (1 + g^{0}_t)\,\frac{lvl_t}{lvl_{t-1}}, \qquad g_{t_0} = g^{0}_{t_0}
\tag{7.28}\]
where

\(lvl_t\) is the GDP level factor used this year (gdp.lvl);
\(Y_t\) is real GDP after the feedback (gdp.pos.usd), USD bn;
\(g^{0}_t\) is baseline real GDP growth (gdp.base) and \(g_t\) real GDP growth after the feedback (gdp.pos.pct).

A steady effect therefore raises the level once and leaves growth unchanged afterwards; it does not compound.
Growth after the feedback is what drives demand in the year: it is computed at the very start of year \(t\), before the power and fuel-use blocks. The fuel-use block reads it raised to the income factor of the elasticities (Python GDPI = \((1+g_t)^{\,inc}-1\), with \(inc\) = inc.ela.adj), together with the demand shock factor SHOCK; see Chapter 3. The road engineer model reads GDP after the feedback too (Chapter 5), and the non-energy GHG drivers read GDP growth (Chapter 6).






TipPseudocode: GDP effects and feedback



# start of year t (before power and fuel use)
def gdp_start(t):
    if t == t0:
        gdp_lvl[t] = 1.0
        gdp_pos_pct[t] = gdp_base[t]
    else:
        gdp_lvl[t] = 1 + gdp_eff[t - 1]                       # last year's effect
        gdp_pos_pct[t] = (1 + gdp_base[t]) * gdp_lvl[t] / gdp_lvl[t - 1] - 1
    GDPI[t] = (1 + gdp_pos_pct[t]) ** inc_ela_adj[t] - 1      # read by fuel use

# end of year t (after revenues)
def gdp_effects(t):
    fis_rev[t] = rnet[t] + rnew[t] + rsr[t] + rpsu[t] + ch4_rev[t]
    fis_sp[t]  = (fis_rev[t] - baseline.fis_rev[t]) / (gdp_usd[t] * M_PER_BN)
    if t < GDPStartYear:
        fis_imp[t] = 0.0
    elif t == t0:
        fis_imp[t] = fis_sp[t]
    else:
        fis_imp[t] = fis_sp[t] - fis_sp[t - 1] * gdp_usd[t - 1] / gdp_usd[t]
    fis_impp[t] = 0.0 if t < CPIntro else fis_imp[t]

    group = multiplier_group(MultipliersSource, income_group)
    sign  = {'Base': 0, 'Low': -1, 'High': +1}[FmAdj]
    def m(i, k):                                  # k = 0..19, held after lag 11
        kk = min(k, 11)
        return median[group, i, kk] + sign * sd[income_group, i, kk]

    eff = {'exc': -sum(fis_imp[t - k] * m('exc', k)
                       for k in range(20) if t - k >= t0)}
    for i, share in [('pit', EXPLabortax), ('cit', EXPCIT), ('capt', EXPCapex),
                     ('gnfs', EXPGoodsandserv), ('trns', EXPTransfers)]:
        eff[i] = share / 100 * sum(fis_impp[t - k] * m(i, k)
                                   for k in range(20) if t - k >= t0)
    gdp_eff[t] = sum(eff.values()) if GDPEndogenous == 'Yes' else 0.0
    gdp_pos_usd[t] = gdp_usd[t] * gdp_lvl[t]




7.3.7 The timing rule
Revenue of year \(t\) changes GDP only from year \(t+1\). GDP growth after the feedback reads the level of the current year, which holds the effect of the previous year. The rule has three consequences, kept as rules of the model:

The fiscal space of year \(t\) reads revenue of year \(t\) only: no later year, no lookup over a whole row.
A same-year GDP effect never reaches same-year demand. The impulse of year \(t\) counts at lag 0 in \(\varepsilon_t\), which acts on GDP from \(t+1\).
No other block reads a later year. With this lag, no revenue line can close a circular reference, whatever it reads (fuel use, power, methane).






flowchart LR
  a1["Year t: GDP level<br/>1 + ε(t−1)"] --> b1["Year t: power,<br/>fuel use"] --> c1["Year t:<br/>revenues"] --> d1["Year t: fiscal space,<br/>impulse, ε(t)"]
  d1 --> a2["Year t+1: GDP level<br/>1 + ε(t)"] --> b2["Year t+1: power,<br/>fuel use"]






This lag is what makes the whole model computable year by year: GDP growth depends only on earlier years.


7.3.8 Memo rows
Three memo rows report the GDP effects in other forms.
Contribution of each use to GDP growth. The change in the use’s effect over the previous year, on the level:
\[
gdpg_{i,t} = \mathbb{1}[\text{GDPEndogenous} = \text{Yes}]\;(1 + g^{0}_t)\,\frac{eff_{i,t-1} - eff_{i,t-2}}{lvl_{t-1}}
\tag{7.29}\]
with \(eff_{i,t-2} = 0\) in the first projection year and \(gdpg = 0\) in the base year. The total \(gdpg_{all}\) uses \(\varepsilon\) in place of \(eff_i\) and equals \(g_t - g^{0}_t\): the channels sum to it.
Year of the reform. \(gdpy_t = t - t^{GDP} + 1\). The growth effect of reform year \(N\) is \(gdpg_{all}\) in the year where \(gdpy = N\).
Change in real GDP. \(\Delta Y_t = Y_t - Y^{0}_t\) (gdp.chg.usd), USD bn.

title: 7  Revenues, GDP and welfare
text:
7.4 External balance
Lower fossil fuel use means lower imports, or more exports, of oil, gas and coal. Block 16b values the change in fuel use at the supply price and scales it by the share of each fuel group that is traded, then adds it to the energy trade balance and to the current account of the baseline. All rows are in USD bn, real (A8.2).

7.4.1 Trade data
For each trade group \(g\) (oil products, gas, coal) the base-year energy balance gives imports \(M_g\), production \(P_g\) and exports \(X_g\) (exports are negative in the balance). From them:
\[
ts_g = \frac{M_g - X_g}{M_g + P_g - X_g} \quad (1 \text{ where the denominator is } 0)
\tag{7.30}\]
\[
TB_{g,t} = -(M_g + X_g)\,\theta\,\frac{p^{int}_{g,t}}{u_g}\,\frac{1}{M}
\tag{7.31}\]
where

\(ts_g\) is the share traded of the group (ts_<group>); Egypt: gas 0.19, oil products 0.47, coal 1.0;
\(TB_{g,t}\) is the baseline energy trade balance, exports minus imports (xtb.<group>);
\(p^{int}_{g,t}\) is the real international price of scenario 1’s price source (oil per barrel, gas per MMBtu on the country’s gas market, coal per tonne), and \(u_g\) the GJ per unit (6.12 GJ per barrel, 1.055056 GJ per MMBtu, 25.14 GJ per tonne).

The oil group holds gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene, jet fuel and other oil products.


7.4.2 Change in net imports
For each fossil fuel, the change in use against the baseline is valued at the supply price and scaled by the share traded of its group:
\[
\Delta NIM_{f,t} = \Delta F_{f,t}\;\theta\;sp_{f,t}\;ts_{g(f)}\;\frac{1}{M}
\tag{7.32}\]
where

\(\Delta F_{f,t}\) is the change in total use of the fuel against scenario 1 (echg, block 11b, Chapter 3), ktoe;
\(sp_{f,t}\) is the supply price (sp, Chapter 2), USD/GJ;
\(\Delta NIM_{f,t}\) is the change in net energy imports (xnim.<fuel>), positive for more imports.

The fuel rows are summed by group (xnim.grp.oil, .nga, .coa) and in total (xnim.all).


7.4.3 Trade balance and current account
The scenario’s energy trade balance is the baseline balance less the change in net imports:
\[
TB^{P}_t = \sum_g TB_{g,t} - \sum_f \Delta NIM_{f,t}
\tag{7.33}\]
Both, and the change in net imports, are also given as shares of baseline real GDP (xtb.pct = \(TB^P/Y^0\), xnim.pct = \(\Delta NIM/Y^0\); 0 where GDP is 0).
The current account starts from the WEO series and adds the change in net imports, in USD and in percent of GDP:
\[
\begin{aligned}
CA^{r}_t &= CA_t\,\nu_t && \text{real current account, pre-policy }(\texttt{bca.r})\\
\Delta CA_{g,t} &= -\Delta NIM_{g,t} && \text{change by fuel group }(\texttt{bca.d})\\
CA^{P}_t &= CA^{r}_t + \textstyle\sum_g \Delta CA_{g,t} && \text{after the policy }(\texttt{bca.p})\\
\hat{Y}_t &= \left|CA^{r}_t / ca_t\right| && \text{implied GDP / 100 }(\texttt{bca.y}\text{; 0 if }ca_t = 0)\\
ca^{P}_t &= ca_t + \textstyle\sum_g \Delta CA_{g,t} / \hat{Y}_t && \text{after the policy, percent of GDP }(\texttt{bca.pp})
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.34}\]
where

\(CA_t\) is the current account balance (WEO BCA, bca), USD bn nominal, held after its last data year;
\(ca_t\) is the current account in percent of GDP (WEO BCA_NGDPD, bca.gdp), held likewise;
\(\nu_t\) is the US CPI index (infl, 1 in the results year);
bca.dp.<group> = \(\Delta CA_{g,t}/\hat{Y}_t\); the memo bca.n is the current account in current prices, 0 after the last data year.

title: 7  Revenues, GDP and welfare
text:
7.5 Carbon pricing indicators
How heavily is carbon priced, once every tax and subsidy on energy is counted? Section 17 answers with revenue per tonne of CO2, by fuel and for the economy, and with the share of emissions the new carbon tax and ETS cover (A7.5). The methodology discusses coverage in section 3.9.3.1.1.

7.5.1 Implicit carbon price and effective carbon rate
Implicit carbon price by fuel. The revenue net of subsidies of the fuel, final use and power generation, divided by its CO2:
\[
tcp_f = \frac{rfu_f + rfg_f}{CO2_f}, \qquad
tcp_{all} = \frac{\sum_{f \in \text{fossil}} rfu_f + \sum_{k \in \{coal,gas,oil\}} rfg_k}{CO2}
\tag{7.35}\]
where \(CO2_f\) is the CO2 of the fuel (power included; Chapter 6), MtCO2, \(rfg_f\) applies to coal, gas and other oil products only, and \(tcp\) is in USD/tCO2 (tcp; 0 where the CO2 is 0). Biomass is left out: it has no CO2.
This is the tax-and-subsidy wedge per GJ divided by the emission factor. A carbon tax of \(\tau\) USD/t raises every fuel’s implicit price by about \(\tau\).
Effective carbon rate. All revenue net of subsidies, per tonne of energy CO2:
\[
ecr = \frac{rev^{net} + rev^{new} + rev^{sr}}{CO2}
\tag{7.36}\]
so VAT, the electricity subsidy gap and electricity VAT count. ecr is the summary row of section 17.


7.5.2 Coverage
CO2 covered by the new carbon tax in each of the 17 coverage sectors \(e\) (power and the 16 subsectors): the CO2 of the fuels whose coverage switch is on, counted only where the sector’s carbon tax rate is above 0:
\[
CO2^{cov}_e = \mathbb{1}[ct_e > 0]\sum_{f} CO2_{e,f}\;\kappa^{ct}_f
\tag{7.37}\]
where \(\kappa^{ct}_f\) is the fuel’s carbon tax coverage switch (ctcov). Power uses the CO2 of coal, gas and oil generation. A sector in a non-complementary ETS has a carbon tax rate of 0 and so no covered CO2.
Coverage shares and effective carbon tax:
\[
cov^{ct}_G = \frac{\sum_{e \in G} CO2^{cov}_e}{CO2}, \qquad
cov^{ets} = \frac{CO2^{ets}}{CO2}, \qquad
cov = cov^{ct}_{all} + cov^{ets}, \qquad
p^{eff} = \tau\;cov^{ct}_{all}
\tag{7.38}\]
where \(G\) is a sector group (transport, buildings, industry, other energy use, power) or all sectors, \(CO2^{ets}\) the CO2 covered by the new ETS (co2.ets, Chapter 6), \(\tau\) the carbon price (cptraj) and \(p^{eff}\) the effective carbon tax (cpeff), USD/tCO2.

title: 7  Revenues, GDP and welfare
text:
7.6 Welfare and externalities
Section 18 puts a money value on what the policy does to society. It values climate damages at the social cost of carbon, air pollution and road transport externalities with the inputs of the two co-benefit modules, and efficiency (deadweight) costs with the tax wedges. From the same building blocks it computes fossil fuel subsidies, explicit and implicit, and efficient prices. The methodology describes the framework in section 3.7, Monetized social costs and benefits.
Results are in USD bn, real, unless stated.

7.6.1 Social cost of carbon
The social cost of carbon (SCC) values a tonne of CO2. The model offers five paths and picks one for the national value and one for the global value (M1.6):
\[
\begin{aligned}
SCC^{tgt}_t &= SCC^{*}\,(1 + g^{scc})^{\,t - T^{*}}\\
SCC^{Rn}_t &= SCC^{R}_{c}\,(1 + g^{scc})^{\,t - t_0}, \qquad SCC^{Rg}_t = SCC^{R}_{world}\,(1 + g^{scc})^{\,t - t_0}\\
SCC^{EPA}_t &= SCC^{EPA}\,(1 + g^{scc})^{\,t - t_0}\\
SCC^{man}_t &= \text{manual path}
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.39}\]
where \(SCC^{R}_c\) is the national value of Ricke et al. (2018) for the chosen pure rate of time preference and elasticity of marginal utility (sheet SCC, key <country>.<rate>.<elasticity>), \(SCC^{R}_{world}\) the global value (key wld.<rate>.<elasticity>), and \(t_0\) the base year. The national SCC (\(SCC^{nat}\), scc.nat) and the global SCC (\(SCC^{glo}\), scc.glo) take the path chosen by NSCCSrc and GSCCSrc (first letter: T, R, M, U or E).

Climate cost per GJ of each fossil fuel, with the generic CO2 factor of the fuel (not calibrated):
\[
cc^{nat}_f = SCC^{nat}\,EF_f, \qquad cc^{glo}_f = SCC^{glo}\,EF_f
\tag{7.40}\]
for coal, gas, other oil products, gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene, where \(EF_f\) is the generic emission factor (tCO2/GJ) and \(cc\) is in USD/GJ (cc.nat, cc.glo).


7.6.2 Climate damages
Climate damages are the SCC times GHG emissions excluding LULUCF (Chapter 6); the welfare gain is the damage avoided against the baseline:
\[
D^{x} = \frac{SCC^{x}\;GHG}{M}, \qquad W^{cli,x} = D^{x,B} - D^{x}, \qquad x \in \{nat, glo\}
\tag{7.41}\]
where \(GHG\) is in Mt CO2e, \(D\) the climate damage (dmg.nat, dmg.glo) and \(W^{cli}\) the damage avoided (wcli.nat, wcli.glo), USD bn.


7.6.3 Efficiency costs
A tax or subsidy drives a wedge between what users pay and what supply costs. When a policy changes fuel use, the welfare cost is the wedge times the change in use: a Harberger triangle plus, with a prior tax, a rectangle (methodology 3.7.1.3). The model takes the average of the wedges of the scenario and the baseline (a trapezoid).
The wedge is revenue net of subsidies per unit of use:
\[
w_f = \frac{rfu_f + rfg_f}{F_f}, \qquad w_{ecy} = \frac{rfu_{ecy}}{F_{ecy}}
\tag{7.42}\]
where \(F_f\) is total use of the fuel (ener, section 11), \(F_{ecy}\) electricity demand (eldem), both ktoe, \(rfg\) applies to coal, gas, other oil products and biomass, and \(w\) is in USD million per ktoe (wdg; 0 where use is 0).
The efficiency cost of each fuel (biomass and the power fuels included) and of electricity:
\[
EC_f = -\,\frac{w_f + w^{B}_f}{2}\;\frac{\Delta F_f}{M}, \qquad EC = \sum_f EC_f + EC_{ecy}
\tag{7.43}\]
where \(\Delta F_f\) is the change in use against the baseline (echg; electricity: eldem − eldem\(^B\)) and \(EC\) is the efficiency cost (eff), USD bn: positive is a cost. With subsidies (negative wedges), a fall in use is a gain.
Efficiency cost of the methane fee. For each methane source \(j\) (oil and gas upstream, downstream gas, coal mines, biomass, livestock, rice, waste), the abatement curve gives the abated share \(a_j\,p^{b_j}\) at a fee \(p\) per tonne of CH4. The fee used on the curve is capped where abatement reaches 1:
\[
p^{mf}_j = \begin{cases} 0 & a_j = 0\\ \min\!\left(m\,GWP_j\,\delta^{mf}_j,\ a_j^{-1/b_j}\right) & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
\tag{7.44}\]
\[
MC_j = E^{0}_j\,\frac{Act_j}{Act^{0}_j}\;abt_j\;p^{mf}_j\;\frac{b_j}{1+b_j}\;\frac{1}{10^{6}}, \qquad MC = \sum_j MC_j
\tag{7.45}\]
where

\(m\) is the methane fee (mfee), USD/tCO2e, \(GWP_j\) the global warming potential and \(\delta^{mf}_j\) 1 if the fee applies to the source;
\(a_j\), \(b_j\) are the parameters of the abatement curve (country, else average); where \(b_j = 0\) or the cap overflows, there is no cap;
\(E^{0}_j\) is the source’s emissions in the inventory year (kt CH4), \(Act_j / Act^{0}_j\) its activity against the base year, and \(abt_j\) its abated share (Chapter 6);
\(p^{mf}_j\) is mfp (USD/tCH4) and \(MC\) the methane fee cost (mfc), USD bn: the area under the abatement curve.



7.6.4 Air pollution costs
The air pollution module provides two things (Chapter 6 gives the pollutant emissions it reads): the marginal damage of each fuel in each subsector, and the value of a change in modelled PM2.5 concentration (A8.3). The methodology describes the economic valuation in chapter 6, section 6.7.
Cost per unit of fuel, by price code. The marginal damage per GJ of each subsector (airpol.mc, computed before the year loop with the Pigouvian taxes, A1.2) is averaged over the subsectors of the price code, weighted by the scenario’s own fuel use of the year:
\[
ap_{c} = u_c\;\frac{\sum_{s \in c} mc^{ap}_{s,f}\,F_{s,f}}{\sum_{s \in c} F_{s,f}}
\quad \Big(\text{the plain average where } \textstyle\sum_{s \in c} F_{s,f} = 0\Big)
\tag{7.46}\]
where \(u_c\) is the GJ per price unit (litres for gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene; 1 for coal, gas and other oil products, which are in USD/GJ) and \(ap_c\) is airpol.cost. The price codes are coal and gas for industry, residential (buildings subsectors) and power (the plant’s own value), the four road and household oil products over all oil-using subsectors, and other oil products for power and industry. Per GJ, \(ap^{gj}_c = ap_c / u_c\) (airpol.cost.gj). Residential coal counts only where buildings’ coal use exceeds ApCoalResMin (0.1%) of buildings’ total fuel use.
Averages for other uses (block 18), weighted by the use of the year (apq): coal and gas “other” average industry, residential (buildings use) and power (power fuel use); “other oil and diesel” (odo) averages diesel in transport and other oil products in power and industry (0 where all three are 0); oop.avg averages other oil products in power and industry.
Air pollution cost of electricity (memo), USD/kWh:
\[
ap_{ecy} = \frac{\sum_{k \in \{coal, gas, oil\}} ap^{gj}_{pow,k}\;PE_k\;\theta}{G^{tot}\,H}
\tag{7.47}\]
Modelled PM2.5 concentration by module source \(m\) (coal, gas and other power plants, road, ground level, other, food), from the pollutant emissions of section 15:
\[
PM_m = 1000 \sum_p AP_{m,p}\;\kappa_{m,p}, \qquad PM = \sum_m PM_m
\tag{7.48}\]
where \(AP_{m,p}\) is the emission of pollutant \(p\) by source \(m\) (aps), kt, \(\kappa_{m,p}\) the module’s concentration coefficient (µg/m³ per t; NOx, SO2, BC, POM, other PM, VOC, CH4, CO, PM2.5, OC) and \(PM\) the modelled ambient PM2.5 (air.con.pm2.mod), µg/m³.


7.6.5 Road transport externalities
The transport co-benefits module gives the cost of accidents, congestion and road damage per vehicle-km. The model turns them into a cost per litre (or kWh) of road fuel, using the road engineer model (Chapter 5) for fuel economy and the split between passenger and freight use (A8.4). The methodology describes these costs in chapter 7, section 7.7.5.
A change in fuel use comes partly from driving less and partly from more efficient vehicles. Only the driving part changes the externalities. Its share, for road fuel \(f\) (gasoline, diesel, LPG, gas, electricity), is:
\[
w_f = 1 - \frac{Q^{fre,B}_f}{Q^{cls,B}_f} \;(w_{gso} = 1), \qquad
\mu_f = \frac{\epsilon^{U}_{die} + w_f\,(\epsilon^{U}_{gso} - \epsilon^{U}_{die})}
{\epsilon^{U}_{die} + \epsilon^{F}_{die} + w_f\,(\epsilon^{U}_{gso} + \epsilon^{F}_{gso} - \epsilon^{U}_{die} - \epsilon^{F}_{die})}
\tag{7.49}\]
where

\(Q^{cls}_f\) is the road fuel use of the vehicle classes of the fuel (tran.cls: passenger and freight; gasoline: passenger and two-three wheelers; electricity: all three), bn litres or kWh, and \(Q^{fre}_f\) its freight part;
\(w_f\) is the passenger weight of the fuel in the baseline (tran.wcl);
\(\epsilon^{U}\), \(\epsilon^{F}\) are the road usage and efficiency elasticities of gasoline and diesel;
\(\mu_f\) is the driving share of the response (tran.mrg), 0 where the baseline class use is 0.

The cost per unit of fuel, for each kind of externality:
\[
\begin{aligned}
acc_f &= a^{km}\;\overline{fe}_f\;\mu_f\;\rho_f && \text{accidents }(\texttt{tran.acc.cost})\\
con_f &= k^{km}\;\overline{fe}_f\;\mu_f\;\rho_f && \text{congestion }(\texttt{tran.con.cost})\\
rdm_f &= r^{km}\;\overline{fe}_f\;\mu_f\;\phi_f\;\rho_f && \text{road damage, not gasoline }(\texttt{tran.rdm.cost})
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.50}\]
where

\(a^{km}\), \(k^{km}\), \(r^{km}\) are the accident, congestion and road-damage costs per vehicle-km of the module (tran.acc.km, tran.con.km, tran.rdm.km), USD/km; road damage is per freight vehicle-km;
\(\overline{fe}_f\) is the average fuel economy of the stock (trafg, trafo, trafe), km per litre or kWh;
\(\phi_f = Q^{fre}_f / Q^{cls}_f\) is the freight share of the scenario (tran.fsh);
\(\rho_f\) is the road share of the fuel’s total use (tran.rsh; electricity: road demand over total demand);
the costs are in USD per litre (USD per kWh for electricity).

Per GJ, for gasoline, diesel and LPG, divide by the GJ per litre (tran.acc.gj, tran.con.gj, tran.rdm.gj). The total road externality excluding climate, USD/GJ (tot.ext):
\[
ext_{gso} = ap^{gj}_{gso} + acc^{gj}_{gso} + con^{gj}_{gso}, \qquad
ext_{die} = ap^{gj}_{die} + acc^{gj}_{die} + con^{gj}_{die} + rdm^{gj}_{die}
\tag{7.51}\]

7.6.6 Welfare gains
The national welfare gain adds the climate damages avoided at the national SCC, the air pollution and road transport co-benefits, and subtracts the efficiency costs (A8.5, methodology 3.7.3).
Air pollution. The value of a change in modelled PM2.5:
\[
W^{air} = v^{PM}\,\left(PM^{B} - PM\right)
\tag{7.52}\]
where \(v^{PM}\) is the value of averted modelled ambient PM2.5 (air.vpm), USD bn per µg/m³, from the air pollution module.
Road transport. The per-km costs times the change in vehicle-km of the road engineer model:
\[
W^{acc} = a^{km}\,(VKT^{B} - VKT), \qquad W^{con} = k^{km}\,(VKT^{B} - VKT), \qquad W^{rdm} = r^{km}\,(VKT^{fre,B} - VKT^{fre})
\tag{7.53}\]
where \(VKT\) is total road vehicle-km (trkmt) and \(VKT^{fre}\) freight vehicle-km (trkmf), bn km, from the road engineer model whatever road model is selected (Chapter 5).
National welfare gain, the summary row of section 18:
\[
W = W^{cli,nat} + W^{air} + W^{acc} + W^{con} + W^{rdm} - EC - MC
\tag{7.54}\]

7.6.8 Fossil fuel subsidies
Explicit subsidies are the gap between the supply cost and the retail price, where users pay less than supply costs. Implicit subsidies are the further gap up to the efficient price: the supply cost plus external costs plus the VAT consumers would pay on both (A8.6). They are computed for 16 lines \(j\): gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene and other oil products; gas and coal for industry, residential, power and “other”; electricity for industry, residential and “other”.
\[
p^{*}_j = sc_j + ext_j + vat_j, \qquad vat_j = (sc_j + ext_j)\;\eta_j\;\bar{v}_t
\tag{7.56}\]
\[
S^{exp}_j = \max(0,\ sc_j - p_j)\;\frac{Q_j}{M}, \qquad
S^{imp}_j = \mathbb{1}[p_j \le p^{*}_j]\;\left(p^{*}_j - \max(p_j, sc_j)\right)\frac{Q_j}{M}
\tag{7.57}\]
where

\(sc_j\) is the supply cost of the scenario (supcost: sp; electricity spe), USD/GJ or USD/kWh;
\(ext_j\) is the external cost (extcost): global climate cost plus tot.ext for gasoline and diesel; plus the air pollution cost for LPG, kerosene, other oil products (the oop.avg average) and coal and gas lines; 0 for electricity;
\(\eta_j\) is the VAT base flag: the household share of the oil product for gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene, 1 for residential lines, 0 for other oil products, industry and power;
\(\bar{v}_t\) is the general VAT rate of the year (vatgen): the WEO VAT rate up to the last historical price year, then held;
\(p_j\) is the retail price of the scenario (rpsub: rpn; electricity rp);
\(Q_j\) is consumption (con), PJ (GWh for electricity): total use for oil products (kerosene with jet fuel), sector use for coal and gas (residential = buildings; power = power fuel use; other = transport and other energy use), electricity demand of industry, buildings, and transport with other energy use;
the “other” lines of coal, gas and electricity take the consumption-weighted averages of \(sc\), \(ext\), \(vat\) and \(p\) of the lines above them (the plain average where consumption is 0);
\(S^{exp}\), \(S^{imp}\) are the explicit and implicit subsidies (expsub.con, impsub.con), USD bn; their totals are also given as shares of GDP (expsubgdp.con, impsubgdp.con).



7.6.9 Efficient prices
The efficient price of a fuel is what it would cost with every externality priced: the supply cost, the Pigouvian taxes (air pollution, climate, road transport) and VAT. The tax gap compares it with the retail price (methodology 3.7.2). It is computed per price unit (USD per litre for oil products, USD/GJ for coal and gas, USD/kWh for electricity) for 12 price codes \(c\): gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene; coal and gas for industry, residential and power; electricity for industry and residential.
\[
pig_c = ap_c + cd_c + acc_c + con_c + rdm_c
\tag{7.58}\]
\[
p^{eff}_c = sc^{B}_c\,u_c + pig_c + \left(sc^{B}_c\,u_c + \chi\,pig_c\right)\eta_c\,\bar{v}_t, \qquad
tg_c = p_c\,u_c - p^{eff}_c
\tag{7.59}\]
where

\(ap_c\) is the air pollution cost (airpol.cost.s): airpol.cost for oil products, airpol.cost.gj for coal and gas, and for electricity the baseline value of the generation-weighted cost \(\sum_k ap^{gj}_{pow,k} G_k / G^{tot}\) converted to USD/kWh (airpol.ecy.g);
\(cd_c\) is the climate damage per unit at the national SCC (scc.cost = cc.code = \(SCC^{nat}\,EF_c\,u_c\)), 0 for electricity;
\(acc_c\), \(con_c\) (gasoline and diesel) and \(rdm_c\) (diesel) are the road externalities per litre of the scenario (Equation 7.50); 0 for other codes;
\(sc^{B}_c\) is the baseline supply cost per GJ (electricity per kWh), \(u_c\) the GJ per price unit;
\(\chi\) is 1 if ExternalityAddVAT = Yes (externalities are part of the VAT base), else 0; \(\eta_c\) is 1 for consumer codes (oil products and residential), else 0;
\(p_c\) is the retail price of the scenario (rpn; electricity rp), so \(p_c u_c\) is rp.eff;
\(pig_c\) is the Pigouvian tax (pig), \(p^{eff}_c\) the efficient price (eff.price; its VAT part is vat.cost) and \(tg_c\) the tax gap (tgap).

Per tonne of CO2. The Pigouvian tax and its air pollution part are also expressed per tonne of CO2, and the baseline excise likewise:
\[
pig^{CO2}_c = pig_c\,\frac{SCC^{glo}}{cd_c}, \qquad app_c = pig^{CO2}_c\,\frac{ap_c}{pig_c}, \qquad
txo^{CO2}_c = txo^{B}_c\,u_c\,\frac{SCC^{glo}}{cd_c}
\tag{7.60}\]
each 0 where its denominator is 0 (and \(txo^{CO2} = 0\) for electricity). The averages pig.co2e.avg and app.avg weight the ten fossil codes by fuel use (effp.q: total use for oil products, kerosene with jet fuel; industry, buildings and power use for coal and gas).

Legacy unit-cost bugs L189-L193 fixed (L192: the residential coal switch tested a typed total; L193: the driving share without class use).
Transport co-benefits (issue I111), as legacy: margins from scenario 1, per-km costs independent of the scenario (congestion does not respond to the policy), welfare a rectangle, road damage only for freight; the road damage cost of 0.12 USD/km is not deflated. Average fuel economy of passenger and freight vehicles, as legacy.
Social costs, FFS and subsidies (LD82): legacy bugs fixed: L176 (other oil products: climate cost per barrel added to costs per GJ), L177 (air pollution cost of electricity), L178 (other-use averages), L179 (FFS coal and gas lines take another sector’s change in use), L180 (FFS conversion and road damage), L181-L182 (retail price of the subsidy lines), L183 (climate cost on gas for power), L184-L185 (VAT base of the subsidy lines), L186 (consumption of the lines), L187 (other-line averages), L188 (GDP of the year in the shares). Replicated issues: I107 (FFS lines value diesel in industry, power and “other” at oil-product costs; FFS uses the global SCC; FFS welfare is a separate measure, not in wel.usd), I108 (electricity external cost 0), I109 (VAT base). Explicit and implicit subsidies are computed in every scenario group with the scenario’s own prices and use; legacy computes scenario 1 only (I110).
VAT of the year: the general VAT rate follows the WEO rate of the year up to the last historical price year (prototype bug M15 fixed: the 2022 rate in every year).
Efficient prices (LD83): as legacy, with the road externalities of the scenario (I118), electricity air pollution from the baseline generation mix (I121), electricity Pigouvian tax 0 (I119), potential VAT on the externalities when ExternalityAddVAT = Yes (I120); txo.co2e is 0 where the climate cost is 0 (L203).
Methodology. The methodology’s efficiency cost is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(ncp - xcp)(F_P - F_B)\); the model uses the average wedge of all taxes and subsidies in the scenario and the baseline, so subsidies count too. The methodology’s footnote says road damage is not in the welfare benefits; the model includes it.

title: 8  Distribution
text:
8.1 The module at a glance
The distribution module shows who bears the cost of a scenario. It takes the price changes and the revenue that mitigation computes for one year, the analysis year, and turns them into a change in the consumption of households, decile by decile. It then gives the revenue back to households through the recycling options chosen in the scenario and reports what is left: the net effect, the inequality it implies and the sectors whose prices rise most.
The methodology describes the module in methodology, chapter 5; its overview of functions is in section 5.1.1.2. This chapter is the model as Excel-AI and CPAT Python compute it, with the places where it simplifies or departs from the methodology.
The module works on one scenario at a time and always against scenario 1, the baseline. Every result has eleven values: the basket (the whole survey sample) and the ten consumption deciles, from the poorest (decile 1) to the wealthiest (decile 10). Most results are given for three samples: overall, urban and rural.
The calculation runs in eleven steps, the sections of the Distribution sheet.
flowchart TD
  M["Mitigation, analysis year<br/>prices, spending, GDP, population, revenue"] --> P["2 Price changes by fuel"]
  P --> I["3 Indirect price changes<br/>(input-output table)"]
  P --> F["4 Price factors"]
  I --> F
  S["5 Budget shares (survey)"] --> E["6 Direct and indirect effects"]
  F --> E
  N["7 Survey to national accounts"] --> E
  N --> R["8 Revenue recycling"]
  M --> R
  E --> T["9 Net effect, compensation, Gini"]
  R --> T
  T --> C["10 Outputs for charts"]
  I --> X["11 Price changes by production sector"]
Budget shares (section 5) come before the price factors (section 4) in the code, because the weighted summary of the price factors uses them; the rebasing (section 7) comes before the effects (section 6), because the mitigation adjustment of section 6 needs national consumption. The order of the sections in the sheet is kept for reading.

title: 8  Distribution
text:
8.3 Inputs from mitigation
The module needs five things from mitigation: the price change of each household fuel, the economy-wide price change of each fuel, what the economy spent on each fuel, GDP and population, and the revenue to recycle. All are read for the analysis year, in the scenario and in scenario 1. The methodology describes the link in section 5.3.1.

8.3.1 Household price change by fuel
The direct effect uses the residential price, the price households pay (M2.5, Chapter 2):
\[
t_f = \frac{p^{P}_{f,\text{res},y}}{p^{B}_{f,\text{res},y}} - 1
\tag{8.1}\]
where

\(t_f\) is the household price change of fuel \(f\) (fraction; code dpr.<f>.res);
\(p_{f,\text{res},y}\) is the residential after-tax price atp of fuel \(f\) in the analysis year (local unit); for electricity, the residential retail price rp.res.ecy;
\(P\) and \(B\) mark the scenario and scenario 1.

This is D1.3. Oil (oil in the survey) takes the price of other oil products (oop).


8.3.2 Economy-wide price change and spending
The indirect effect uses the price that producers pay. It is the change in the average price over sectors (rpn, Chapter 2):
\[
t^{a}_f = \frac{\bar{p}^{P}_{f,y}}{\bar{p}^{B}_{f,y}} - 1
\tag{8.2}\]
where

\(t^{a}_f\) is the economy-wide price change of fuel \(f\) (code dpa.<f>);
\(\bar{p}_{f,y}\) is the average price rpn of the industry sector for coal and natural gas, of all sectors for other oil products, gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene, and the industrial retail price rp.ind.ecy for electricity.

Each fuel is weighted by what the economy spent on it, in scenario 1 and in the base year:
\[
S_f = \text{pav.sp}^{B}_{f,t_0} \times
\begin{cases} 0.041868 & f \neq \text{electricity} \\ 1 & f = \text{electricity} \end{cases}
\tag{8.3}\]
where

\(S_f\) is the base-year spending on fuel \(f\) (USD million; code spend.<f>);
\(\text{pav.sp}\) is the economy-wide spending on the fuel, all sectors, from the price block (Chapter 2);
\(0.041868\) is PJ per ktoe, which turns the fuels’ spending into USD million (electricity’s already is);
\(t_0\) is the base year. The spending of the base year is paired with the price changes of the analysis year (issue I76, below).

title: 8  Distribution
text:
8.4 Budget shares
A household loses more from a price rise the more of its budget goes to the good. The budget shares come from household budget surveys, prepared as the methodology describes in section 5.2.1 (eq-5_1):
\[
\pi^{g}_{j} = \frac{C^{g}_{j}}{C_j}, \qquad
\pi^{dg} = \underset{j \in d}{\text{mean, median, p25 or p75}}\ \pi^{g}_{j}
\tag{8.4}\]
where

\(\pi^{g}_{j}\) is household \(j\)’s share of its consumption \(C_j\) spent on item \(g\);
\(\pi^{dg}\) is the population-weighted statistic over the households of decile \(d\) (percent; code bsh.<g>.dec.<s>).

This is D1.1. The survey tables (HHSurvey) already hold the decile statistics; the model reads them by sample (overall, urban, rural), by the statistic QuantilesStatistic and by decile. The basket reads the whole-sample row (quantile code 9999).
The items are the eight household fuels, the 14 consumption categories and, in the overall sample, three biomass fuels (charcoal, ethanol, firewood). Biomass has a budget share but no price change. The energy budget share, fuels plus biomass, is the summary row of the section.

title: 8  Distribution
section: 8.5 Indirect price changes through the input-output table
text:
8.5 Indirect price changes through the input-output table
A carbon price also raises the price of food, transport and everything else made with energy. The module finds these indirect price changes with the GTAP input-output table of the country: how much of each fuel group is embedded, directly and upstream, in one unit of each sector’s output. The methodology describes the approach in section 5.3.1 (eq-5_3) and the scaling in section 5.3.2.4.
The table has 64 GTAP sectors: five fuel groups and 59 non-fuel sectors, which map to the 14 categories. CPAT’s eight fuels map to the five GTAP fuel groups:



Table 8.3: CPAT fuels and GTAP fuel groups









GTAP group \(k\)
CPAT fuels




Coal (coa)
coal


Electricity (ely)
electricity


Gas (nga)
natural gas


Crude oil (oil)
other oil products


Petroleum and coke products (p_c)
gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene







8.5.1 Step 1: the price factor of each fuel group
First, the spending-weighted price change of each group, and the group’s total use:
\[
R_k = \sum_{f \in k} S_f\, t^{a}_f
\tag{8.5}\]
\[
U_k = \frac{D_{t_R}}{D_{GTAP}} \Big( \sum_{i \notin \text{fuels}} (TD_i + X_i)\, L_{i,k} + TD_k \Big)
\tag{8.6}\]
where

\(R_k\) is the extra cost of group \(k\) at base-year spending (USD million; code grev.<k>);
\(U_k\) is the total use of group \(k\): embedded in the total demand \(TD_i\) and exports \(X_i\) of the non-fuel sectors, plus the group’s own demand \(TD_k\) (USD million; code gtot.<k>, DIOTot on DistMapping);
\(L_{i,k}\) is GTAP’s total-requirement (Leontief) coefficient of group \(k\) in sector \(i\);
\(D_{t_R} / D_{GTAP}\) is the WEO GDP deflator of the results year over that of the GTAP year (issue I77).

Equation 8.6 is B1.1. The price factor of the group is
\[
\phi_k =
\begin{cases}
R_k / U_k & \texttt{ScaleGTAP} = \text{Yes} \\[2pt]
R_k / \sum_{f \in k} S_f & \texttt{ScaleGTAP} = \text{No}\ (0 \text{ without spending})
\end{cases}
\tag{8.7}\]
where \(\phi_k\) is the factor applied to the Leontief coefficients of group \(k\) (code gfac.<k>).
With ScaleGTAP = Yes the extra cost CPAT computes for the fuels is spread over everything the group is used for. With ScaleGTAP = No, \(\phi_k\) is simply the spending-weighted economy-wide price change of the group’s fuels.


8.5.2 Step 2: the price change of each category
\[
t_g = \sum_k \bar{L}_{g,k}\, \phi_k, \qquad
\bar{L}_{g,k} = \frac{\sum_{i \in g} H_i\, L_{i,k}}{\sum_{i \in g} H_i}
\tag{8.8}\]
where

\(t_g\) is the price change of category \(g\) (fraction; code dpr.<g>);
\(\bar{L}_{g,k}\) is the household-demand weighted Leontief coefficient of the category (DLcat on DistMapping);
\(H_i\) is GTAP household demand for the output of sector \(i\).

This is D1.2. The summary row of the section is the budget-share weighted average of \(t_g\) over the categories, overall sample.






TipPseudocode: indirect price changes



# data step (once per country)
ratio = weo_deflator[results_year] / weo_deflator[gtap_year]
for k in [coa, ely, nga, oil, p_c]:
    gtot[k] = ratio * (sum((TD[i] + X[i]) * L[i, k] for i in nonfuel_sectors) + TD[k])
    for g in categories:
        DLcat[g, k] = sum(H[i] * L[i, k] for i in g) / sum(H[i] for i in g)

# each scenario
for k in groups:
    grev[k]   = sum(spend[f] * dpa[f] for f in fuels_of[k])
    gspend[k] = sum(spend[f] for f in fuels_of[k])
    if ScaleGTAP == 'Yes':
        gfac[k] = grev[k] / gtot[k]
    else:
        gfac[k] = grev[k] / gspend[k] if gspend[k] > 0 else 0
for g in categories:
    dpr[g] = sum(DLcat[g, k] * gfac[k] for k in groups)








NoteWhy one factor per fuel group is legacy’s rescaling





Legacy CPAT (with ScaleGTAP = Yes, its default) rescales the raw price change of each GTAP sector \(s\) by
\[
\kappa_s = \frac{\sum_k \sigma_{k,s}\, R_k}{\sum_k Emb_{k,s}\, t_{k,s}},
\]
where \(Emb_{k,s}\) is the use of group \(k\) embedded in sector \(s\), \(\sigma_{k,s}\) its share in the group’s total use and \(t_{k,s}\) the price change of the fuel for that sector. With \(Emb_{k,s} = Y_s L_{s,k}\) and \(\sigma_{k,s} = Emb_{k,s} / U_k\), the sector’s adjusted price change becomes
\[
\kappa_s \sum_k L_{s,k}\, t_{k,s} = \sum_k L_{s,k}\, \frac{R_k}{U_k} = \sum_k L_{s,k}\, \phi_k .
\]
The sector-specific fuel prices cancel. The model therefore keeps one factor per group. Checked on legacy’s cache: all 59 sectors agree to 4e-16, and the 14 categories to 3e-6 (legacy prints six digits).
